15124.m: Robert Grimm led the general strike of 1918.

15125.q: Which demand of the 1918 general strike was put into practice in industry as early as 1919 and 1920?
15125.e: The 48-hour week was introduced in industry in 1919 and 1920. Women’s right to vote at federal level, on the other hand, only came in 1971.
15125.m: The 48-hour week was introduced soon after the general strike.

15126.q: Which social insurance, demanded during the 1918 general strike, only came into force in 1948?
15126.e: Old-age and survivors’ insurance (AHV) was one of the demands of the general strike. In the end it only came into force in 1948.
15126.m: The AHV was demanded in 1918 and introduced in 1948.

15127.q: What did the Federal Council use against the general strike in 1918?
15127.e: The Federal Council called up soldiers and gave the strikers an ultimatum. After three days the strike leaders called off the general strike. In Grenchen, three young workers were shot dead.
15127.m: The Federal Council ended the 1918 general strike with the army.

15128.q: Which day is known around the world as the labour movement’s “Labour Day”?
15128.e: On 1 May, trade unions in many countries demonstrate for employees’ rights. In some Swiss cantons it is a public holiday.

15129.q: What term did Marx and Engels use for the working class, which owns nothing but its ability to work?
15129.e: Proletarians do not own factories or machines. They live by selling their labour for wages.
15129.m: The proletariat is the working class that owns no property.

15130.q: Which Italian built the first usable battery, the voltaic pile, around 1800?
15130.e: Alessandro Volta presented his pile to the Royal Society in London in 1800. For the first time it produced a steady electric current.
15130.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

15131.q: Which unit of electrical voltage is named after Alessandro Volta?
15131.e: Voltage is measured in volts, in honour of Alessandro Volta. A plug socket in Switzerland, for example, has 230 volts.

15132.q: Which English scientist discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
15132.e: In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that a moving magnet in a coil of wire produces electricity. Generators in power stations work on this principle.
15132.m: Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831.

15133.q: What does a dynamo, like the one Werner von Siemens improved in 1866, produce?
15133.e: A dynamo turns movement into electricity. Werner von Siemens made it so powerful that electricity could be produced cheaply and in large amounts.
15133.m: A dynamo makes electricity from movement.

15134.q: Which American inventor received a patent for his light bulb in 1880 and had it mass-produced?
15134.e: Thomas Edison applied for a patent for his light bulb in 1879 and received it in 1880. He was not the only inventor, but he made the bulb practical and cheap.
15134.m: Thomas Edison made the light bulb fit for everyday use.

15135.q: Which material did Edison soon use for especially long-lasting filaments?
15135.e: In his first successful experiment in 1879, Edison used a carbon filament. Later he used carbonised bamboo fibres from Japan, which lasted over 1,000 hours.
15135.m: Edison used carbonised bamboo for his filaments.

15136.q: Where did the first electric light in Switzerland shine in 1879?
a: in a hotel in St Moritz
in the Federal Palace in Bern
15136.e: On 18 July 1879 the hotelier Johannes Badrutt had electric arc lamps lit in the dining room of his Kulm Hotel in St Moritz. The electricity came from a small power plant of his own.
15136.m: Switzerland’s first electric light shone in St Moritz in 1879.

15137.q: From which energy source has Switzerland got most of its electricity for over a hundred years?
15137.e: Switzerland has many rivers and reservoirs in the Alps. That is why it built lots of hydroelectric power stations early on.
15137.m: Switzerland gets most of its electricity from hydropower.

15138.q: Why was hydropower in Switzerland also called “white coal”?
a: It replaced the coal the country lacked as a source of energy.
The water was pressed into white stones.
White coal was found in the Alps.
Coal was painted white before burning.
15138.e: Other countries had lots of coal for their industry, but Switzerland had hardly any. Water from the snow-covered mountains therefore became its most important source of energy.

15139.q: What advantage did the electric motor have over the steam engine in factories?
a: Each machine could have its own small drive.
It needed no energy at all.
It was much louder and more dangerous.
15139.e: A steam engine drove many machines at once through long belts. Electric motors were small and could drive each machine separately.
15139.m: Electric motors made powering factories simpler and more flexible.

15140.q: Which material became standard for light bulb filaments around 1910?
15140.e: Tungsten only melts at very high temperatures. That is why a tungsten filament lasts a long time and shines brightly.
15140.m: Filaments are usually made of tungsten.

15141.q: Was Thomas Edison the only inventor of the light bulb?
a: No, others such as Joseph Swan built light bulbs too.
Yes, nobody else was working on it.
No, the Romans already had light bulbs.
Yes, the idea was protected by law.
15141.e: The Englishman Joseph Swan showed a light bulb as early as February 1879. But Edison made it especially well known and cheap. In 1883 their companies merged.
15141.m: The light bulb had several inventors.

15142.q: How did electric light change life in towns and cities?
a: Streets and factories could be brightly lit at night too.
People had to go to bed earlier.
Candles suddenly became much more expensive.
Towns became completely dark at night.
15142.e: Electric lamps lit up the night without an open flame. Factories could work at night and streets became safer.
15142.m: Electric light made towns and factories bright at night too.

17022.e: Asia is the biggest continent. It has the most area.
17022.m: Asia is the biggest continent on Earth.

17023.e: Australia is the smallest continent. Most of it belongs to the country of Australia.

17024.e: A continent is a very large landmass. There are often many countries on it.
17024.m: A continent is a huge piece of land.

17025.e: The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean. Its name means “peaceful ocean”.
17025.m: The Pacific is the biggest ocean on Earth.

17026.q: Which ocean lies between Europe and America?
17026.e: The Atlantic separates Europe and Africa from America. Ships need many days to cross it.
17026.m: The Atlantic lies between Europe and America.

17027.q: What does the water in the ocean taste like?
17027.e: A lot of salt is dissolved in seawater. That is why you cannot drink it.
17027.m: The water in the ocean is salty.

17028.q: What colour are oceans usually on maps?
17028.e: On maps and globes, water is almost always drawn in blue. That way you recognise it at once.
17028.m: Oceans are usually blue on maps.

17029.q: Which country is the biggest in the world?
17029.e: Russia has the largest area of all countries. It lies in Europe and in Asia.
17029.m: Russia is the biggest country in the world by area.

17030.q: Which country is the smallest in the world?
17030.e: Vatican City is smaller than half a square kilometre. The Pope lives there.
17030.m: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world.

17031.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland is very small and lies to the east?
17031.e: Liechtenstein lies between Switzerland and Austria. It is one of the smallest countries in Europe.
17031.m: Liechtenstein is a small neighbouring country of Switzerland.

17032.q: What does the Swiss flag look like?
17032.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background. It is square.
17032.m: The Swiss flag has a white cross on a red background.

17033.q: Which country has a white flag with a red circle?
17033.e: The red circle on the Japanese flag stands for the sun. Japan is also called the “Land of the Rising Sun”.
17033.m: The flag of Japan shows a red circle on white.

17034.q: How many stars does the flag of the USA have?
17034.e: Each of the 50 stars stands for one state of the USA. The 13 stripes are a reminder of the first colonies.
17034.m: The flag of the USA has 50 stars.

17035.q: In which city is the seat of the Swiss government?
17035.e: The Federal Council and Parliament work in Bern. Bern is called the federal city.

17036.q: What is the capital of Austria?
17036.e: Vienna is the capital and the largest city of Austria. The famous Schönbrunn Palace is there.
17036.m: Vienna is the capital of Austria.

17037.q: What is the capital of Spain?
17037.e: Madrid lies roughly in the middle of Spain. It is the largest city in the country.
17037.m: Madrid is the capital of Spain.

17038.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17038.e: Tokyo is the capital of Japan. A great many people live in the Tokyo region.
17038.m: Tokyo is the capital of Japan.

17039.q: What money do people pay with in Switzerland?
17039.e: In Switzerland people pay with francs and centimes (Rappen). One franc has 100 Rappen.
17039.m: In Switzerland you pay with francs.

17040.q: What is the capital of Germany?
17040.e: Berlin is the capital and the largest city of Germany. The Brandenburg Gate is there.
17040.m: Berlin is the capital of Germany.

17041.q: What is the highest mountain in Germany called?
17041.e: The Zugspitze is about 2960 metres high. It lies on the border with Austria.
17041.m: The Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.

17042.q: In which direction is Germany from Switzerland?
17042.e: Germany lies north of Switzerland. Basel and Schaffhausen are close to the border.
17042.m: Germany lies to the north of Switzerland.

17043.q: How many federal states does Germany have?
17043.e: Germany is divided into 16 federal states, for example Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

17044.q: In which city is the Eiffel Tower?
17044.e: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris. It is made of iron and is about 330 metres high.
17044.m: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris.

17045.q: What colours is the flag of France?
17045.e: The French flag has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red.
17045.m: The flag of France is blue, white and red.

17046.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the west of Switzerland?
17046.e: France lies to the west of Switzerland. The city of Geneva is right on the border with France.
17046.m: France lies to the west of Switzerland.

17047.q: What does Italy look like on the map?
17047.e: Italy is long and narrow and looks like a boot. The toe points into the Mediterranean.
17047.m: On the map, Italy looks like a boot.

17048.q: What is the capital of Italy?
17048.e: Rome is the capital of Italy. The Colosseum is there.
17048.m: Rome is the capital of Italy.

17049.q: Which dish originally comes from Italy?
17049.e: Pizza as we know it comes from Naples in Italy.

17050.q: In which Italian city do people travel by boat instead of by car?
17050.e: Venice is built on lots of small islands. Instead of roads there are canals and narrow lanes, and people travel by boat and gondola.
17050.m: In Venice people travel by boat on canals.

17051.q: Which sea lies to the south of Europe?
17051.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe and Africa. Many people go on beach holidays there.
17051.m: The Mediterranean lies to the south of Europe.

17052.q: Which mountain range forms a border between Europe and Asia?
17052.e: The Urals are a long mountain range in Russia. They are seen as the border between Europe and Asia.
17052.m: The Urals separate Europe and Asia.

17053.q: What is the money that people pay with in many countries of Europe called?
17053.e: Many countries in Europe share the euro as their money. Switzerland is not one of them.
17053.m: In many countries of Europe people pay with euros.

17054.q: What is the highest mountain in Africa called?
17054.e: Kilimanjaro is in Tanzania and is almost 5900 metres high. There is snow at the top, even though it is hot at the bottom.
17054.m: Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa.

17055.q: In which African country are the famous pyramids of Giza?
17055.e: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt. They were built more than 4000 years ago.
17055.m: The pyramids of Giza are in Egypt.

17056.q: Which big river flows through Egypt?
17056.e: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world. It flows through Egypt into the Mediterranean.

17057.q: Which animal lives in the wild in Africa?
17057.e: Giraffes live in the African savannah. With their long necks they eat leaves from tall trees.
17057.m: Giraffes live in the wild in Africa.

17058.q: In which country is the Great Wall?
17058.e: The Great Wall of China is a very long structure in China. It was built for protection against enemies.
17058.m: The Great Wall is in China.

17059.q: In which country do giant pandas live in the wild?
17059.e: Giant pandas live in mountain forests in China. They mainly eat bamboo.
17059.m: Giant pandas live in the wild in China.

17060.q: Which country has had the most inhabitants in the world since 2023?
17060.e: Since 2023, more people have lived in India than in any other country. There are over 1.4 billion (as of 2025).
17060.m: India has had the most inhabitants since 2023.

17061.q: On which continent do the most people live?
17061.e: More than half of all people live in Asia. Some very populous countries are there.

17062.q: Which two parts make up America?
17062.e: America is made up of North America and South America. Central America lies in between.
17062.m: America is made up of North America and South America.

17063.q: In which city is the Statue of Liberty?
17063.e: The Statue of Liberty stands on a small island near New York. France gave it to the USA as a gift.
17063.m: The Statue of Liberty is in New York.

17064.q: Which is the biggest country in South America?
17064.e: Brazil is the biggest country in South America. People there speak Portuguese.
17064.m: Brazil is the biggest country in South America.

17065.q: Who came to America by ship in 1492?
17065.e: Christopher Columbus sailed across the Atlantic in 1492. He reached islands off America.

17066.q: Which animal carries its baby in a pouch and lives in Australia?
17066.e: The kangaroo is a marsupial. The baby grows up in its mother's pouch.
17066.m: The kangaroo lives in Australia and has a pouch.

17067.q: Which animal sleeps a lot and eats eucalyptus leaves?
17067.e: The koala lives in Australia in eucalyptus trees. It sleeps almost all day.

17068.q: What is the capital of Australia?
17068.e: Many people think of Sydney, but the capital is Canberra. Sydney is the biggest city.
17068.m: Canberra is the capital of Australia.

17069.q: What is the famous red rock in Australia called?
17069.e: Uluru is a huge red rock in the middle of Australia. It is sacred to the Aboriginal people.
17069.m: Uluru is a big red rock in Australia.

17070.q: What is Antarctica almost completely covered with?
17070.e: Antarctica is almost completely covered by a thick layer of ice. In many places the ice is kilometres thick.
17070.m: Antarctica is covered with thick ice.

17071.e: Penguins cannot fly, but they swim well. Many species live in the south, for example in Antarctica.

17072.q: Who lives in Antarctica for a while?
17072.e: There are no towns in Antarctica. Researchers live there in stations and study the ice and weather.
17072.m: Researchers live in stations in Antarctica.

17073.q: What is the weather usually like in Antarctica?
17073.e: Antarctica is the coldest place on Earth. Temperatures below minus 80 degrees have been measured there.
17073.m: It is very cold in Antarctica.

17074.q: What is the highest mountain in the world called?
17074.e: Mount Everest is in the Himalayas. It is about 8849 metres high.
17074.m: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

17075.q: Which pointed mountain stands near Zermatt?
17075.e: The Matterhorn is in Valais near Zermatt. Its pyramid shape is known all over the world.

17076.q: What do you call the highest point of a mountain?
17076.e: The summit is the very top of a mountain. There is often a summit cross there.
17076.m: The highest point of a mountain is called the summit.

17077.q: What do you call the place where a river begins?
17077.e: At the source, the water often comes out of the ground. From there it flows on as a stream.
17077.m: A river begins at its source.

17078.e: The Rhine flows through Basel and then on into Germany. Basel has a Rhine port.

17079.q: Which sea does the Rhone flow into?
17079.e: The Rhone begins at the Rhone Glacier in Valais. It flows through France into the Mediterranean.
17079.m: The Rhone flows into the Mediterranean.

17080.q: Which river flows through the city of Bern?
17080.e: In Bern the Aare makes a big loop around the old town. In summer lots of people swim in it.

17081.q: Which lake is the largest in Switzerland?
17081.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland. Part of it belongs to France.
17081.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.

17082.q: Which lake do Switzerland, Germany and Austria all border?
17082.e: Lake Constance lies between three countries. Towns such as Konstanz and Bregenz are on its shores.

17083.q: Which lake is the city of Lucerne on?
17083.e: Lucerne lies on Lake Lucerne. Many boats sail across the lake from there.

17084.q: What kind of water do most lakes have?
17084.e: Most lakes are filled with fresh water. There is hardly any salt in it.

17085.q: Does Switzerland have a coastline on the sea?
17085.e: Switzerland is a landlocked country. That means it has no access to the sea.
17085.m: Switzerland is not by the sea.

17086.q: In which sea can you float on top almost without swimming?
17086.e: The Dead Sea is extremely salty. All that salt holds your body up, so you float on top.
17086.m: In the Dead Sea you float on top because of the salt.

17087.q: What is it called when the sea goes back from the beach?
17087.e: At low tide the water level drops and the beach gets wider. At high tide the water rises again.
17087.m: At low tide the sea goes back.

a: Land surrounded by water on all sides
17088.e: An island is a piece of land completely surrounded by water. You can often only reach it by ship or plane.
17088.m: An island is surrounded by water on all sides.

17089.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
17089.e: Greenland is the largest island in the world. Most of it is covered with ice.
17089.m: Greenland is the largest island in the world.

17090.q: Which large island lies off the east coast of Africa?
17090.e: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean off Africa. Lemurs live there.
17090.m: Madagascar lies off the coast of Africa.

17091.e: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and belongs to Italy. The volcano Etna is there.
17091.m: Sicily is an island of Italy.

17092.q: Which animal often carries loads in the desert?
17092.e: Camels can go a long time without water. That is why they are good pack animals in the desert.
17092.m: The camel is a pack animal in the desert.

17093.q: What do you call a place with water and palm trees in the desert?
17093.e: In an oasis there is water from the ground. That is why plants such as date palms grow there.
17093.m: An oasis is a place with water in the desert.

17094.q: What is there very little of in a desert?
17094.e: It hardly ever rains in the desert. That is why only a few plants grow there.
17094.m: It rains very little in the desert.

17095.q: What is the largest rainforest in the world called?
17095.e: The Amazon rainforest is in South America. It is the largest rainforest on Earth.
17095.m: The Amazon rainforest is the largest rainforest.

17096.q: What is the weather like in the tropical rainforest?
17096.e: It is warm all year in the tropical rainforest. It rains almost every day.
17096.m: The tropical rainforest is warm and wet.

17097.q: Which animal lives in the rainforest?
17097.e: Very many kinds of animals live in the rainforest. Colourful parrots live high up in the trees.

17098.e: People cut down trees for wood, fields and pastures. So a lot of rainforest disappears every year.
17098.m: Rainforests are getting smaller because trees are cut down.

17099.q: Which large predator lives near the North Pole?
17099.e: Polar bears live in the Arctic around the North Pole. They mainly hunt seals.
17099.m: Polar bears live in the Arctic.

17100.q: What do you stand on at the North Pole?
17100.e: There is no land at the North Pole. A layer of ice floats on the sea there.
17100.m: At the North Pole you stand on ice over the sea.

17101.q: Which way does the needle of a compass point?
17101.e: The compass needle is magnetic and points north. That is how you find your way.

17102.q: On which continent is the South Pole?
17102.e: The South Pole lies in the middle of the continent of Antarctica. There are no towns and no trees there.
17102.m: The South Pole is in Antarctica.

17103.q: Who was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911?
17103.e: The Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole with dog sleds in December 1911. The Briton Robert Scott got there about a month later.
17103.m: Roald Amundsen was the first to reach the South Pole in 1911.

17104.q: Roughly how long does it stay dark at the South Pole in winter?
17104.e: At the South Pole the sun does not rise for about half a year in winter. In summer, on the other hand, it shines non-stop for about half a year.
17104.m: At the South Pole the winter night lasts about half a year.

17105.e: A globe shows the Earth as a small ball. That way you can see countries and seas in their correct positions.
17105.m: A globe is a model of the Earth.

17106.e: The Earth is round like a ball. That is why a globe is also shaped like a sphere.
17106.m: A globe is shaped like a sphere.

17107.q: What is the line that runs around the middle of the globe called?
17107.e: The equator divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half. In lowlands near the equator it is warm all year.
17107.m: The equator runs around the middle of the Earth.

17108.q: What does a world map show?
17108.e: A world map shows all the continents and seas on a flat sheet.
17108.m: A world map shows the whole Earth on a flat sheet.

17109.q: What do you call a book with lots of maps?
17109.e: In an atlas you find maps of countries, continents and the whole world.
17109.m: A book with lots of maps is called an atlas.

17110.q: Which compass direction is at the top of most maps?
17110.e: On most maps north is at the top and south at the bottom. East is on the right, west on the left.
17110.m: On most maps north is at the top.

17111.q: Which country lies entirely in Europe and is the largest by area?
17111.e: Ukraine is about 600,000 km² in size. Russia is bigger, but most of it lies in Asia.
17111.m: Ukraine is the largest country that lies entirely in Europe.

17112.q: Which of these countries does not border Switzerland?
17112.e: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. Belgium lies further to the north-west.

17113.q: Which country in the European Union has the most inhabitants?
17113.e: Germany has over 80 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That makes it the most populous country in the EU.
17113.m: Germany is the most populous country in the EU.

17114.q: Which is the smallest country in the European Union by area?
17114.e: Malta is an island state in the Mediterranean and only about 316 km² in size. Luxembourg, at around 2,600 km², is much bigger.
17114.m: Malta is the smallest country in the EU.

17115.q: What is the capital of Portugal?
17115.e: Lisbon lies where the Tagus flows into the Atlantic. Porto is the second largest city in Portugal.
17115.m: The capital of Portugal is Lisbon.

17116.q: What is the capital of Poland?
17116.e: Warsaw lies on the Vistula and is the largest city in Poland. Kraków was a royal city for a long time.
17116.m: The capital of Poland is Warsaw.

17117.q: What is the capital of Croatia?
17117.e: Zagreb lies inland in the north of Croatia. Split and Dubrovnik are well-known cities on the Adriatic coast.
17117.m: The capital of Croatia is Zagreb.

17118.q: Officially, Switzerland has no capital. What is Bern called instead?
17118.e: The Federal Council and the Federal Assembly have their seat in Bern. But the Federal Constitution names no capital, so people speak of the federal city.

17119.q: Which has been the largest country in Africa by area since 2011?
17119.e: When South Sudan split from Sudan in 2011, Algeria, at around 2.4 million km², became the largest country in Africa. Much of it is desert.
17119.m: Algeria is the largest country in Africa.

17120.q: Which country in Africa has the most inhabitants?
17120.e: Nigeria in West Africa has over 200 million inhabitants (as of 2025). That means about one in six people in Africa lives there.
17120.m: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa.

17121.q: Which country is Kilimanjaro, the highest mountain in Africa, in?
17121.e: Kilimanjaro is about 5,895 m high and lies in north-eastern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya. Its highest peak is the volcano Kibo, which has been dormant for a long time.

17122.q: Which country is completely surrounded by the territory of South Africa?
17122.e: Lesotho is an enclave and lies entirely inside South Africa. It is a mountainous country with high valleys.
17122.m: Lesotho lies in the middle of South Africa.

17123.q: What is the capital of Japan?
17123.e: Tokyo lies on the main island of Honshu. Kyoto was the imperial city for over 1,000 years.
17123.m: The capital of Japan is Tokyo.

17124.q: Which country lies entirely in Asia and is the largest by area?
17124.e: China is about 9.6 million km² in size. Russia is bigger, but part of it lies in Europe.
17124.m: China is the largest country that lies entirely in Asia.

17125.q: Which island state in South-East Asia is made up of around 17,000 islands?
17125.e: Indonesia is the largest island state in the world. Among the best-known islands are Java, Bali and Sumatra.
17125.m: Indonesia is the largest island state on Earth.

17126.q: Which landlocked country lies between Russia and China?
17126.e: Mongolia borders only Russia and China and has no access to the sea. A large part of the country is steppe and the Gobi Desert.
17126.m: Mongolia is squeezed in between Russia and China.

17127.q: Which is the largest country in South America by area?
17127.e: Brazil is about 8.5 million km² in size. It takes up almost half the area of South America.
17127.m: Brazil is the largest country in South America.

17128.q: What is the capital of Canada?
17128.e: Ottawa is in the province of Ontario. Toronto is the largest city in Canada, but not the capital.
17128.m: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

17129.q: Which language is the official language of Brazil?
17129.e: Brazil was a colony of Portugal for a long time. That is why people there speak Portuguese, while Spanish is spoken in most neighbouring countries.

17130.q: In which country is the canal that links the Atlantic with the Pacific in Central America?
17130.e: The Panama Canal opened in 1914 and is about 82 km long. Ships no longer have to sail round the southern tip of South America.
17130.m: The Panama Canal links two oceans.

17131.q: Which mountain range is seen as the border between Europe and Asia?
17131.e: The Urals stretch about 2,500 km from north to south in Russia. They are usually used as the border between the two continents.
17131.m: The Urals separate Europe from Asia.

17132.q: Which mountain range forms the border between France and Spain?
17132.e: The Pyrenees reach from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. The tiny country of Andorra lies in the middle of these mountains.
17132.m: The Pyrenees lie between France and Spain.

17133.q: Which large mountain range stretches across western North America from Canada into the USA?
17133.e: The Rocky Mountains are over 4,000 km long. Well-known national parks such as Yellowstone are in these mountains.
17133.m: The Rocky Mountains are in western North America.

17134.q: Which mountain range lies in north-western Africa, mainly in Morocco?
17134.e: The Atlas Mountains run through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. They separate the Mediterranean coast from the Sahara.
17134.m: The Atlas Mountains are in north-western Africa.

17135.q: What is the highest mountain in the Alps called?
17135.e: Mont Blanc is about 4,806 m high. It lies on the border between France and Italy.
17135.m: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in the Alps.

17136.q: What is the highest peak in Switzerland called?
17136.e: The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif in Valais is 4,634 m high. It is named after the Swiss general Guillaume-Henri Dufour.
17136.m: The Dufourspitze is the highest mountain in Switzerland.

17137.q: How many countries have a share of the Alps?
17137.e: The Alps lie in France, Monaco, Italy, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. That makes eight countries.

17138.q: How high is Mount Everest according to the 2020 measurement?
17138.e: Nepal and China measured Mount Everest again together in 2020. The result was 8,848.86 m, rounded to 8,849 m.
17138.m: Mount Everest is about 8,849 m high.

17139.q: How many mountains on Earth are higher than 8,000 m?
17139.e: There are 14 eight-thousanders in the world. All of them are in the Himalayas or the neighbouring Karakoram in Asia.

17140.q: On the border of which two countries is Mount Everest?
17140.e: The summit lies exactly on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. It can be climbed from both sides.
17140.m: Mount Everest lies between Nepal and China.

17141.q: Who were the first people proven to reach the summit of Mount Everest, in 1953?
17141.e: On 29 May 1953, the New Zealander Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit. They were part of a British expedition.
17141.m: Hillary and Tenzing were the first to climb Everest, in 1953.

17142.q: What does the name “Himalaya” mean when translated from Sanskrit?
17142.e: The word is made of “hima” for snow and “alaya” for home. “Roof of the world”, on the other hand, is a nickname for the Tibetan Plateau.

17143.q: Roughly how far do the Andes in South America stretch from north to south?
17143.e: The Andes run along the west coast of South America for about 7,500 km from Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego. They are seen as the longest mountain range above sea level.
17143.m: The Andes are the longest mountain range on land.

17144.q: What is the highest mountain in the Andes and in all of the Americas called?
17144.e: Aconcagua in Argentina is about 6,961 m high. It is the highest mountain outside Asia.
17144.m: Aconcagua is the highest mountain in the Americas.

17145.q: What is the famous Inca ruined city high in the Andes of Peru called?
17145.e: Machu Picchu was built by the Incas in the 15th century and lies at around 2,400 m above sea level. Chichén Itzá and Tikal are Maya cities.
17145.m: Machu Picchu is an Inca city in Peru.

17146.q: Which large lake lies in the Andes on the border between Peru and Bolivia?
17146.e: Lake Titicaca lies at around 3,800 m above sea level. It is seen as the highest large navigable body of water in the world.
17146.m: Lake Titicaca lies high in the Andes.

17147.q: Which sea does the Nile flow into?
17147.e: The Nile reaches the sea in Egypt with a large delta. A great many people live in the fertile Nile Delta.
17147.m: The Nile ends in the Mediterranean.

17148.q: In which city do the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet?
17148.e: Khartoum is the capital of Sudan. From there the river flows on northwards as the Nile.
17148.m: The White Nile and Blue Nile join in Khartoum.

17149.q: From which large lake in East Africa does the White Nile flow out?
17149.e: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa. It lies between Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania.
17149.m: The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria.

17150.q: Which large reservoir was created in Egypt by the Aswan Dam?
17150.e: The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970. It dams the Nile to form Lake Nasser and protects the country from floods.
17150.m: Lake Nasser is a reservoir on the Nile.

17151.q: Which river carries the most water of all the rivers in the world?
17151.e: On average the Amazon carries over 200,000 m³ of water per second into the sea. That is more than the next seven largest rivers put together.
17151.m: The Amazon is the river with the most water on Earth.

17152.q: Which sea does the Amazon flow into?
17152.e: The Amazon flows east right across South America. It reaches the sea in Brazil through a huge estuary.
17152.m: The Amazon flows into the Atlantic.

17153.q: In which country does the Amazon begin?
17153.e: The headwaters of the Amazon rise high in the Andes of Peru. From there the water flows east.

17154.q: In which country is most of the Amazon rainforest?
17154.e: Around 60 percent of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil. It is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.
17154.m: Most of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil.

17155.q: In which mountains does the Danube begin?
17155.e: At Donaueschingen, the streams Brigach and Breg from the Black Forest flow together. From there the river is called the Danube.
17155.m: The Danube begins in the Black Forest.

17156.q: Which sea does the Danube flow into?
17156.e: The Danube reaches the sea on the border of Romania and Ukraine. There it forms a large delta with many birds.
17156.m: The Danube flows into the Black Sea.

17157.q: How many countries does the Danube flow through?
17157.e: The Danube flows through or along Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine. No other river in the world touches so many countries.

17158.q: Which of these capital cities does the Danube not flow through?
17158.e: The Vltava flows through Prague. The capitals Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade are on the Danube.
17158.m: The Danube flows through four capital cities.

17159.q: Which river from the Engadine carries water from Switzerland into the Danube?
17159.e: The Inn rises in the Upper Engadine and flows through Austria to Germany. At Passau it flows into the Danube.
17159.m: The Inn flows from the Engadine to the Danube.

17160.q: In which canton does the Rhine begin?
17160.e: The Anterior Rhine starts at Lake Toma in Graubünden. At Reichenau the Anterior and Posterior Rhine flow together.

17161.q: Which sea does the Rhine flow into?
17161.e: The Rhine flows into the North Sea in the Netherlands. The large port of Rotterdam lies where it reaches the sea.
17161.m: The Rhine ends in the North Sea.

17162.q: Near which town are the Rhine Falls?
17162.e: The Rhine Falls are at Neuhausen am Rheinfall, right next to Schaffhausen. They are among the largest waterfalls in Europe.
17162.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

17163.q: Near which Swiss city are the Rhine ports from which cargo ships sail to the North Sea?
17163.e: The Swiss Rhine ports are at Basel. From there cargo ships travel along the Rhine to the North Sea.
17163.m: In Basel, Switzerland has access to the sea via the Rhine.

17164.q: Which lake does the Rhine flow through between Switzerland, Austria and Germany?
17164.e: The Alpine Rhine flows into Lake Constance in Vorarlberg (Austria), and the Rhine leaves the lake again at Stein am Rhein. Lake Constance borders three countries.
17164.m: The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.

17165.q: Which strait links the Mediterranean with the Atlantic?
17165.e: The Strait of Gibraltar lies between Spain and Morocco. At its narrowest point it is only about 14 km wide.
17165.m: At Gibraltar the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic.

17166.q: Which canal links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea?
17166.e: The Suez Canal in Egypt opened in 1869. Since then ships from Europe to Asia no longer have to sail round Africa.
17166.m: The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

17167.q: Which is the largest island in the Mediterranean?
17167.e: Sicily belongs to Italy and is about 25,700 km² in size. The volcano Etna is on the island.
17167.m: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean.

17168.q: How many continents does the Mediterranean border?
17168.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe to the north, Africa to the south and Asia to the east. Its name means “sea in the middle of the lands”.

17169.q: Which ocean is the second largest on Earth?
17169.e: The Atlantic covers about a fifth of the Earth's surface. It lies between America to the west and Europe and Africa to the east.
17169.m: The Atlantic is the second largest ocean.

17170.q: Which warm ocean current gives western Europe a mild climate?
17170.e: The Gulf Stream brings warm water from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic to Europe. That is why winters there are milder than in Canada at the same latitude.
17170.m: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe.

17171.q: Which island country lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
17171.e: In Iceland the North American and Eurasian plates drift apart. That is why there are many volcanoes and hot springs there.
17171.m: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

17172.q: Which group of islands in the middle of the Atlantic belongs to Portugal?
17172.e: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Portugal. The Canary Islands belong to Spain.
17172.m: The Azores are Portuguese islands in the Atlantic.

17173.q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
17173.e: The Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface. It is bigger than all the land on Earth put together.
17173.m: The Pacific is the largest ocean.

17174.q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point in the Mariana Trench?
17174.e: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is just under 11,000 m deep. Even Mount Everest would disappear completely inside it.
17174.m: The Mariana Trench is the deepest point in the oceans.

17176.q: Where does the Pacific get its name from?
a: from the name of a king
17176.e: In 1520 the seafarer Ferdinand Magellan called the sea “Mar Pacífico” because it was calm during his voyage. Pacífico means peaceful.
17176.m: The name Pacific means the peaceful one.

17177.q: Which US state is made up of islands in the middle of the Pacific?
17177.e: Hawaii lies about 3,800 km off the coast of North America. The islands were formed by volcanoes.
17177.m: Hawaii is a US island state in the Pacific.

17178.q: Which island country is made up of around 1,200 flat coral islands in the Indian Ocean?
17178.e: The Maldives lie south-west of India. Most of the islands rise only a little above sea level.
17178.m: The Maldives are made up of many flat coral islands.

17179.q: Which large island off the east coast of Africa lies in the Indian Ocean?
17179.e: Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world. Many animals live there that are found only on this island, such as lemurs.
17179.m: Madagascar lies off the east coast of Africa.

17180.q: What is the wind over the Indian Ocean called that changes direction with the seasons and brings rainy seasons to South Asia?
17180.e: In summer the monsoon blows from the sea onto the land and brings heavy rain. In winter it blows the other way and it is dry.
17180.m: The monsoon brings South Asia its rainy season.

17181.q: Off which island did an undersea earthquake set off a devastating tsunami in the Indian Ocean in December 2004?
17181.e: The earthquake off the northern tip of Sumatra on 26 December 2004 was one of the strongest ever measured. The waves hit coasts in many countries around the Indian Ocean.
17181.m: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra set off a huge tsunami in 2004.

17182.q: Ideally, how many degrees of longitude does one time zone cover?
17182.e: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours. 360 divided by 24 is 15 degrees per hour.
17182.m: One hour of time difference equals 15 degrees of longitude.

17183.q: Through which part of London does the prime meridian run?
17183.e: In 1884 the prime meridian was set through the Greenwich observatory. Lines of longitude are counted east and west from there.
17183.m: The prime meridian runs through Greenwich.

17184.q: What changes when you cross the International Date Line?
17184.e: The date line runs roughly along the 180th line of longitude through the Pacific. If you travel west across it, you jump forward a day; if you travel east, you go back a day.
17184.m: At the date line the date changes.

17185.q: In winter it is 12 noon in Zurich (UTC+1). What time is it then in New York (UTC−5)?
17185.e: The difference is 1 minus (minus 5), so 6 hours. New York is further west, so you work out 12 minus 6 = 6 am.
17185.m: In the west it is earlier than in the east.

17186.q: During summer time, what time does Switzerland use compared with Coordinated Universal Time (UTC)?
17186.e: In summer the clocks in Switzerland are put forward one hour. This time is called Central European Summer Time.
17186.m: In summer Switzerland uses Central European Summer Time.

17187.q: Which climate zone is Switzerland in?
17187.e: Switzerland lies in the middle latitudes with four clear seasons. In the mountains, however, it is much colder than in the Central Plateau.
17187.m: Switzerland lies in the temperate zone.

17188.q: Between which lines do the tropics lie?
a: Between the two tropics of Cancer and Capricorn
Between the equator and the North Pole
Between the prime meridian and the date line
17188.e: The tropics of Cancer and Capricorn lie at about 23.4 degrees north and south. Between them, the sun is directly overhead at midday at least once a year.
17188.m: The tropics lie between the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.

17189.q: Which climate zone is the Sahara mainly in?
17189.e: The Sahara lies around the Tropic of Cancer. Dry air sinks there, which is why it very rarely rains.
17189.m: Many large deserts lie in the subtropics.

17190.q: What is the treeless landscape with mosses and lichens in the subpolar zone called?
17190.e: In the tundra the summer is too short and too cool for trees. Deep down, the ground often stays frozen all year.
17190.m: No trees grow in the tundra.

17191.q: Where can you see the midnight sun in summer?
a: Only on the Tropic of Cancer
17191.e: North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set for at least one day in midsummer. This is true, for example, in northern Norway.
17191.m: The midnight sun can be seen north of the Arctic Circle.

17192.q: Roughly how many people live on Earth (as of 2025)?
17192.e: According to the United Nations, the world population passed 8 billion in 2022. The number is still growing, but more slowly than before.
17192.m: About 8 billion people live on Earth.

17193.q: On which continent do about 60 percent of the world's people live?
17193.e: Asia has several countries with very large populations. That is why more than half of all people live there.

17194.q: Which country is the most densely populated in the world?
17194.e: Monaco is only about 2 km² in size but has about 38,000 inhabitants (as of 2023). That is over 18,000 people per km².
17194.m: Monaco is the most densely populated country.

17195.q: A country has 1,000,000 inhabitants and an area of 5,000 km². What is its population density?
17195.e: Population density is the number of inhabitants divided by the area. 1,000,000 divided by 5,000 is 200 inhabitants per km².
17195.m: For population density, you divide the number of inhabitants by the area.

17196.q: What was the Taj Mahal in India built as?
17196.e: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had the Taj Mahal built in Agra in the 17th century for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is a mausoleum made of white marble.
17196.m: The Taj Mahal is a magnificent tomb.

17197.q: In which city is the large statue of Christ on Corcovado mountain?
17197.e: The statue “Christ the Redeemer” is about 30 m tall and was unveiled in 1931. It looks out over the city and the bay.
17197.m: The statue of Christ watches over Rio de Janeiro.

17198.q: In which country is the rock city of Petra?
17198.e: Over 2,000 years ago the Nabataeans carved buildings straight into the reddish rock. Petra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
17198.m: Petra is a rock city in Jordan.

17199.q: Which country gave the USA the Statue of Liberty in New York?
17199.e: The Statue of Liberty was unveiled in 1886 and was a gift from France to mark the friendship between the two countries. Its inner steel frame was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
17199.m: The Statue of Liberty is a gift from France.

17200.q: In which city is the opera house with sail-shaped roofs by the harbour?
17200.e: The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973. It was designed by the Danish architect Jørn Utzon.
17200.m: The famous opera house with sail roofs is in Sydney.

17201.q: Which is the largest lake on Earth by area?
17201.e: Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is a lake with no outlet to the sea. It is about 370,000 km² in size (a little more or less depending on the water level), about nine times the size of Switzerland.
17201.m: The Caspian Sea is the largest lake on Earth.

17202.q: Which lake is the deepest on Earth?
17202.e: Lake Baikal in Siberia is up to about 1,640 m deep. It holds about a fifth of the liquid fresh water on the Earth's surface.
17202.m: Lake Baikal is the deepest lake in the world.

17203.q: Which is the largest island on Earth?
17203.e: Greenland is over 2 million km² in size and mostly covered with ice. Australia counts as a continent, not an island.
17203.m: Greenland is the largest island on Earth.

17204.q: Where is the lowest point on land?
17204.e: The shore of the Dead Sea is more than 430 m below sea level. The water is so salty that you can hardly sink in it.
17204.m: The Dead Sea is the lowest place on land.

17205.q: In which country is the highest waterfall on Earth, Angel Falls?
17205.e: Angel Falls plunge about 979 m. They are in a national park in south-eastern Venezuela.
17205.m: The highest waterfall on Earth is in Venezuela.

17597.q: How many fingers do you have on one hand?
17597.e: On each hand there is a thumb and four other fingers. Together that makes five fingers.
17597.m: I have five fingers on each hand.

17598.q: Which part of the body connects the head to the trunk?
17598.e: The neck holds up the head. Thanks to it you can turn your head and nod.
17598.m: The neck connects the head to the body.

17599.q: What is the joint in the middle of the leg called?
17599.e: The knee is between the thigh and the lower leg. Thanks to it you can bend your leg.
17599.m: With my knee I can bend my leg.

17600.q: What is the joint in the middle of the arm called?
17600.e: The elbow is between the upper arm and the forearm. You use it to bend your arm.
17600.m: With my elbow I can bend my arm.

17601.e: The thumb is the strongest finger. With it we can grab and hold things well.
17601.m: My thumb helps me grab things.

17603.q: Which sense tells you whether something is soft or hard?
17603.e: When you touch something, you feel with your skin whether it is soft, hard, rough or smooth.
17603.m: With my sense of touch I feel what something is like.

17604.q: Which sense helps you enjoy music?
17604.e: Music is made of sounds. You take in sounds with your ears.
17604.m: I take in music with my hearing.

17605.q: What do you call the parts of the body we use to sense things?
17605.e: Eyes, ears, nose, tongue and skin pick up signals from the world around us. That is why they are called sense organs.
17605.m: With my sense organs I take in the world.

17606.q: Which sense warns you about burnt food before you see it?
17606.e: The smell of burning reaches the nose quickly. So you often notice from the next room that something is burning.
17606.m: My nose can warn me of danger.

17607.q: What is the black hole in the middle of the eye called?
17607.e: Light enters the eye through the pupil. In the dark it gets bigger, in bright light smaller.
17607.m: Light comes into my eye through the pupil.

17608.q: Which part of the eye decides eye colour?
17608.e: The iris is the coloured ring around the pupil. It can be, for example, blue, green or brown.
17608.m: The iris gives my eyes their colour.

17609.q: What protects the eye when we blink?
17609.e: When you blink, the eyelid closes briefly. It spreads tear fluid and keeps dust away.
17609.m: When I blink, the eyelid protects my eye.

17610.q: What do our eyes need in order to see?
17610.e: Our eyes take in light. In total darkness we cannot see anything.
17610.m: Without light I cannot see anything.

17611.q: What helps many people to see clearly again?
17611.e: Glasses have special lenses. They help the eye to see things clearly.

17612.q: What is the thin skin in the ear that vibrates with sounds called?
17612.e: Sounds make the eardrum vibrate. These vibrations are passed on into the inner parts of the ear.
17612.m: The eardrum vibrates when sounds come into the ear.

17613.q: Apart from hearing, what is the inner ear also important for?
17613.e: In the inner ear there is a balance organ. It notices how we move and how our head is positioned.
17613.m: My ear also helps me keep my balance.

17614.q: Where in the body is the smallest bone?
17614.e: The smallest bone is called the stirrup. It sits in the middle ear and helps with hearing.
17614.m: The smallest bone is in my ear.

17615.q: What protects your ears from very loud noise?
17615.e: Very loud noise can damage your hearing for good. Ear protection makes the noise quieter.
17615.m: When it is very loud, I protect my ears.

17616.q: What helps people who are hard of hearing to hear better?
17616.e: A hearing aid makes sounds louder. That way people who are hard of hearing can follow conversations better.
17616.m: A hearing aid makes sounds louder.

17617.q: What are the little hairs in your nose good for?
17617.e: Nose hairs catch dust and tiny particles from the air. That keeps the lungs cleaner.

17618.q: Why does food often taste bland when you have a cold?
a: Because your nose cannot smell well
17618.e: Smell and taste work closely together. If your nose is blocked, lots of things taste weaker.

17619.q: What does your nose do with the air you breathe in?
17619.e: In the nose, the air is warmed and moistened. That is good for the lungs.
17619.m: The nose warms the air you breathe.

17620.q: How many nostrils does a person have?
17620.e: The nose has two nostrils. Between them is the wall called the septum.

17621.q: Which taste goes with a lemon?
17621.e: Lemons contain a lot of acid. That is why they taste sour.

17622.e: Honey contains a lot of sugar. Sugar tastes sweet.

17623.q: What is on the tongue and helps with tasting?
17623.e: There are thousands of tiny taste buds on the tongue. We taste our food with them.
17623.m: I taste with my taste buds.

17624.q: Apart from tasting, what does the tongue help with?
17624.e: The tongue moves very easily. Without it we could not say many sounds.

17625.q: Why do we sweat when we are hot?
17625.e: Sweat evaporates on the skin. As it does so, it cools the body down.

17626.q: What protects the skin from sunburn in summer?
17626.e: Sun cream blocks some of the sun's rays. A hat, clothes and shade protect the skin too.
17626.m: In summer I protect my skin from the sun.

17627.q: What is unique to every person?
17627.e: The fine lines on your fingertips are different for every person. Even twins have different fingerprints.
17627.m: My fingerprint belongs only to me.

17628.q: What do you call it when the tiny hairs on your skin stand up in the cold?
17628.e: When you are cold or get a fright, tiny muscles in the skin tighten. Then the tiny hairs stand up.
17628.m: When it is cold I sometimes get goose bumps.

17630.q: What do we think and learn with?
17630.e: The brain processes everything we see, hear and feel. It also stores what we learn.
17630.m: I think and learn with my brain.

17631.q: What protects your head when you ride a bike?
17631.e: A helmet cushions knocks if you fall. That way it protects your head and brain.
17631.m: I wear a helmet when I ride my bike.

17632.q: What does the brain need to recover well?
17632.e: During sleep the brain rests and sorts out what we have learnt. Afterwards we can concentrate better.
17632.m: Sleep is good for my brain.

17633.q: How do messages get from the brain to the hands?
17633.e: Nerves run like cables through the whole body. They pass messages between the brain and the parts of the body.
17633.m: Nerves carry messages through my body.

17634.e: The heart is a pump. It pumps blood around the whole body.
17634.m: My heart pumps blood around my body.

17635.q: What is the heart mainly made of?
17635.e: The heart is a strong muscle. It tightens again and again and so pumps the blood along.

17636.e: The heart is in the ribcage, a little to the left of the middle. You can sometimes feel it beating there.
17636.m: My heart is in my chest.

17637.q: What happens to your heartbeat when you run fast?
17637.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. That is why the heart beats faster.
17637.m: When I do sport, my heart beats faster.

17638.q: Where can you feel your pulse easily?
17638.e: At the wrist, blood flows close under the skin. There you can feel every heartbeat as your pulse.
17638.m: I can feel my pulse at my wrist.

17639.q: How many lungs does a person have?
17639.e: People have a right lung and a left lung. Both are in the ribcage.

17640.q: Which organ takes oxygen out of the air?
17640.e: When you breathe in, air flows into the lungs. There the oxygen from the air gets into the blood.
17640.m: My lungs take oxygen out of the air.

17641.q: What is very harmful to the lungs?
17641.e: Tobacco smoke contains many poisonous substances. They damage the lungs and make people ill.

17642.q: What protects the lungs from the outside?
17642.e: The ribs form the ribcage. It surrounds the lungs like a cage.

17643.q: Where does food end up after you swallow it?
17643.e: After you swallow, the food slides down into the stomach. There it is digested further.
17643.m: Swallowed food goes into the stomach.

17644.q: What does the stomach do with food?
a: It pumps it into the heart
It sends it to the nose
17644.e: The stomach kneads the food and mixes it with gastric juice. That turns it into a mush.
17644.m: My stomach turns food into a mush.

17645.q: Why does your tummy sometimes rumble?
17645.e: An empty stomach still moves. Air and liquid are pushed back and forth, and we hear that.
17645.m: A rumbling tummy often means you are hungry.

17646.q: What does gastric juice contain that makes bacteria harmless?
17646.e: Gastric juice is very acidic. The acid kills many germs in food.

17647.q: Roughly how many bones does an adult have?
17647.e: An adult human has about 206 bones. Babies have more, because some bones grow together later.

17648.q: What do you call all the bones together?
17648.e: All the bones together make up the skeleton. It supports the body and gives it its shape.

17649.e: The skull is a hard case of bone. Inside it lies the delicate brain.

17650.q: Where is the longest bone in the body?
17650.e: The thigh bone is the longest and one of the strongest bones. It carries a large part of the body's weight.
17650.m: The longest bone is in the thigh.

17651.q: What do people often wear when they have broken an arm?
17651.e: A plaster cast keeps the broken bone still. That way it can grow back together properly.
17651.m: A plaster cast helps a broken bone heal.

17652.q: What do we need to move an arm?
17652.e: Muscles pull on the bones. That way we can move our arms, legs and fingers.

17653.q: What happens to a muscle when it works?
17653.e: A working muscle gets shorter and thicker. As it does, it pulls on a bone.
17653.m: A muscle tightens when it works.

a: Through sitting for a long time
17654.e: When we use our muscles often, they get stronger. Sport and playing outside help with this.

17655.q: What do you call sore muscles the day after lots of sport?
17655.e: After unusual effort, muscles often hurt the next day. This is called muscle soreness, and it goes away by itself after a few days.
17655.m: Muscle soreness goes away after a few days.

17656.q: What is the muscle at the front of the upper arm called?
17656.e: The biceps is at the front of the upper arm. It bends the arm at the elbow.

17657.q: How many milk teeth does a child have?
17657.e: Children have 20 milk teeth. Later they are replaced one by one by permanent teeth.
17657.m: A child has twenty milk teeth.

17658.q: How many times a day should you brush your teeth?
17658.e: Dentists recommend brushing your teeth at least twice a day. Best in the morning and in the evening before bed.
17658.m: I brush my teeth at least twice a day.

17659.q: What is especially bad for your teeth?
17659.e: Bacteria in the mouth turn sugar into acid. The acid attacks the teeth.
17659.m: Too much sugar is bad for your teeth.

17660.q: What is the hard white layer on the teeth called?
17660.e: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the whole body. It protects the tooth.

17661.q: What is the disease called in which holes form in the teeth?
17661.e: With tooth decay, the tooth is attacked by acid. Holes form, and the dentist has to treat them.
17661.m: Tooth decay makes holes in the teeth.

17662.e: Blood is red because it contains a huge number of red blood cells. They give the blood its colour.

17663.q: What does blood carry around the body?
17663.e: Blood collects oxygen from the lungs. It takes it to every part of the body.
17663.m: Blood brings oxygen into my body.

17664.q: In which tubes does blood flow around the body?
17664.e: Blood flows in blood vessels, which are also called veins and arteries. They reach right into your fingertips.
17664.m: My blood flows in my blood vessels.

17665.q: What forms when a small wound heals?
17665.e: The blood clots at the wound and becomes firm. This crust closes the wound until new skin has grown.
17665.m: A crust protects a healing wound.

17666.q: Roughly how much blood does an adult have?
17666.e: An adult has about 5 to 6 litres of blood. Children have less, because they are smaller.
17666.m: An adult has about five litres of blood.

17667.q: Which gas from the air do we need to live?
17667.e: Our body needs oxygen to get energy. Without oxygen we could only survive for a short time.

17668.q: Which gas do we mainly breathe out?
17668.e: When we breathe out, we give off carbon dioxide. It is made in the body as a waste product.
17668.m: When I breathe out, I give off carbon dioxide.

17669.q: What is the tube through which air flows into the lungs called?
17669.e: The windpipe leads from the neck into the chest. There it splits and leads into both lungs.
17669.m: Air comes into the lungs through the windpipe.

17670.q: What rises and falls when you breathe deeply?
17670.e: When you breathe in, the chest expands, and when you breathe out, it gets smaller again. You can feel this with your hand.
17670.m: When I breathe, my chest moves.

17671.q: What gets faster when you run?
17671.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen. That is why we breathe faster and more deeply.
17671.m: When I work hard, I breathe faster.

17672.e: Food is already broken up by the teeth in the mouth. That is where digestion begins.

17673.q: Through which tube does food get from the mouth to the stomach?
17673.e: The food pipe is a tube made of muscle. It pushes food down into the stomach.
17673.m: The food pipe leads to the stomach.

17674.q: Which long organ comes after the stomach?
17674.e: After the stomach, the food mush moves into the gut. There the nutrients are taken into the blood.
17674.m: After the stomach comes the gut.

17675.q: What is the liquid in your mouth that helps with eating called?
17675.e: Saliva makes food moist and slippery. That makes it easier to swallow.

17676.q: Why should you chew your food well?
a: So that it is easier to digest
So that there is more of it
17676.e: Well-chewed food is in small pieces. Then the stomach has less work to do.
17676.m: Food that is well chewed is half digested.

17677.q: Roughly how many hours of sleep do school-age children need each night?
17677.e: Experts recommend about 9 to 12 hours of sleep for children aged 6 to 12. Children need more sleep than adults.

17678.q: What do we often experience while we sleep?
17678.e: During sleep the brain processes lots of impressions. We often dream while it does, even if we forget it by the morning.
17678.m: I often dream while I sleep.

17679.e: Darkness and quiet tell the body that it is time to sleep. Screens, on the other hand, keep you awake.
17679.m: I sleep better in a dark, quiet room.

17680.q: What happens to children's bodies mainly while they sleep?
a: They get as cold as ice
17680.e: During sleep the body makes particularly a lot of growth hormone. That is why sleep is very important for children.
17680.m: My body grows while I sleep.

17681.q: How do people often feel after too little sleep?
17681.e: People who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate. They get tired and grumpy more quickly.
17681.m: When I have slept well, I can concentrate better.

17682.q: According to experts, at least how long should children be active every day?
17682.e: The World Health Organization recommends at least 60 minutes of activity a day for children and teenagers. Playing counts too.
17682.m: I am active for at least an hour every day.

17683.q: What is a healthy way to get to school?
17683.e: If you walk or cycle to school, you move every day. That strengthens your heart and muscles.

17684.q: What should you do before sport?
17684.e: Warming up gets your muscles and joints ready for the effort. That way you are less likely to get injured.

17685.q: What is best to drink after sport?
17685.e: During sport the body loses water through sweat. Water replaces the liquid without any sugar.

17686.q: Which vitamin is found in large amounts in oranges?
17686.e: Oranges and other citrus fruits contain a lot of vitamin C. It is important for our body's defences.
17686.m: Oranges provide lots of vitamin C.

17687.q: How many portions of vegetables and fruit are recommended per day?
17687.e: In Switzerland, five portions a day are recommended: three portions of vegetables and two portions of fruit. One portion is about a handful.
17687.m: I eat five portions of vegetables and fruit every day.

17688.q: Which mid-morning snack is especially healthy?
17688.e: An apple provides vitamins and fills you up. Sweets, on the other hand, contain a lot of sugar.
17688.m: An apple is a healthy mid-morning snack.

17689.q: What do milk and cheese provide for your bones?
17689.e: Dairy products contain a lot of calcium. Calcium makes bones and teeth strong.

17690.q: What does the food pyramid show?
a: How to eat a balanced diet
17690.e: The food pyramid shows what you should eat a lot of and what you should eat little of. At the bottom is what you need most.
17690.m: The food pyramid helps me eat a balanced diet.

17691.q: When should you always wash your hands?
a: Before going to sleep in bed
17691.e: After using the toilet there may be germs on your hands. That is why you always wash your hands thoroughly afterwards.
17691.m: After the toilet I always wash my hands.

17692.q: What makes your hands properly clean when you wash them?
17692.e: Soap loosens dirt and grease from the skin. Water then rinses the germs away.

17693.q: Where should you sneeze if you have no tissue?
a: Into the crook of your elbow
17693.e: If you sneeze into the crook of your elbow, you spread fewer germs. Your hands stay clean and do not infect others.
17693.m: Without a tissue, I sneeze into the crook of my elbow.

17694.q: Why should everyone use their own toothbrush?
a: So that no germs are passed on
So that the toothpaste tastes better
17694.e: Germs from the mouth stick to a toothbrush. If you share it, illnesses can be passed on.

17695.q: What should you do before eating?
17695.e: Lots of germs collect on your hands. They should be clean before eating, so the germs do not get into your mouth.
17695.m: I wash my hands before eating.

17696.q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
17696.e: The thigh bone (femur) is the longest and one of the strongest bones in the body.
17696.m: The thigh bone is the longest human bone.

17697.q: Where is the smallest human bone?
17697.e: The stirrup in the middle ear is only a few millimetres long. It helps to pass sound on to the inner ear.
17697.m: The stirrup in the ear is the smallest bone.

17698.q: How many pairs of ribs does a person usually have?
17698.e: People usually have 12 pairs of ribs, so 24 ribs. Together with the breastbone they form the ribcage.
17698.m: The ribcage is made of 12 pairs of ribs and the breastbone.

17699.q: What is made in the red bone marrow?
17699.e: Red and white blood cells and platelets are made in the red bone marrow.
17699.m: Red bone marrow is the factory for our blood cells.

17700.q: Which mineral makes bones hard and firm?
17700.e: Bones contain a lot of calcium in the form of calcium phosphate. This substance gives them their hardness.

17701.q: Which type of joint is found in the shoulder and the hip?
17701.e: In a ball-and-socket joint, a ball-shaped end of bone sits in a socket. That is why you can move your arm and leg in many directions.
17701.m: Ball-and-socket joints allow movement in all directions.

17702.q: Which type of joint, like a door hinge, only allows bending and straightening?
17702.e: A hinge joint only moves in one plane, much like a door hinge. Examples are the joints between the bones of the fingers.
17702.m: A hinge joint only moves back and forth in one direction.

17703.q: What covers the joint surfaces of bones so that they glide smoothly?
17703.e: Smooth cartilage covers the ends of the bones in a joint. It reduces friction and cushions knocks.
17703.m: Cartilage protects the ends of the bones in a joint.

17704.q: What is the fluid that lubricates a joint called?
17704.e: The joint fluid (synovial fluid) is made by the joint capsule. It makes sure the joint moves easily.
17704.m: Joint fluid keeps our joints moving.

17705.q: In a joint, what connects two bones to each other?
17705.e: Ligaments are tough bands of connective tissue that connect bone to bone. They keep the joint stable.
17705.m: Ligaments hold the bones in a joint together.

17706.q: Which human joint is a saddle joint?
a: The joint at the base of the thumb
17706.e: The saddle joint of the thumb is at the base of the thumb, between the wrist bones and the hand bone. It lets you place the thumb opposite the other fingers.
17706.m: Thanks to the saddle joint we can grip with our thumb.

17707.q: Which three types of muscle are there in the human body?
17707.e: Skeletal muscles move the body, the heart muscle pumps blood and smooth muscles work, for example, in the gut.
17707.m: Humans have skeletal muscles, smooth muscles and the heart muscle.

17708.q: What connects a muscle to a bone?
17708.e: Tendons pass the force of the muscle on to the bone. The best known is the Achilles tendon at the heel.

17709.q: Which muscle straightens the arm when the biceps is relaxed?
17709.e: The biceps and triceps are opposing muscles. The biceps bends the arm and the triceps straightens it.
17709.m: Muscles work together in opposing pairs.

17710.q: Why does every skeletal muscle need an opposing muscle?
a: Because muscles can only pull, not push
Because muscles tear after every movement
Because muscles only work once a day
Because muscles need no energy themselves
17710.e: A muscle can only tighten. To move the joint back again, another muscle on the opposite side has to pull.
17710.m: A muscle can only pull and never push.

17711.q: What is a skeletal muscle made of on the inside?
17711.e: A skeletal muscle is built from many bundles of fibres. Each muscle fibre is a long cell that can shorten.
17711.m: Muscles are made of many long muscle fibres.

17712.q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
17712.e: Arteries carry blood away from the heart into the body. Veins bring it back to the heart.
17712.m: Arteries lead away from the heart, veins lead back to it.

17713.q: What are the tiniest blood vessels, where substances are exchanged, called?
17713.e: Capillaries are extremely thin. Oxygen and nutrients pass through their walls into the cells.
17713.m: In the capillaries, blood and cells exchange substances.

17714.e: Red blood cells contain the red pigment haemoglobin. Oxygen attaches to it.
17714.m: Red blood cells are the oxygen carriers in the blood.

a: They help the blood to clot
17715.e: Platelets (thrombocytes) stick together at a wound and help to close it.
17715.m: Platelets stop bleeding when you are injured.

17716.q: Roughly how much blood does an adult have?
17716.e: An adult has about 4.5 to 6 litres of blood, which is about 7 to 8 per cent of body weight.
17716.m: An adult has about 5 to 6 litres of blood.

17717.q: Where does blood flow in the pulmonary circulation?
a: From the heart to the lungs and back
From the heart to the brain and back
From the liver to the gut
From the kidneys to the bladder
17717.e: In the small or pulmonary circulation, the blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives off carbon dioxide.
17717.m: In the pulmonary circulation the blood is loaded with oxygen.

17719.q: Roughly how many times a minute does an adult's heart beat at rest?
17719.e: An adult's resting pulse is usually about 60 to 80 beats per minute; about 50 to 100 counts as normal. In children it is higher.
17719.m: At rest, an adult heart beats about 60 to 80 times per minute.

17720.q: A heart beats 70 times a minute. How many times does it beat in an hour?
17720.e: An hour has 60 minutes. So you calculate 70 times 60, which makes 4,200 beats.
17720.m: A heart beats several thousand times an hour.

17721.q: What are the heart valves for?
a: They filter poisons out of the blood
17721.e: The heart valves work like valves on a pipe. They only let blood flow in one direction.
17721.m: Heart valves make blood flow in one direction.

17722.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood into the main artery and so into the whole body?
17722.e: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. Its wall is especially thick and strong.
17722.m: The left ventricle supplies the whole body with blood.

a: Electrical signals in the heart itself
17723.e: In the right atrium there is a natural pacemaker, the sinus node. It regularly sends out electrical signals that make the heart muscle tighten.
17723.m: The heart sets its own rhythm with electrical signals.

17724.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
17724.e: In the tiny air sacs (alveoli), oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the air.
17724.m: Oxygen gets into the blood in the air sacs.

17725.q: Which muscle is the most important for breathing in?
17725.e: The diaphragm separates the chest from the belly. When it tightens and moves down, air flows into the lungs.
17725.m: The diaphragm is our most important breathing muscle.

17726.q: What stops food getting into the windpipe when you swallow?
17726.e: The epiglottis closes the entrance to the windpipe when you swallow. That way the food slides into the food pipe.
17726.m: The epiglottis protects the windpipe when you swallow.

17727.q: Roughly what percentage of the air we breathe in is oxygen?
17727.e: Air is made up of about 78 per cent nitrogen and about 21 per cent oxygen.
17727.m: Air contains about one fifth oxygen.

17728.q: Which gas do we breathe out in larger amounts than we breathe in?
17728.e: Cells make carbon dioxide when they produce energy. It is taken by the blood to the lungs and breathed out.
17728.m: When we breathe out, we give off carbon dioxide.

17729.q: Which nutrient is already broken down by saliva in the mouth?
17729.e: Saliva contains the enzyme amylase. It starts to break starch down into sugar. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time.
17729.m: Digestion already begins in the mouth.

17730.q: Which acid does the stomach make?
17730.e: The stomach lining makes hydrochloric acid. It kills many germs and helps to digest protein.
17730.m: Stomach acid kills germs and helps with digestion.

17731.q: In which organ are most nutrients taken into the blood?
17731.e: The small intestine has many folds and tiny finger-like villi. This gives it a huge surface so it can take in lots of nutrients.
17731.m: The small intestine takes in most of the nutrients.

17732.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
a: It removes water from the food mush
17732.e: In the large intestine, water and salt are taken out of what is left of the food. What remains is the thickened faeces.
17732.m: The large intestine takes water back out of the food mush.

17733.e: The liver makes bile, and the gall bladder only stores it. Bile helps to digest fats.
17733.m: The liver makes bile for digesting fat.

17734.q: What is the technical term for a nerve cell?
17734.e: Neurons are cells that receive and pass on electrical signals. The brain is made of billions of them.

17735.q: What does the central nervous system consist of?
17735.e: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. The nerves in the rest of the body belong to the peripheral nervous system.
17735.m: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system.

17736.q: What is the contact point where a nerve cell passes a signal on to the next cell called?
17736.e: At the synapse, messenger substances are released. They pass the signal on to the next cell.
17736.m: Nerve cells pass on signals at synapses.

17737.q: Why do we pull our hand away from a hot hob in a flash?
a: Because of a reflex through the spinal cord
Because the muscles feel the heat
17737.e: In a reflex, the signal is already switched in the spinal cord. The movement starts before the brain consciously registers the pain.
17737.m: Reflexes protect us from danger in a flash.

17738.q: Which part of the nervous system gets the body ready for fight or flight under stress?
17738.e: The sympathetic nervous system speeds up heartbeat and breathing. Its opposite number, the parasympathetic nervous system, brings rest and recovery.
17738.m: The sympathetic nervous system activates the body under stress.

17739.q: Which part of the brain is especially important for balance and coordinating movement?
17739.e: The cerebellum fine-tunes movements. It helps you keep your balance, for example, when riding a bike.

17740.q: Which part of the brain controls vital processes such as breathing and heartbeat?
17740.e: The brainstem connects the brain and spinal cord. It automatically controls breathing, heartbeat and swallowing.

17741.q: Which side of the body is mainly controlled by the left half of the brain?
a: The right side of the body
The left side of the body
17741.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain mainly controls the right side.
17741.m: Each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.

17742.q: Roughly how heavy is an adult's brain?
17742.e: An adult brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms. That is only about 2 per cent of body weight.
17742.m: Our brain weighs a little more than one kilogram.

17743.q: Which part of the brain is especially important for storing new things in your memory?
17743.e: The hippocampus lies deep in the temporal lobe. It helps to move new experiences and knowledge into long-term memory.
17743.m: The hippocampus helps with learning and remembering.

17744.q: Why is enough sleep important for the brain?
a: Because it strengthens what you have learnt while you sleep
Because it needs no energy while you sleep
Because it makes new bones while you sleep
Because it makes blood while you sleep
17744.e: During sleep the brain processes the impressions of the day. What you have learnt is strengthened in your memory.
17744.m: If you sleep well, you can learn better.

17745.q: What is the body's first protective barrier against germs?
17745.e: Unbroken skin and the mucous membranes keep many germs out before they even get into the body.
17745.m: The skin is our first wall of protection against germs.

17746.q: What do you call white blood cells that surround and break down germs?
17746.e: Phagocytes (macrophages) recognise invaders, swallow them up and digest them.
17746.m: Phagocytes eat up germs that have got in.

17747.q: Which proteins does the immune system make to mark particular germs?
17747.e: Antibodies are made by certain white blood cells. They fit exactly to one germ and mark it for the body's defences.
17747.m: Antibodies recognise and mark very particular germs.

17748.q: Why do many people only get chickenpox once?
a: Because memory cells recognise the germ again
Because the germ dies out afterwards
Because the blood dilutes the germ
17748.e: After the illness, memory cells stay in the body. If you come into contact with the germ again, they fight it very quickly.
17748.m: The immune system remembers germs it already knows.

a: An overreaction to substances that are actually harmless
17749.e: With an allergy, the immune system fights harmless substances such as pollen. This leads, for example, to sneezing or itching.
17749.m: With an allergy, the immune system reacts too strongly.

17750.q: Why can a fever be useful during an infection?
a: It makes it harder for many germs to multiply
17750.e: The raised temperature slows down many germs and speeds up the body's defences. A very high fever, however, must be treated by a doctor.
17750.m: Fever is one of the body's defence reactions.

17751.q: Which of these groups does NOT belong to the germs that cause disease?
17751.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites can cause diseases. Vitamins, on the other hand, are vital nutrients.
17751.m: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites can make you ill.

17752.q: Which diseases can ticks pass on in Switzerland?
17752.e: Ticks can pass on the tick-borne encephalitis virus and Borrelia bacteria. That is why you should check yourself after spending time in the woods.
17752.m: After being in the woods, you check your body for ticks.

17753.q: What do you call it when germs are passed on by coughing or sneezing?
17753.e: When you cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with germs get into the air. Other people breathe them in.
17753.m: Sneezing into the crook of your elbow protects others from droplets.

17754.q: What do you call the time between catching an illness and the first signs of it?
17754.e: During the incubation period, the germs multiply in the body before you feel any symptoms.
17754.m: The incubation period lies between infection and the outbreak of the illness.

17755.e: Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites (plasmodia). They are passed on by Anopheles mosquitoes.
17755.m: Malaria is passed on by mosquitoes.

17756.q: Why are viruses not considered living things in their own right?
a: They can only multiply inside other cells
They are made only of fat
17756.e: Viruses have no metabolism of their own. They need a host cell that makes new viruses for them.
17756.m: Viruses need other cells in order to multiply.

17757.q: Why do antibiotics not help against flu?
a: Because flu is caused by viruses
Because flu does not last long enough
Because antibiotics only work against fungi
Because flu is not an illness
17757.e: Antibiotics work against bacteria. Flu, however, is caused by influenza viruses.
17757.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

17758.q: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
