17758.e: Measles is caused by the measles virus and is very contagious. The other diseases are caused by bacteria.
17758.m: Measles is a contagious viral disease.

17759.q: How big are viruses usually compared with bacteria?
17759.e: Most viruses are so tiny that you can only see them with an electron microscope. Bacteria are usually much bigger.
17759.m: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.

17760.q: Which germs usually cause an ordinary cold?
17760.e: Colds are usually caused by viruses, for example rhinoviruses. They normally get better by themselves after a few days.
17760.m: A cold is usually caused by viruses.

17761.q: What do bacteria lack compared with human cells?
17761.e: Bacteria are single cells without a true nucleus. Their genetic material lies loose in the cytoplasm.
17761.m: Bacteria are single cells without a nucleus.

17762.e: A bacterium splits into two identical daughter cells. In good conditions this happens very quickly.

17763.e: Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould stopped bacteria from growing. This led to penicillin, one of the first and most famous antibiotics.
17763.m: Penicillin was one of the first antibiotics.

17764.q: Which bacteria help to make yoghurt?
17764.e: Lactic acid bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid. This makes the milk thick and slightly sour.

17765.q: What does it mean when bacteria are “resistant”?
a: An antibiotic no longer works against them
They only live in the gut
17765.e: Resistant bacteria survive despite an antibiotic. That is why you should only take antibiotics as a doctor tells you.
17765.m: Only take antibiotics as a doctor tells you.

17766.q: What job do the many bacteria in our gut have?
17766.e: The gut bacteria help to break down food, make some vitamins and protect against harmful germs.

17767.q: Which English doctor vaccinated a boy with cowpox in 1796 to protect him from smallpox?
17767.e: With his experiments, Edward Jenner showed that harmless cowpox protects against dangerous smallpox. He made smallpox vaccination scientifically known and spread it around the world.
17767.m: Edward Jenner is seen as a pioneer of vaccination.

17768.q: What does an active vaccination do in the body?
a: The immune system makes antibodies and memory cells
The body is given ready-made medicines
The germs are filtered out of the blood straight away
The skin becomes thicker and tighter
17768.e: The vaccine contains weakened or killed germs or parts of them. In this way the immune system learns to recognise the real germ.
17768.m: A vaccination trains the immune system.

17769.q: What are you given in a passive vaccination?
17769.e: In a passive vaccination you are injected with antibodies. The protection works at once but only lasts a few weeks to months.
17769.m: A passive vaccination protects quickly, but only for a short time.

17770.q: Which disease did the World Health Organization declare wiped out in 1980?
17770.e: Thanks to vaccination programmes all over the world, smallpox has officially no longer existed since 1980.
17770.m: Smallpox was wiped out by vaccination.

17771.q: What is a booster vaccination for?
a: It extends the protection of a vaccination
17771.e: With some vaccinations, for example against tetanus, the protection fades over time. A booster strengthens it again.
17771.m: Some vaccinations need to be boosted regularly.

17772.q: Which federal office publishes the official vaccination schedule in Switzerland?
17772.e: The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) publishes the Swiss vaccination schedule together with the Federal Commission for Vaccination.
17772.m: The Swiss vaccination schedule comes from the FOPH.

17773.q: Which three main nutrients give the body energy?
17773.e: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins provide energy. Vitamins, minerals and water are important but do not provide energy.
17773.m: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are our energy suppliers.

17774.q: Which nutrient provides the most energy per gram?
17774.e: One gram of fat provides about 9 kilocalories, one gram of carbohydrate or protein only about 4 kilocalories.
17774.m: Fat is the most energy-rich nutrient.

17775.q: One gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kilocalories. How much energy do 25 grams of carbohydrate provide?
17775.e: You calculate 25 times 4 kilocalories. That makes 100 kilocalories, about as much as the carbohydrates in a banana.
17775.m: Carbohydrates provide about 4 kilocalories per gram.

17776.q: Which disease is caused by a severe lack of vitamin C?
17776.e: In the past, sailors without fresh fruit and vegetables got scurvy. Typical signs are bleeding gums and weakness.
17776.m: Fresh fruit and vegetables provide vitamin C.

17777.q: Which vitamin does the body make in the skin with the help of sunlight?
17777.e: In sunlight the skin makes vitamin D. It is important for building calcium into the bones.
17777.m: Sunlight helps the body to make vitamin D.

17778.q: What is on the bottom level of the Swiss food pyramid?
17778.e: The food pyramid of the Swiss Society for Nutrition recommends unsweetened drinks such as water as the base.
17778.m: Water is the best drink for every day.

17779.q: Where do the long bones grow in length?
17779.e: The growth plates are zones of cartilage near the ends of the bones. New bone tissue forms there.
17779.m: Bones grow longer at the growth plates.

17780.q: Which gland in the brain makes growth hormone?
17780.e: The pituitary gland releases growth hormone. It encourages bones and muscles to grow.
17780.m: Growth hormone comes from the pituitary gland.

17781.q: When does the body release particularly a lot of growth hormone?
17781.e: A large part of the growth hormone is released during deep sleep. That is why enough sleep is important for children.

17782.q: Why does a person stop growing taller after puberty?
a: Because the muscles become too heavy
Because the heart beats more slowly
Because the skin can no longer stretch
17782.e: Towards the end of puberty, the growth plates turn into bone. After that, the bones can no longer get longer.
17782.m: After puberty the growth plates close.

17783.q: Through which process are new body cells made as you grow?
17783.e: In cell division (mitosis), one cell becomes two identical daughter cells. That is how the body grows.
17783.m: The body grows through cell division.

17784.q: Which hormone is especially important for boys in puberty?
17784.e: Testosterone, for example, makes the beard grow, the voice get deeper and the muscles get stronger.
17784.m: Testosterone controls many changes in boys.

17785.q: What triggers the changes in the body during puberty?
17785.e: Hormones are messengers in the blood. In puberty the body makes more of them, and they control growth and many other changes.

17787.q: Why do boys' voices break during puberty?
a: Because the voice box and vocal cords grow
17787.e: Under the influence of hormones, the voice box and vocal cords grow. This makes the voice deeper.
17787.m: When the voice breaks, it gets deeper.

17788.q: Why do many teenagers get spots in puberty?
a: Because the oil glands make more oil
Because they drink too much water
Because the skin has fewer cells
17788.e: Hormones stimulate the oil glands. If the pores get blocked, spots can form.
17788.m: Hormones in puberty can cause spots.

17875.q: Which risk factor for heart and circulation diseases can be influenced by your own behaviour?
17875.e: Smoking damages the walls of the blood vessels and encourages hardening of the arteries. Age, sex and family history, on the other hand, cannot be changed.
17875.m: Not smoking lowers your risk of heart and circulation diseases.

18192.q: Which instrument measures how warm or cold it is?
18192.e: A thermometer shows the temperature. You read it in degrees Celsius.

18193.q: What is the forecast called that tells you what the weather will be like tomorrow?
18193.e: In the weather forecast, experts say what the weather will be like over the next few days. You find it on the radio, on TV or on the internet.
18193.m: The weather forecast tells you the weather in advance.

18194.q: What are the little drops of water on the grass early in the morning called?
18194.e: During the cool night, water forms from the damp air. In the morning, little drops sparkle on the grass.
18194.m: Dew is little drops of water in the morning.

18195.q: What do you call a cloud that lies right down on the ground?
18195.e: Fog is a cloud that lies right down on the ground. Then you cannot see very far.
18195.m: Fog is a cloud on the ground.

18196.q: What are the small balls of ice that fall from the sky in a storm called?
18196.e: Hailstones are balls of ice. They form in big thunderclouds.
18196.m: Hail is made of small balls of ice.

18197.q: In which direction does the sun set in the evening?
18197.e: In the evening the sun disappears in the west. After that it gets dark.
18197.m: The sun sets in the west.

18198.q: What protects your skin from sunburn in summer?
18198.e: Sun cream blocks some of the strong rays of the sun. A hat and clothes protect you too.
18198.m: Sun cream protects your skin from sunburn.

18199.q: Why must you never look straight at the sun?
18199.e: Bright sunlight can injure your eyes. That is why you never look straight at it.
18199.m: Looking straight at the sun harms your eyes.

18200.q: Apart from light, what does the sun give us?
18200.e: The sun sends light and warmth to the Earth. Without it, the Earth would be freezing cold.
18200.m: The sun gives us light and warmth.

18201.q: What is a raindrop made of?
18201.e: A raindrop is a little drop of water. Lots of drops together are rain.

18202.q: What is often left on paths and roads after it rains?
18202.e: The rainwater collects in little dips. That is how puddles form.

18203.q: What do plants need rain for?
18203.e: Plants need water to grow. The rain brings them this water.

18204.q: Which animal often comes out of the ground after it rains?
18204.e: After rain, earthworms often crawl up to the surface. You can see them on paths and meadows.
18204.m: Lots of earthworms come out after rain.

18205.q: What do you take with you to keep your head dry in the rain?
18205.e: An umbrella keeps off the drops from above. That way you stay dry.
18205.m: An umbrella keeps the rain off.

18206.q: How many points does a snowflake usually have?
18206.e: Snow crystals usually have six points or sides. Even so, every flake looks a little different.
18206.m: A snowflake usually has six points.

18207.q: What happens to snow when it gets warm?
18207.e: When it is warm, snow melts. The snow turns into water.
18207.m: Snow melts into water when it is warm.

18208.q: What can you build out of snow?
18208.e: With wet snow you can roll balls. You use them to build a snowman.
18208.m: You can build a snowman out of snow.

18209.q: What do you call a large amount of snow that slides down a mountain?
18209.e: An avalanche is snow that slides quickly down a slope. Avalanches are dangerous.
18209.m: An avalanche is snow sliding down a mountain.

18210.e: Wind is air that moves. You cannot see it, but you can feel it.

18211.q: Which toy do you fly in the wind in autumn?
18211.e: A kite is lifted into the air by the wind. In autumn it is often windy.
18211.m: A kite flies with the wind.

18212.q: What is a very strong wind that can blow trees over called?
18212.e: A storm is a very strong wind. It can blow trees over and damage roofs.
18212.m: A storm is a very strong wind.

18213.q: What turns on a wind turbine when the wind blows?
18213.e: The wind turns the blades of the wind turbine. This makes electricity.
18213.m: The wind turns the blades of a wind turbine.

18214.q: What is the warm wind called that blows down into the valleys of the Swiss Alps?
18214.e: The föhn is a warm, dry wind. In Switzerland it blows, for example, in the canton of Uri and in the Rhine valley.
18214.m: The föhn is a warm wind in the Alps.

18215.q: What is the cold wind called that often blows from the north-east in Switzerland?
18215.e: The bise is a cold, dry wind from the north-east. It often blows across the Swiss Plateau.
18215.m: The bise is a cold wind from the north-east.

18216.e: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They float in the air.
18216.m: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets.

18217.q: What colour are clouds often before it rains heavily?
18217.e: Thick rain clouds let little light through. That is why they look dark grey.

18218.q: What do fleecy “sheep” clouds look like?
a: Like little balls of cotton wool
18218.e: Fleecy clouds are lots of small white clouds. They look like a flock of sheep.
18218.m: Fleecy clouds look like little balls of cotton wool.

18219.q: What do you see flash in the sky during a thunderstorm?
18219.e: Lightning is a bright electric spark in the air. It only flashes for a very short time.

18220.q: What is the loud crash after a flash of lightning called?
18220.e: Lightning heats the air very strongly. This makes a loud bang: the thunder.
18220.m: After the lightning comes the thunder.

18221.q: In a thunderstorm, what reaches you first?
18221.e: Light is much faster than sound. That is why you see the lightning before you hear the thunder.
18221.m: You see the lightning before the thunder.

18222.q: Where are you safest during a thunderstorm?
18222.e: In a house or a car you are protected from lightning. Trees, hills and water are dangerous.
18222.m: In a thunderstorm, go into a house.

18223.q: In which season are there the most thunderstorms in Switzerland?
18223.e: In summer the air is warm and damp. Thunderstorms often form from it.

18224.q: What protects a house from being struck by lightning?
18224.e: A lightning conductor carries the lightning safely into the ground. That way the house is not damaged.
18224.m: A lightning conductor protects the house from lightning.

18225.q: What is needed for a rainbow to appear?
18225.e: A rainbow appears when sunlight shines on raindrops. The drops split the light into colours.
18225.m: For a rainbow you need sun and rain.

18226.q: Which colour is on the very outside of a rainbow?
18226.e: In a rainbow, red is on the outside. Violet is right on the inside.
18226.m: In a rainbow, red is on the very outside.

18227.e: A rainbow is a coloured arch in the sky. From an aeroplane you can sometimes see a whole circle.
18227.m: A rainbow is shaped like an arch.

18228.q: Where must the sun be when you see a rainbow?
18228.e: You only see a rainbow with the sun behind you. The rain is then in front of you.
18228.m: You see a rainbow with the sun behind you.

18229.q: Which colour is NOT in a rainbow?
18229.e: A rainbow has red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. Brown is not one of them.
18229.m: Brown is not in a rainbow.

18230.q: In which season do the leaves fall from many trees?
18230.e: In autumn the leaves turn colourful and fall off. This helps the trees save water in winter.

18231.q: In which season do the first flowers such as snowdrops bloom?
18231.e: In spring it gets warmer. Then the first flowers bloom.
18231.m: The first flowers bloom in spring.

18232.q: In which season are the days longest?
18232.e: In summer the sun shines for the longest time. That is why it stays light late in the evening.
18232.m: The days are longest in summer.

18233.e: The order is spring, summer, autumn, winter. After winter comes spring again.

18234.q: What is the highest point of a mountain called?
18234.e: The summit is the highest place on a mountain. There is often a summit cross there.
18234.m: The summit is the highest point of a mountain.

18235.q: What is the big mountain range in Switzerland with very high mountains called?
18235.e: The Alps are the highest mountains in Switzerland. They cover more than half of the country.
18235.m: The Alps are the highest mountains in Switzerland.

18236.q: Which Swiss mountain is famous for its pointed shape?
18236.e: The Matterhorn near Zermatt has a very pointed shape. It is one of the best-known mountains in the world.
18236.m: The Matterhorn is famous for its pointed shape.

18237.q: What are the mountains in the north-west of Switzerland called?
18237.e: The Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland. Its mountains are lower than the Alps.
18237.m: The Jura is in the north-west of Switzerland.

18238.q: How does the temperature usually change when you climb a high mountain?
18238.e: The higher you climb, the colder the air gets. That is why there is often snow on high mountains.
18238.m: The higher you climb, the colder it gets.

18239.e: A valley is lower land between mountains. A river often flows along the bottom.
18239.m: A valley lies low between mountains.

18240.q: What often flows along the bottom of a valley?
18240.e: A river flows through many valleys. The water often helped to shape the valley itself.
18240.m: A river flows through many valleys.

18241.q: Which letter shape does a valley carved out by a glacier have?
18241.e: A glacier grinds the valley out wide. That is why it is shaped like a U.
18241.m: A glacier valley is shaped like a U.

18242.q: Which letter shape does a valley dug by a river have?
18242.e: A river digs deep and narrow into the ground. That is why the valley looks like a V.
18242.m: A river valley is shaped like a V.

18243.q: Which big river flows through Valais?
18243.e: The Rhône flows through the main valley of Valais. Then it flows into Lake Geneva.

18244.q: What is the place where a river begins called?
18244.e: At the source, water comes out of the ground. That is where a stream or river begins.
18244.m: A river begins at its source.

18245.q: What is the place called where a river flows into another river, a lake or the sea?
18245.e: The mouth is the end of a river. There it flows into another body of water.
18245.m: A river ends at its mouth.

18246.q: Which big river flows through Basel?
18246.e: The Rhine flows through Basel and on to the North Sea. Basel has an important Rhine port.

18247.q: What do you call a small river?
18247.e: A stream is a small, narrow flowing water. Several streams together can form a river.
18247.m: A small river is called a stream.

18248.q: What is the edge of a river called?
18248.e: The bank is the land right next to the water. You can go for a walk there.
18248.m: The edge of a river is called the bank.

18249.e: A lake is still water in the middle of the land. All around it is land.
18249.m: A lake is water surrounded by land.

18250.q: Which is the largest lake in Switzerland?
18250.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland. Part of it belongs to France.
18250.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in Switzerland.

18251.q: Which big lake lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria?
18251.e: Lake Constance lies in the north-east of Switzerland. Three countries border it.

18252.q: What is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland?
18252.e: Lake Neuchâtel lies completely in Switzerland. We share Lake Geneva and Lake Constance with other countries.
18252.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely in Switzerland.

18253.q: What is a small, often shallow body of still water called?
18253.e: A pond is a small body of still water. Frogs and dragonflies often live there.
18253.m: A pond is a small body of water.

18254.q: Is the water in Swiss lakes salty or fresh?
18254.e: Swiss lakes have fresh water. The water in the sea is salty.

18255.q: What is a glacier made of?
18255.e: A glacier is a huge mass of ice. It forms from snow that is pressed together over many years.
18255.m: A glacier is made of ice.

18256.q: What is the longest glacier in the Alps called?
18256.e: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the longest glacier in the Alps. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
18256.m: The Aletsch Glacier is the longest glacier in the Alps.

a: Yes, as fast as a car
18257.e: A glacier flows very slowly down the valley. You cannot see the movement with your eyes.

18258.q: What is happening to most glaciers in Switzerland at the moment?
18258.e: Because it is getting warmer, the glaciers are melting. Many have shrunk a lot in recent years.

18259.q: What are deep cracks in glacier ice called?
18259.e: Crevasses are deep cracks in the ice. They are very dangerous, so people only cross them roped together.
18259.m: Crevasses are deep cracks in the ice.

18260.q: What is the hot, liquid rock that flows out of a volcano called?
18260.e: Lava is melted rock from deep inside the Earth. It is about 800 to 1200 degrees hot.
18260.m: Lava is liquid rock from a volcano.

18261.q: What is the opening at the top of a volcano called?
18261.e: The crater is the hole at the top of the volcano. Lava and ash come out of it during an eruption.
18261.m: The crater is at the top of the volcano.

18262.q: What do you call it when a volcano throws out lava and ash?
18262.e: In an eruption, lava, ash and gases come out of the volcano. That can be very dangerous.

18263.q: Are there active volcanoes in Switzerland today?
18263.e: There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland today. Active volcanoes in Europe can be found, for example, in Italy and Iceland.
18263.m: There are no active volcanoes in Switzerland.

18264.q: Which famous volcano is on the Italian island of Sicily?
18264.e: Etna is on Sicily. It is one of the most active volcanoes in Europe.

18265.e: In an earthquake the Earth moves and the ground shakes. Strong earthquakes can damage houses.
18265.m: In an earthquake the ground shakes.

18266.q: Where is the best place to hide in a house during an earthquake?
18266.e: Under a sturdy table you are protected from things falling down. Windows and lifts are dangerous.
18266.m: In an earthquake, protect yourself under a sturdy table.

18267.q: In which canton is the risk of earthquakes highest in Switzerland?
18267.e: Valais has the highest earthquake risk in Switzerland. But most earthquakes there are so weak that you cannot feel them.
18267.m: Valais has the highest earthquake risk.

18268.q: Can you feel most earthquakes in Switzerland?
18268.e: There are many earthquakes in Switzerland every year. But most are so weak that only measuring instruments notice them.
18268.m: Most earthquakes are too weak to feel.

18269.q: Which present-day Swiss city was destroyed by a strong earthquake in 1356?
18269.e: The Basel earthquake of 1356 is the strongest known earthquake in Central Europe. Large parts of the city were destroyed.
18269.m: Basel was destroyed by an earthquake in 1356.

18270.q: At how many degrees Celsius does water freeze?
18270.e: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. Below that it stays solid.

18271.q: At how many degrees Celsius does water boil?
18271.e: Water boils at about 100 degrees Celsius. Then it turns into steam.
18271.m: Water boils at a hundred degrees.

18272.q: Why is Switzerland often called the “water tower of Europe”?
18272.e: Big rivers such as the Rhine and the Rhône start in the Swiss Alps. They flow into many countries in Europe.
18272.m: Switzerland is called the water tower of Europe.

18273.q: What covers most of the Earth’s surface?
18273.e: More than two thirds of the Earth’s surface is covered with water. Most of it is sea water.
18273.m: Most of the Earth is covered with water.

18274.q: Does ice float in water or sink?
18274.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why it floats on top, like ice cubes in a glass.

18275.q: What are the pointed sticks of ice that hang from the roof in winter called?
18275.e: When water drips from the roof and freezes, icicles grow. They hang downwards.
18275.m: Icicles hang from the roof in winter.

18276.q: What is a huge chunk of ice floating in the sea called?
18276.e: An iceberg is a big chunk of ice in the sea. Most of it is hidden under the water.
18276.m: Most of an iceberg is under the water.

18277.q: What is dangerous on a frozen lake?
18277.e: Thin ice can break. Only go onto the ice when grown-ups have said it is allowed.

18278.q: What is spread on roads in winter to make the ice melt?
18278.e: Salt makes ice melt even when it is cold. That is why municipalities spread salt on the roads in winter.
18278.m: Salt makes ice on the road melt.

18279.q: What happens when the sun warms the water in the sea?
18279.e: The sun warms the water. Some of it rises into the air as invisible water vapour.

18280.q: What forms when water vapour cools high up?
18280.e: High up in the air it is cold. The cooled vapour gathers there and clouds form.

18281.q: How does the water from the clouds get back down to Earth?
18281.e: The water falls to Earth as rain, snow or hail. Experts call this precipitation.
18281.m: Rain or snow falls from clouds.

18282.q: Where does the rainwater in streams and rivers flow in the end?
18282.e: Streams and rivers carry the water back to the sea. There the cycle starts all over again.
18282.m: Rivers carry the water back to the sea.

18283.q: Why doesn’t the Earth run out of water?
a: It moves round in a cycle
18283.e: Water evaporates, forms clouds, rains down and flows back to the sea. It is used again and again.
18283.m: Water moves round in a cycle.

18284.q: What is the water called that soaks into the ground and collects under the earth?
18284.e: Some of the rain soaks into the ground and collects as groundwater. In Switzerland, a large part of the drinking water comes from groundwater.

18285.q: Into how many main layers is the Earth divided according to its chemical make-up?
18285.e: We distinguish the crust, the mantle and the core. These layers differ in their materials and their density.
18285.m: The Earth is made up of crust, mantle and core.

18286.q: Which layer makes up most of the Earth’s volume?
18286.e: The mantle makes up around four fifths of the Earth’s volume. Compared with it, the crust is only a thin skin.
18286.m: The mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth.

18287.q: Roughly what is the radius of the Earth?
18287.e: The mean radius of the Earth is about 6371 km. The diameter is twice as big, around 12,740 km.
18287.m: From the centre of the Earth to the surface is about 6370 kilometres.

18288.q: How did scientists mainly find out about the inner structure of the Earth?
a: With deep boreholes down to the core
18288.e: Earthquake waves are bent and refracted at the boundaries between the layers. Their travel times can be used to work out the structure.
18288.m: Earthquake waves tell us how the inside of the Earth is built.

18289.q: What does the lithosphere consist of?
a: The crust and the uppermost mantle
18289.e: The lithosphere is the solid, rigid outer shell of the Earth. It includes the crust and the top part of the mantle and is broken into plates.
18289.m: The lithosphere is the rigid rocky shell of the Earth.

18290.q: What is the soft, slowly flowing layer in the upper mantle on which the plates slide called?
18290.e: The asthenosphere lies below the lithosphere and can partly be deformed slightly. The lithospheric plates can move slowly on top of it.
18290.m: The Earth’s plates slide on the asthenosphere.

18291.q: Roughly how thick is the oceanic crust?
18291.e: The oceanic crust beneath the seas is thin and consists mainly of basalt. The continental crust is much thicker.
18291.m: The Earth’s crust is thinnest beneath the oceans.

18292.q: Where is the Earth’s crust thickest?
18292.e: Beneath mountain ranges such as the Alps or the Himalayas, the crust reaches deep down like a root. There it can be 60 to 70 km thick.
18292.m: The crust is especially thick beneath big mountain ranges.

18293.q: Which chemical element is the most common in the Earth’s crust?
18293.e: Almost half the mass of the Earth’s crust is oxygen. It is bound up in rocks, for example in quartz and feldspar.
18293.m: The most common element in the Earth’s crust is oxygen.

18294.q: Which metal is the most common in the Earth’s crust?
18294.e: Aluminium makes up around 8 per cent of the Earth’s crust. But it never occurs pure, only bound up in minerals.
18294.m: Aluminium is the most common metal in the Earth’s crust.

18295.q: What are the three main layers of the Earth called, from the outside in?
18295.e: On the outside is the thin crust, below it the thick mantle. Right in the middle is the core of iron and nickel.
18295.m: The Earth consists of crust, mantle and core.

18296.q: Roughly how deep does the mantle go?
18296.e: The mantle begins beneath the crust and reaches down to a depth of around 2900 km. That is where the outer core begins.
18296.m: The mantle is almost 3000 kilometres thick.

18297.q: What lies directly beneath the Earth’s crust?
18297.e: Beneath the crust the mantle begins. It is made of dark, heavy rock and reaches down to around 2900 km.
18297.m: The mantle lies beneath the Earth’s crust.

18298.q: What makes the rock in the mantle move very slowly?
18298.e: Hot rock rises slowly and cooler rock sinks. This convection also drives the movement of the Earth’s plates.
18298.m: Heat currents in the mantle move the Earth’s plates.

18299.q: What state is most of the mantle in?
18299.e: The mantle is solid almost everywhere. But over millions of years it can bend and flow like a very thick, sticky mass.
18299.m: The mantle is solid, but flows very slowly over long periods.

18300.q: What changes at the boundary between the mantle and the core?
a: Rock gives way to liquid metal
18300.e: At a depth of about 2900 km, the solid rocky mantle ends. Below it lies the outer core of liquid iron and nickel.
18300.m: Beneath the rocky mantle begins the metal core.

18301.q: Which metals is the Earth’s core mainly made of?
18301.e: The Earth’s core consists mainly of iron with some nickel. That is why it is much denser than the other layers.
18301.m: The Earth’s core is mainly iron and nickel.

18302.q: Roughly how much of the Earth’s total mass is the core?
18302.e: The core has only about 16 per cent of the Earth’s volume, but around 32 per cent of its mass. This is because of its very high density of iron and nickel.
18302.m: The small core is very heavy and holds about a third of the Earth’s mass.

18303.q: Why is the inner core solid despite the great heat?
a: Because it is made of ice
Because it is colder than the surface
18303.e: There is huge pressure at the centre of the Earth. It squeezes the iron so hard that it cannot melt.
18303.m: The huge pressure keeps the inner core solid.

18304.q: Roughly how hot is it in the Earth’s core?
18304.e: The inner core is estimated to reach about 5000 to 6000 °C. That is roughly as hot as the surface of the sun.
18304.m: The Earth’s core is about as hot as the sun’s surface.

18305.q: What produces the Earth’s magnetic field?
a: Currents in the liquid outer core
18305.e: In the outer core, liquid iron flows and produces electric currents. This geodynamo builds up the Earth’s magnetic field, which a compass lines up with.
18305.m: The Earth’s magnetic field is produced in the liquid outer core.

a: Lava cools quickly in the sea
18306.e: Granite is a plutonic rock. Because the magma cools slowly, clearly visible crystals form.
18306.m: Granite is magma that solidified slowly deep down.

18307.q: Which group of rocks does limestone belong to?
18307.e: Limestone usually forms from the deposited shells and skeletons of sea creatures. Such rocks made of deposits are called sedimentary rocks.
18307.m: Limestone is a sedimentary rock from the sea.

a: From limestone through pressure and heat
18308.e: If limestone is strongly heated and squeezed deep in the Earth, it recrystallises. This forms the metamorphic rock marble.

a: Lava solidifies quickly at the surface
18309.e: Basalt is a dark volcanic rock. Because the lava cools quickly, its crystals are very small.
18309.m: Basalt is lava that solidified quickly.

18310.q: Which rock is the Rigi mostly made of?
18310.e: Nagelfluh is a sedimentary rock of rounded river pebbles held together by a natural cement. It formed from rubble worn away from the young Alps.
18310.m: The Rigi is made mainly of Nagelfluh.

18311.q: Which group of rocks does gneiss belong to?
18311.e: Gneiss forms when rocks such as granite are changed under high pressure and high temperature. It is common in the Alps.

18312.q: Which mineral is the hardest on the Mohs scale?
18312.e: The Mohs scale ranks minerals from 1 to 10 by how hard they are to scratch. Diamond has hardness 10 and scratches all the others.
18312.m: Diamond is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale.

18313.q: Which mineral is the softest on the Mohs scale?
18313.e: Talc has hardness 1 and can be scratched with a fingernail. It feels soapy.
18313.m: Talc is the softest mineral on the Mohs scale.

18314.q: Rock crystal is a see-through form of which mineral?
18314.e: Rock crystal is pure, clear quartz. In the Swiss Alps, crystal hunters search for such crystals in rock clefts.

18315.q: What is the mineral that table salt is made of called?
18315.e: Halite is sodium chloride and is also called rock salt. In Switzerland, salt is obtained, for example, at Bex and on the Rhine near Basel.
18315.m: Table salt is made of the mineral halite.

18316.q: Which three minerals together make up granite?
18316.e: An old German rhyme says that feldspar, quartz and mica are three you will never forget. You can see these minerals as grains in granite.
18316.m: Granite is made of feldspar, quartz and mica.

18317.q: In which type of rock are fossils found most often?
a: In plutonic rocks such as granite
18317.e: Living things get buried in mud or sand that later turns into rock. Heat and melting, on the other hand, would destroy them.
18317.m: Fossils are found mainly in sedimentary rocks.

a: Sea creatures with a spiral shell
18318.e: Ammonites were cephalopods, related to today’s squid. They died out about 66 million years ago, together with the dinosaurs.
18318.m: Ammonites were cephalopods with snail-like shells.

18319.q: Which mountain in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils?
18319.e: Exceptionally well-preserved fish and marine reptiles from the Triassic were found on Monte San Giorgio. It has been a World Heritage Site since 2003.
18319.m: Monte San Giorgio is a famous fossil site.

18320.q: What is the science that studies fossils called?
18320.e: Palaeontology studies living things from past ages of the Earth using fossils. Archaeology, by contrast, studies human history.

18321.q: What do you call melted rock while it is still below the Earth’s surface?
18321.e: Underground, melted rock is called magma. Only when it comes out at the surface is it called lava.
18321.m: Underground the melt is called magma; above ground it is called lava.

18322.q: What is the belt of many volcanoes around the Pacific called?
18322.e: Many of the Earth’s plates collide around the Pacific. That is why there are so many volcanoes and earthquakes there.
18322.m: Most of the world’s volcanoes lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire.

18323.q: Which volcano buried the city of Pompeii in AD 79?
18323.e: Vesuvius near Naples buried Pompeii under ash and pumice. As a result, the ancient city has stayed well preserved to this day.

a: A glowing avalanche of gas and ash
18324.e: A pyroclastic flow races down the side of a volcano at over 100 km/h. It is several hundred degrees hot and therefore extremely dangerous.
18324.m: Pyroclastic flows are among the most dangerous effects of an eruption.

18325.q: Which type of volcano has gentle slopes made of runny lava, as in Hawaii?
18325.e: Runny lava flows a long way and forms broad, flat cones. They are called shield volcanoes because they look like a shield lying down.
18325.m: Shield volcanoes are made of runny lava.

18326.q: Which volcano on Sicily is one of the most active volcanoes in Europe?
18326.e: Etna erupts very often and is over 3300 m high. It is the highest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus.
18326.m: Etna on Sicily is a very active volcano.

18327.q: Which instrument is used to measure earthquakes?
18327.e: A seismograph records the movements of the ground. The recordings can be used to work out the strength and location of the earthquake.

18328.q: What is the point on the Earth’s surface directly above the source of an earthquake called?
18328.e: The actual source inside the Earth is called the hypocentre. The point directly above it on the surface is called the epicentre.
18328.m: The epicentre is on the surface above the source of the earthquake.

18330.q: Which body monitors earthquakes in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich
18330.e: The Swiss Seismological Service runs a network of measuring stations across the whole country. It gives information about earthquakes and assesses earthquake risk.
18330.m: The Seismological Service at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes in Switzerland.

18331.q: What does it mean if an earthquake has a magnitude 1 higher?
a: It releases many times more energy
It lasts exactly one minute longer
Its source is one kilometre deeper
It releases exactly the same energy
18331.e: The magnitude scale is built so that each step means many times more energy. So one step higher is a much stronger earthquake.
18331.m: One magnitude higher means many times more energy.

18332.q: What is the most common cause of earthquakes?
a: Stresses between moving plates of the Earth
18332.e: Plates get stuck and build up stress. When the stress is suddenly released, the Earth shakes.
18332.m: Most earthquakes happen at plate boundaries.

18333.q: What does the Japanese word “tsunami” mean?
18333.e: Fishermen out at sea hardly noticed the wave, but in the harbour it caused great damage. Hence the name harbour wave.

18334.q: What most often causes a tsunami?
18334.e: In an undersea earthquake, the sea floor suddenly rises or sinks. This sets the whole column of water above it moving.
18334.m: Most tsunamis are caused by undersea earthquakes.

18335.q: In which ocean did the devastating tsunami of 26 December 2004 happen?
18335.e: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra set off huge waves. They hit many coasts around the Indian Ocean and killed a great many people.
18335.m: The 2004 tsunami hit the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

18336.q: Which warning sign can appear on the coast shortly before a tsunami?
a: The sea suddenly pulls back a long way
The waves become very small and regular
18336.e: Often the trough of the wave reaches the coast first and the water draws back. Then you should flee to higher ground at once.
18336.m: If the sea suddenly pulls back, get away from the beach at once.

18337.q: How fast can a tsunami travel in the deep ocean?
a: About as fast as an aeroplane
About as fast as a bicycle
About as fast as a person walking
About as fast as a rowing boat
18337.e: In deep water, a tsunami reaches up to around 800 km/h. Only at the coast does it slow down, and then it becomes much higher.
18337.m: Out in the open sea, a tsunami is extremely fast.

18338.q: On which Swiss lake did a rockfall set off a tsunami in the year 563?
18338.e: In the Tauredunum event, a mountainside collapsed at the upper end of Lake Geneva. The flood wave also reached the city of Geneva after about an hour.
18338.m: Lakes can be hit by a tsunami too.

18339.q: What is the region in the USA where especially many tornadoes occur called?
18339.e: On the Great Plains, warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico meets cold, dry air. That is why there are very many tornadoes there.
18339.m: There are especially many tornadoes in Tornado Alley.

18340.q: Which scale is used to give the strength of tornadoes?
18340.e: The Fujita scale estimates the wind speed from the damage done. It runs from F0 to F5.
18340.m: Tornadoes are rated on the Fujita scale.

18341.q: Which type of cloud do tornadoes form from?
18341.e: Tornadoes usually form from huge thunderclouds, called cumulonimbus. Rotating thunderstorms, known as supercells, are especially dangerous.

18342.q: What do you call a tornado over a lake or the sea?
18342.e: Over water, the whirl sucks up spray and droplets and so becomes visible. Waterspouts occasionally occur on Swiss lakes too.
18342.m: A tornado over water is called a waterspout.

18343.e: Hurricanes need sea water of at least about 26 °C. Evaporation gives them their energy.
18343.m: Hurricanes get their energy from warm sea water.

18344.q: What is the calm centre of a hurricane called?
18344.e: In the eye there is almost no wind and often no clouds. All around it, the strongest winds rage in the eyewall.
18344.m: It is calm in the eye of a hurricane.

18345.q: What is a tropical cyclone in the western Pacific called?
18345.e: Tropical cyclones have different names in different regions. In the Atlantic they are called hurricanes, in the Indian Ocean cyclones.
18345.m: In the western Pacific, these storms are called typhoons.

18346.q: Apart from strong wind, what does a hurricane often bring to the coast?
18346.e: The storm pushes sea water against the coast. The water level rises sharply and floods low-lying areas.
18346.m: Hurricanes often cause storm surges on coasts.

18347.q: From what wind speed is a storm called a hurricane?
18347.e: A tropical cyclone becomes a hurricane at hurricane force, which is about 119 km/h. Below that it is called a tropical storm.
18347.m: A hurricane has at least hurricane-force winds.

18348.q: What is built along rivers to protect villages from floods?
18348.e: Embankments are walls of earth along the bank. During a flood they keep the water in the riverbed so that it does not flow into the villages.

18349.q: Which kind of weather most often leads to floods in Switzerland?
18349.e: When it rains heavily for days, the ground and rivers can no longer take in the water. If snow is melting as well, the water levels rise even faster.
18349.m: Constant rain can make rivers burst their banks.

18350.q: Why do tarmac and concrete surfaces make a flood worse?
a: They warm up the river water
18350.e: On sealed ground, the water runs straight off into streams and drains. So the water levels rise faster and higher.
18350.m: Sealed ground makes water run off quickly.

18351.q: Which measure gives a river more space again and so protects against floods?
a: Restoring the river to a natural state
18351.e: When a river is restored, it gets wider banks and areas that can flood. The water can spread out there during a flood.
18351.m: Rivers with more space can cope better with floods.

18352.q: Which big project from the 19th century was meant to protect the Seeland from flooding?
18352.e: In the Jura water correction, the Aare was diverted into Lake Biel and the lakes were lowered. This drained the Seeland and made it usable.
18352.m: The Jura water correction protects the Seeland from floods.

18353.q: Which institute publishes the avalanche bulletin in Switzerland?
18353.e: The WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos assesses the avalanche danger every day. In winter the bulletin is available for the whole of Switzerland.
18353.m: The SLF in Davos warns about avalanches.

18354.q: How many danger levels does the European avalanche danger scale have?
18354.e: The scale runs from level 1 “low” to level 5 “very high”. Many accidents already happen at level 3 “considerable”.
18354.m: Avalanche danger is given in five levels.

18355.q: From what slope angle do slab avalanches usually break away?
18355.e: Most slab avalanches break away on slopes of 30 degrees or steeper. That is why ski tourers measure the slope angle on the map.
18355.m: Steep slopes from about 30 degrees are at risk of avalanches.

18356.q: Which device helps to locate people buried in an avalanche?
18356.e: The avalanche transceiver sends and receives radio signals. With it, companions can quickly find a buried person.
18356.m: An avalanche transceiver helps find buried people faster.

18357.q: What protects villages in the Alps from avalanches in a natural way?
18357.e: Trees hold the snow cover in place and stop avalanches breaking away. In Switzerland, about half of the forest is protection forest.

a: Snow turns into firn over years and then into ice
18358.e: New snow is pressed together by new layers. Over several years it becomes grainy firn and finally dense glacier ice.
18358.m: Glacier ice forms from snow pressed together.

18359.q: What is the rubble that a glacier carries along and leaves behind called?
18359.e: Glaciers push stones, gravel and sand in front of them and along their sides. These deposits are called moraines and remain as hills after the ice melts.
18359.m: Moraines are ridges of rubble left by glaciers.

18360.q: Which valley shape do glaciers leave behind?
18360.e: The ice planes the valley out wide, creating steep sides with a flat floor. Rivers, by contrast, cut V-shaped valleys.

a: The wearing away of soil and rock
18361.e: Water, wind and ice wear away soil and bits of rock and carry them off. This process is called erosion.
18361.m: Erosion wears away soil and rock.

18362.q: What is the weathering called in which water freezes in cracks in the rock and breaks it apart?
18362.e: Water expands by about 9 per cent when it freezes. This forces cracks in the rock further and further apart.
18362.m: Freezing water can break rocks apart.

18363.q: Which river carved out the Grand Canyon?
18363.e: Over millions of years, the Colorado River dug deep into the rock. This created a canyon up to 1800 m deep.
18363.m: Over a long time, rivers can dig deep gorges.

18364.q: What best protects the soil from erosion by rain and wind?
a: A slope with the trees cut down
18364.e: Roots hold the soil in place, and leaves slow down the raindrops. On bare ground, by contrast, a lot of soil is washed away.
18364.m: Plants hold the soil in place.

18365.q: How did the earth pyramids of Euseigne in Valais form?
a: Through erosion, with a capstone protecting each pillar
18365.e: Rain washed away the soft moraine rubble. Where a big stone lay on top, a pillar was left standing beneath it.
18365.m: Earth pyramids form when a capstone protects the ground from rain.

18366.q: Which federal office is responsible for weather forecasts in Switzerland?
a: The Federal Office for the Environment
The Swiss Federal Office of Energy
18366.e: MeteoSwiss is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology. It makes forecasts and issues severe weather warnings.
18366.m: MeteoSwiss makes Switzerland’s official weather forecast.

18367.e: A barometer shows the air pressure. If the pressure falls, the weather may get worse.
18367.m: Air pressure is measured with a barometer.

18368.q: What weather does an area of high pressure usually bring?
18368.e: In a high, the air sinks and warms up. As it does, clouds usually disappear.
18368.m: An area of high pressure usually brings fine weather.

18369.q: What are today’s weather forecasts mainly worked out with?
18369.e: Supercomputers use the equations of physics to calculate how the atmosphere will develop. They use measurements from stations, balloons and satellites.
18369.m: Weather forecasts are worked out with computer models.

18370.q: Why do weather forecasts become uncertain for more than about a week ahead?
a: Because small measurement errors in the atmosphere grow a lot
Because satellites only work for a week
Because the weather never repeats itself
Because there are too few weather stations
18370.e: The atmosphere is a chaotic system. Small differences at the start lead to completely different results after a few days.
18370.m: The further ahead a forecast reaches, the less certain it becomes.

18371.q: Over at least how many years is the weather averaged to describe the climate?
18371.e: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at one short moment. Climate describes the average weather over at least 30 years.
18371.m: Climate is the weather averaged over many years.

18372.q: Which ocean current gives western Europe a milder climate?
18372.e: The Gulf Stream and its continuation, the North Atlantic Current, carry warm water from the Caribbean to Europe. That is why winters here are milder than in Canada at the same latitude.
18372.m: The Gulf Stream works like a hot-water heater for Europe.

18373.q: Roughly how much does the temperature drop when you climb 100 metres higher?
18373.e: In the air, the temperature falls on average by about 0.6 °C every 100 metres of height. Over a height difference of 1000 m, that is about 6 °C.
18373.m: In the mountains, it gets cooler the higher you climb.

18374.q: How much has Switzerland warmed since pre-industrial times compared with the world average (as of 2024)?
18374.e: According to MeteoSwiss, Switzerland is now about 2.9 °C warmer than in 1871 to 1900, while the world is about 1.3 °C warmer. Land areas warm faster than oceans.
18374.m: Switzerland is warming faster than the world average.

18375.q: Which greenhouse gas do humans release in the largest amount?
18375.e: Carbon dioxide, or CO2, comes mainly from burning coal, oil and natural gas. It is the most important driver of human-made warming.
18375.m: CO2 is the most important greenhouse gas caused by humans.

18376.q: On average, how cold would the Earth be without the natural greenhouse effect?
18376.e: Today the average temperature at the Earth’s surface is about +15 °C. Without greenhouse gases it would be about 33 °C lower, so about −18 °C.
18376.m: The natural greenhouse effect makes the Earth fit to live on.

18377.q: Which greenhouse gas is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows?
18377.e: Cattle give off methane as they digest. Molecule for molecule, methane is much stronger than CO2, but it stays in the air for a shorter time.
18377.m: Cows give off methane as they digest.

18378.q: How do greenhouse gases work in the atmosphere?
a: They hold back heat radiated by the Earth
18378.e: Sunlight warms the ground, which gives off heat radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb some of this radiation and send it back to Earth.
18378.m: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

18379.q: What goal does the 2015 Paris climate agreement set?
a: To get rid of the greenhouse effect completely
To halve the number of cars
18379.e: Almost every country in the world, including Switzerland, has signed the agreement. It even aims to limit warming to 1.5 °C.
18379.m: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming.

19040.q: At how many degrees does water boil at sea level?
19040.e: At sea level, pure water starts to boil at 100 degrees Celsius. High up in the mountains it boils at a little less than 100 degrees.
19040.m: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees.

19041.q: What colour is clean water in a glass?
19041.e: Clean water is clear and see-through. You can look through a glass of water.
19041.m: Clean water is clear and see-through.

19042.q: What does clean drinking water smell of?
19042.e: Pure water has no smell and no taste. If water smells strange, you should not drink it.

19043.q: Where does most of the drinking water in Switzerland come from?
19043.e: In Switzerland, about 80 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
19043.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.

19044.q: What happens to a puddle on a hot day?
19044.e: The sun warms the water, and it slowly goes into the air as invisible vapour. That is how the puddle disappears.
19044.m: Puddles dry up in the sun.

19045.q: What is water like at room temperature?
19045.e: At room temperature water is liquid. You can pour it and drink it.
19045.m: At room temperature water is liquid.

19046.q: Where on Earth is there the most water?
19046.e: Almost all the water on Earth is salt water in the seas. Fresh water in rivers and lakes is only a small part.
19046.m: Most of the Earth’s water is in the seas.

19047.q: What do we call water that falls from the clouds?
19047.e: When the droplets in a cloud get too heavy, they fall down. That is rain.
19047.m: Rain is water that falls from clouds.

19048.e: Air is see-through and has no colour. But you can feel it, for example as wind.
19048.m: Air is invisible, but you can feel it.

19049.q: What is inside a blown-up balloon?
19049.e: When you blow up a balloon, you blow air into it. The air pushes the skin of the balloon outwards.
19049.m: A blown-up balloon is filled with air.

19050.q: Which part of the air do we need to breathe?
19050.e: Our body needs the oxygen in the air. We breathe it in with every breath.
19050.m: We need oxygen from the air to breathe.

19051.q: What is air mostly made of?
19051.e: About four fifths of air is nitrogen. The rest is mainly other gases.
19051.m: Air is mostly made of nitrogen.

19052.q: What happens if you push an empty glass upside down into water?
19052.e: There is air in the “empty” glass. It takes up space and does not let all the water in.
19052.m: Air takes up space, even though you cannot see it.

19053.q: Where does the air get thinner?
19053.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is. That is why mountaineers find it harder to breathe on high peaks.
19053.m: The air is thinner high up in the mountains.

19054.q: What does a fire need to burn?
19054.e: A fire needs something that can burn, oxygen from the air and enough heat. If one of these is missing, it goes out.
19054.m: Fire needs fuel, air and heat.

19055.q: What happens to a candle if you put a glass over it?
19055.e: Under the glass, the oxygen runs out. Without enough oxygen, the flame goes out.
19055.m: Without fresh air a flame goes out.

19056.q: What is left when wood has burnt completely?
19056.e: When wood burns, most of it turns into gas and smoke. Grey ash is left behind.
19056.m: Ash is left over from burnt wood.

19057.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland if there is a fire?
19057.e: In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118. 117 is the police and 144 is the ambulance.
19057.m: In Switzerland the fire brigade’s number is 118.

19058.q: What does a fire give off?
19058.e: A flame shines and is hot. That is why people like sitting round a campfire.
19058.m: Fire gives off light and warmth.

19059.q: What happens when wet wood burns?
19059.e: Wet wood burns badly and makes lots of smoke. Dry wood burns better.
19059.m: Wet wood makes lots of smoke when it burns.

19060.q: Who is allowed to light a fire?
a: Only adults, or children with them
Little brothers and sisters on their own
19060.e: Fire is dangerous and can spread quickly. Children only light fires together with adults.
19060.m: Children only light fires with adults.

19061.e: When water gets very cold, it becomes solid. We call this solid water ice.

19062.q: Does an ice cube float in water or sink?
19062.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why it floats on top.

19063.e: Ice is solid and therefore hard. It cools everything it touches.

19064.q: What is glacier ice made from?
19064.e: Lots of snow is pressed together over many years. This turns it into solid glacier ice.
19064.m: Glacier ice is made from snow that has been pressed together.

19065.q: Why is a frozen lake dangerous?
19065.e: Thin ice cannot hold a person’s weight. You may only go onto ice that has been declared safe.
19065.m: Only go onto a frozen lake when the ice has been declared safe.

19066.q: Where do you put water to make ice cubes?
19066.e: In the freezer it is much colder than 0 degrees. The water turns to ice there.
19066.m: You make ice cubes in the freezer.

19067.q: What rises from a saucepan of boiling water?
19067.e: Boiling water turns into water vapour. The white clouds above it are tiny droplets of water.

19068.q: Why do you have to be careful with steam?
19068.e: Steam from boiling water is very hot. It can scald your skin.
19068.m: Hot steam can scald your skin.

19069.q: What happens to steam on a cold mirror in the bathroom?
19069.e: The steam cools down on the cold mirror. It turns back into little drops of water, and the mirror steams up.
19069.m: Steam turns back into water on cold surfaces.

19070.e: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They form when moist air cools down.
19070.m: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets.

19071.q: What do you see in winter when you breathe out outside?
19071.e: Our breath contains water vapour. In the cold air it turns into tiny droplets, which you see as a white cloud.
19071.m: In winter you can see your breath as a little cloud.

19072.q: Where does the steam go when you cook?
19072.e: Warm steam is lighter than the cool air. That is why it rises.

19073.q: What forms when steam collects on the saucepan lid?
19073.e: The lid is cooler than the steam. So the steam turns back into water there and drips down.
19073.m: On the lid, steam turns back into drops of water.

19074.q: Which of these is a solid?
19074.e: A stone has a fixed shape and stays the way it is. Milk, juice and air are not solid.

19075.q: What is typical of a solid?
19075.e: Solids have their own shape. A wooden block stays a block, whatever box it is in.

19076.q: Which of these objects is solid?
19076.e: Wood is a solid. Soup and syrup are liquid, and fog is made of air and droplets.

19077.e: Sand can trickle, but every single grain is solid. That is why sand counts as a solid.
19077.m: Every grain of sand is solid.

19078.q: Which solid is hard and see-through?
19078.e: Window panes are made of glass. Glass is solid and hard, and you can see through it.
19078.m: Glass is a solid that is see-through.

19079.q: Which of these is a solid?
19079.e: Cold chocolate is hard and keeps its shape. Tea and juice are liquid, and steam is a gas.

19080.q: Can you hold a solid in your hand?
19080.e: You can hold solids because they do not flow away. A cube stays a cube in your hand.
19080.m: You can hold solids in your hand.

19081.q: Which of these is a liquid?
19081.e: You can pour milk, and it flows. Wood, stone and glass are solid.

19082.q: What shape is water in a bottle?
19082.e: Liquids do not have their own shape. They take the shape of the container they are in.
19082.m: Liquids take the shape of their container.

19083.q: What can you do with a liquid?
19083.e: Liquids flow. That is why you can pour them from one glass into another.

19084.q: Which of these flows most slowly?
19084.e: Honey is thick. It flows much more slowly than water, juice or milk.
19084.m: Honey is thick and flows slowly.

19085.q: What is the surface of water like in a glass that is standing still?
19085.e: Still water forms a flat, level surface at the top. This is true of all liquids.
19085.m: Still water has a flat surface on top.

19086.q: What happens if you spill water on the table?
19086.e: Water has no fixed shape. On the table it flows apart and forms a puddle.

19087.q: Which oil do you often find in the kitchen?
19087.e: In the kitchen you use cooking oil for frying and for salad. It is a liquid.
19087.m: Cooking oil is a liquid from the kitchen.

19088.q: Which of these is a gas?
19088.e: Air is a gas. It is invisible and spreads out everywhere in a room.

19089.q: What does a gas do in a room?
19089.e: Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume. They spread out through the whole room.
19089.m: Gases spread out through the whole room.

19090.q: How can you tell that there is a gas in the room that you cannot see?
19090.e: Many gases are invisible. But some have a smell, for example the scent of freshly baked bread.

19091.q: Which gas makes a balloon so light that it floats upwards?
19091.e: Helium is lighter than air. That is why a helium balloon rises.
19091.m: A helium balloon rises because helium is lighter than air.

19092.q: What are the bubbles in sparkling mineral water?
19092.e: The bubbles in sparkling mineral water are a gas, usually carbon dioxide. It rises to the top and tingles in your mouth.
19092.m: The bubbles in sparkling water are a gas.

19093.q: Which gas do people breathe out much more of than they breathe in?
19093.e: The body makes carbon dioxide and gets rid of it when we breathe out. Plants take the carbon dioxide in again.
19093.m: People breathe out a lot of carbon dioxide.

19094.e: Gases are easy to squash. That is how you can pump a lot of air into a bicycle tyre.

19095.q: What happens to an ice cube in your warm hand?
19095.e: The warmth of your hand turns the ice back into water. This process is called melting.

a: Both melt at the same speed
19096.e: A small ice cube has less ice that needs to melt. That is why it is gone sooner.
19096.m: Small pieces of ice melt faster than big ones.

19097.q: What happens to butter in a hot frying pan?
19097.e: The heat of the pan makes the butter melt. Solid butter becomes liquid butter.
19097.m: Butter melts in a hot pan.

19098.q: When something melts, what does a solid become?
19098.e: When it melts, a solid becomes liquid. This needs warmth.
19098.m: When a solid melts, it becomes liquid.

19099.q: What happens to the snow in the mountains in spring?
19099.e: In spring it gets warmer, and the snow melts. The water then flows into streams and rivers.

19100.q: What happens to a candle when it burns?
19100.e: The flame is hot and makes the wax melt. Liquid wax collects around the wick.
19100.m: When a candle burns, the wax melts.

19101.q: At what temperature does water freeze?
19101.e: Pure water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. Below that, it stays solid.

19102.q: What happens to water when it freezes?
19102.e: When it freezes, liquid water becomes solid. It turns to ice.
19102.m: When water freezes, it becomes solid.

19103.q: Why should you not put a full glass bottle in the freezer?
19103.e: Water expands when it freezes and needs more space. The bottle can then crack.
19103.m: Water needs more space as ice.

19104.q: When does a pond freeze over?
a: When it is very cold for a long time
When it is calm and warm
19104.e: If it stays below 0 degrees for many days, the surface of the pond freezes. Underneath there is often still water.
19104.m: A pond freezes over when it is cold for a long time.

19105.q: What do you get if you put syrup in a mould in the freezer?
19105.e: In the freezer, syrup freezes into a solid stick. This makes a simple ice lolly.
19105.m: Frozen syrup becomes an ice lolly.

19106.q: When a lake freezes over, where does the water freeze first?
a: At the top, on the surface
19106.e: The cold air cools the lake from above. That is why ice forms first on the surface.
19106.m: A lake freezes from the top down.

19107.q: What are the fine ice crystals on the grass on cold mornings called?
19107.e: When it is freezing, water vapour from the air turns straight into fine ice crystals on grass and leaves. This is called frost.
19107.m: Frost is made of fine ice crystals.

19108.q: What happens to water when it boils for a long time?
19108.e: When water boils, it turns into steam and goes into the air. That is why there is less and less of it in the pan.

19109.q: Why does washing dry on the line?
a: The wind takes the fabric away
19109.e: The water in the washing slowly goes into the air as vapour. This is called evaporation.
19109.m: Wet washing dries because the water evaporates.

a: When it is warm and windy
When it is cold and foggy
19110.e: Warmth and wind help the water to evaporate. That is why washing dries quickly on warm, windy days.
19110.m: Warmth and wind make washing dry quickly.

19111.q: What is left when salt water in a bowl evaporates?
19111.e: Only the water evaporates. The salt stays behind as a white crust in the bowl.
19111.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

19112.q: When a liquid evaporates, what does it become?
19112.e: When it evaporates, a liquid becomes a gas. This needs warmth.
19112.m: When a liquid evaporates, it becomes a gas.

19113.q: Why does sweat cool the body?
19113.e: When sweat evaporates on the skin, it takes warmth with it. That is how the body cools down.

19114.q: Where does the water go when a puddle evaporates?
19114.e: The water turns into invisible water vapour and mixes with the air. Later it can come back as rain.
19114.m: Evaporated water goes into the air.

19115.q: What do you get if you pour sand and stones together?
19115.e: The sand and stones just lie jumbled together. You can separate them again, so it is a mixture.
19115.m: Sand and stones together make a mixture.

19116.q: What happens if you mix oil and water and wait?
a: The oil sinks to the bottom
19116.e: Oil and water do not mix well. The lighter oil collects on top.

19117.q: What do you use to separate pasta from the cooking water?
19117.e: The water runs through the holes in the sieve. The pasta stays inside.
19117.m: You use a sieve to separate pasta from water.

19118.q: What can you use to get iron nails out of sand?
19118.e: A magnet attracts iron, but not sand. So you can pull the nails out.

19119.e: In muesli, flakes, nuts and fruit are mixed together. You can still see the separate parts.
19119.m: Muesli is a mixture of many ingredients.

19120.q: What happens if you mix blue and yellow paint?
19120.e: When you paint with watercolours, blue and yellow together make green.
19120.m: Blue and yellow together make green.

19121.q: What is the easiest way to separate peas and rice?
19121.e: The peas are bigger than the grains of rice. A suitable sieve lets the rice through and keeps the peas back.
19121.m: A sieve separates big and small grains.

19122.q: What happens to sugar in warm tea when you stir it?
19122.e: The sugar spreads out in the tea in tiny particles. You can no longer see it, but you can taste it.

19123.q: Does sugar dissolve faster in warm or in cold water?
19123.e: In warm water the particles move faster. That is why the sugar dissolves faster.
19123.m: Sugar dissolves faster in warm water.

19124.q: Which substance does NOT dissolve in water?
19124.e: Sand stays in the water and sinks to the bottom. Salt, sugar and syrup dissolve.
19124.m: Sand does not dissolve in water.

19125.q: How can you tell that salt is dissolved in water, even though you cannot see it?
19125.e: Dissolved salt is invisible. But you can tell it is there by the taste.
19125.m: You can taste dissolved salt, even if you cannot see it.

19126.q: What helps sugar to dissolve faster?
19126.e: When you stir, the sugar keeps meeting fresh water. That makes it dissolve faster.

19127.q: What happens to a fizzy tablet in water?
19127.e: The tablet dissolves and makes gas bubbles as it does so. That is why the water fizzes.
19127.m: A fizzy tablet fizzes as it dissolves in water.

19128.q: Why does sea water taste salty?
19128.e: There is a lot of salt dissolved in sea water. That is why you cannot drink it.
19128.m: Salt is dissolved in sea water.

19129.q: What do you do in an experiment?
a: You try something out and watch
19129.e: In an experiment you test an idea. Then you look closely at what happens.
19129.m: In an experiment you try things out and watch closely.

19130.q: What should you do before an experiment?
19130.e: Before you start, you think about what will probably happen. Afterwards you compare your guess with the result.
19130.m: Before an experiment you write down a guess.

19131.q: What happens if you pour vinegar onto baking powder?
19131.e: Vinegar and baking powder react with each other. A gas forms, and it foams.
19131.m: Vinegar and baking powder foam up together.

19132.q: What does a raw egg do in very salty water?
19132.e: In tap water a raw egg sinks. If you dissolve a lot of salt in the water, the water becomes heavier and the egg floats.
19132.m: An egg floats in very salty water.

19133.q: What must you never do in an experiment without asking?
19133.e: Some substances are not meant to be eaten. That is why you never taste anything in experiments without permission.
19133.m: In experiments, never eat anything without permission.

19134.q: What happens to a jelly bear left in water overnight?
19134.e: The jelly bear soaks up water. That is why it is much bigger and softer in the morning.
19134.m: A jelly bear gets bigger in water.

19135.q: What happens to a paper clip that you place very carefully on water?
19135.e: The surface of the water acts like a thin skin. A light paper clip can stay lying on it.
19135.m: Water has a surface like a thin skin.

19136.q: What happens if you mix red cabbage juice with vinegar?
19136.e: Red cabbage juice changes colour. With vinegar it turns reddish, with soapy water more green or blue.
19136.m: Red cabbage juice turns red with vinegar.

19137.q: Which three kinds of particles is an atom made of?
19137.e: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. The electrons move around the nucleus in the electron shell.
19137.m: An atom is made of protons, neutrons and electrons.

19138.q: What electric charge does a proton have?
19138.e: Protons are positively charged and sit in the nucleus. Their charge is the same size as an electron’s, but with the opposite sign.

19139.q: Where are the electrons of an atom?
19139.e: The electrons move in the shell around the tiny nucleus. The shell is much bigger than the nucleus.
19139.m: Electrons move in the shell around the nucleus.

19140.q: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
a: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of neutrons in the nucleus
The number of atoms in the molecule
19140.e: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. It decides which element it is.
19140.m: The atomic number counts the protons in the nucleus.

19141.q: What do we call an atom that has given away or taken in electrons?
19141.e: If an atom gives away or takes in electrons, it becomes electrically charged. A charged particle like this is called an ion.
19141.m: An electrically charged atom is called an ion.

19142.q: What does the Greek word “atomos”, from which “atom” comes, mean?
19142.e: The Greek thinker Democritus called the smallest particles “atomos”, meaning indivisible. Today we know that atoms are made of even smaller particles.
19142.m: The word atom originally means indivisible.

19143.q: Which atoms make up a water molecule (H2O)?
19143.e: In the formula H2O, the small 2 after the H stands for two hydrogen atoms. The O without a number stands for one oxygen atom.
19143.m: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

19144.q: How many atoms does a molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2) have?
19144.e: CO2 is made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. Together that makes 1 + 2 = 3 atoms.
19144.m: The numbers in a formula show how many atoms of each kind are in the molecule.

19145.q: What is the formula of the oxygen molecule we breathe in?
19145.e: In the air, oxygen exists as a molecule made of two oxygen atoms. That is why we write O2.
19145.m: The oxygen in the air is made of molecules with two atoms.

19146.q: What is a molecule of ozone made of?
19146.e: Ozone has the formula O3. In the stratosphere the ozone layer protects us from UV radiation, while near the ground ozone irritates the airways in summer.
19146.m: Ozone is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms.

19147.q: How many atoms does a methane molecule (CH4) contain?
19147.e: Methane is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. That makes 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.
19147.m: Methane is the main part of natural gas.

a: A substance made of atoms with the same number of protons
A compound of two kinds of atom
A substance that is always a gas
19148.e: All the atoms of an element have the same number of protons in the nucleus. An element cannot be broken down chemically into other substances.
19148.m: An element is made of just one kind of atom.

19149.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
19149.e: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word “aurum” for gold. Ag is the symbol for silver.

19150.q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
19150.e: Fe comes from the Latin word “ferrum” for iron. Many symbols come from Latin or Greek.

19151.q: Which element has the symbol Na?
19151.e: Na stands for sodium, from the Latin “natrium”. Nitrogen has the symbol N, neon Ne and nickel Ni.

19152.q: Which element has the symbol K?
19152.e: K comes from the Latin name “kalium”. Calcium has the symbol Ca, krypton Kr and cobalt Co.

19153.q: Which element has the symbol Pb?
19153.e: Pb comes from the Latin “plumbum” for lead. Platinum is Pt, phosphorus P and palladium Pd.

19154.q: Which chemist published a periodic table of the elements in 1869?
19154.e: The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by their properties in 1869. He even predicted elements that were not yet known. At almost the same time, Lothar Meyer was working on a similar arrangement.
19154.m: Mendeleev is seen as one of the fathers of the periodic table.

19155.q: What are the horizontal rows in the periodic table called?
19155.e: The horizontal rows are called periods. The vertical columns are called groups.
19155.m: In the periodic table, the rows are periods and the columns are groups.

19156.q: What is the group containing helium, neon and argon called?
19156.e: The noble gases hardly ever react with other substances. They are in the last column of the periodic table.

19157.q: Which group do lithium, sodium and potassium belong to?
19157.e: The alkali metals are in the first main group. They are soft and react violently with water.
19157.m: Alkali metals are in the first main group.

19158.q: Which group do fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine belong to?
19158.e: Halogens are in the seventh main group. The name means “salt formers”, because they form salts with metals.

19159.q: Which element comes first in the periodic table?
19159.e: The elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Right at the front is the element with only one proton in its nucleus.
19159.m: The periodic table arranges the elements by atomic number.

19160.q: How many chemical elements are known and officially named (as of 2026)?
19160.e: So far, 118 elements have been detected and named by IUPAC. The heaviest ones were made artificially in laboratories.

19161.q: Roughly what percentage of dry air is oxygen?
19161.e: Dry air contains around 21 per cent oxygen by volume. Another gas makes up the largest part.
19161.m: About one fifth of the air is oxygen.

19162.q: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
19162.e: The symbol O comes from the scientific name “oxygenium”. S is the symbol for sulphur.

19163.q: In which process do green plants make oxygen?
19163.e: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released in the process.
19163.m: Plants give off oxygen during photosynthesis.

19164.q: What is the atomic number of oxygen?
19164.e: An oxygen atom has 8 protons in its nucleus. That is why its atomic number is 8.

19165.q: Which element is the most common in the Earth’s crust by mass?
19165.e: Almost half the mass of the Earth’s crust is oxygen. It is bound up in rocks and minerals, for example in quartz.
19165.m: A lot of oxygen is bound up in the rocks of the Earth’s crust.

19166.q: Which test is used to detect oxygen in the laboratory?
19166.e: A glowing wooden splint bursts back into bright flame in pure oxygen. This shows that oxygen helps things burn.
19166.m: A glowing splint relights in oxygen.

19167.q: What is the lightest chemical element?
19167.e: A hydrogen atom usually consists of just one proton and one electron. That makes it the lightest atom of all.

19168.q: Which element is the most common in the universe?
19168.e: About three quarters of the normal matter in the universe is hydrogen. Stars like the Sun are mostly made of it.
19168.m: The universe is mostly made of hydrogen.

19169.q: Which test is used to detect hydrogen in the laboratory?
19169.e: If you hold a test tube of hydrogen to a flame, there is a bang or a squeaky pop. Hydrogen and oxygen react violently.
19169.m: Hydrogen shows itself with a pop in the squeaky pop test.

19170.q: Which substance forms when hydrogen burns with oxygen?
19170.e: Hydrogen combines with oxygen to form H2O. Because no carbon dioxide is produced, hydrogen is seen as a clean source of energy.
19170.m: When hydrogen burns, only water is produced.

19171.q: What is the process called in which water is split into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity?
19171.e: In electrolysis, electric current drives a chemical reaction. In this way, water produces hydrogen and oxygen.
19171.m: Electricity can split water into its elements.

19172.q: What is the formula of a hydrogen molecule?
19172.e: Hydrogen gas is made of molecules with two hydrogen atoms. That is why we write H2.
19172.m: Hydrogen gas is made of H2 molecules.

19173.q: What is the chemical symbol for carbon?
19173.e: C comes from the Latin “carbo” for coal. K stands for potassium, Ca for calcium.

19174.q: Which gemstone is made of pure carbon, like graphite?
19174.e: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms. They differ in how the atoms are arranged, which is why diamond is extremely hard.

19175.q: What is the lead of a pencil mainly made of?
19175.e: Despite its name, a pencil contains no lead. The core is a mixture of graphite and clay.
19175.m: Pencil leads contain graphite, not lead.

19176.q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
19176.e: Carbon atoms have 6 protons in their nucleus. The number 12 is the mass number of the most common carbon atom.

19177.q: Which gas is produced when carbon burns completely with enough oxygen?
19177.e: In complete combustion, each carbon atom joins with two oxygen atoms. This produces CO2.
19177.m: Complete combustion of carbon produces carbon dioxide.

19178.q: What is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds called?
19178.e: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds such as sugars, fats and plastics. People used to believe that only living things could make such substances.
19178.m: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon.

19179.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
19179.e: Mercury melts at about -39 °C. It is poisonous, so it is hardly used in thermometers any more.
19179.m: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

19180.q: Which property do all metals have in common?
a: They are solid at room temperature
19180.e: Metals contain electrons that can move freely. That is why all metals conduct electricity and heat.

19181.q: Which metals is bronze mainly made of?
19181.e: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. It gave the Bronze Age its name.
19181.m: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

19182.q: Which of these metals is attracted by a magnet?
19182.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic. Copper, aluminium and gold are not attracted by an ordinary magnet.

19183.q: Which metal is usually used for electric cables in the home because it conducts so well?
19183.e: Copper conducts electricity very well and is easy to shape into wires. Only silver conducts slightly better, but it is much more expensive.
19183.m: Electric cables are usually made of copper.

a: An alloy of iron and carbon
An alloy of copper and zinc
19184.e: Steel is iron with a little carbon and often other additives. This makes it stronger and easy to work with.
19184.m: Steel is an alloy of iron and a little carbon.

19185.q: Which light metal is used for drinks cans and kitchen foil?
19185.e: Aluminium is light, easy to shape and does not rust through. In Switzerland, used aluminium cans can be collected separately and recycled.
19185.m: Aluminium is a light metal that is easy to shape.

19186.q: Which non-metal is liquid at room temperature?
19186.e: Bromine is a red-brown, poisonous liquid. It is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

19187.q: Which yellow, solid non-metal is often found at volcanoes?
19187.e: Sulphur forms yellow crystals that are deposited from gases at volcanoes. When it burns, it has a sharp smell.

19188.q: Which property do most non-metals have?
