23223.m: Reindeer herds travel long distances every year.

23224.q: How did people in the Old Stone Age transport their belongings?
23224.e: There were no carts and no tame horses yet. Everything had to be carried on your back or in your arms.

23225.q: Why did people who moved around a lot have only a few belongings?
23225.e: If you often move on, you cannot take much with you. So people only owned what they really needed.
23225.m: If you move around a lot, you have little luggage.

23226.q: What did people take from their tent when they moved on?
23226.e: The skins were valuable and light enough to carry. At the new place they were used to build a tent again.
23226.m: When moving on, people took the tent skins with them.

23227.q: How did people know where the herds would go?
23227.e: The herds took similar routes every year. The old people knew these routes and told others about them.
23227.m: Experience showed hunters the routes of the herds.

23228.q: Did people sometimes come back to old camps?
a: Yes, often at the same time of year
Yes, but only once in a lifetime
23228.e: Good places were used again and again. People came back when animals or plants could be found there at the right time.
23228.m: Good camps were visited again and again.

23229.q: How did people in the Old Stone Age travel long distances?
23229.e: Horses and reindeer were only tamed much later, and there were no carts yet. People in the Old Stone Age walked everywhere.
23229.m: In the Old Stone Age, people went everywhere on foot.

a: A place where you live for a while
23230.e: At the camp, the group put up its tents. When it moved on, it looked for a new camp.
23230.m: At a camp, you live for a while.

23231.q: What is the most famous room in the Lascaux cave called?
23231.e: In the Hall of the Bulls, large aurochs, horses and deer are painted on the walls and ceiling.
23231.m: The Hall of the Bulls is the best-known room at Lascaux.

23232.q: Next to which animal is a human painted in the shaft at Lascaux?
23232.e: In the deep shaft of the cave you see a bison that has been hit by a spear. Next to it lies a man with a bird's head.
23232.m: In the shaft at Lascaux, a man is painted next to a bison.

23233.q: Which animal with antlers is painted at Lascaux?
23233.e: At Lascaux you can see, among other things, a row of deer heads with large antlers.

23234.q: What is mainly painted on the walls of the Lascaux cave?
23234.e: At Lascaux you mainly see horses, aurochs and deer.
23234.m: At Lascaux, people mainly painted animals.

23235.q: Which large type of cattle is often painted at Lascaux?
23235.e: The aurochs was a large wild ox. One painted bull at Lascaux is over 5 metres long.
23235.m: The aurochs is a prehistoric wild ox.

23236.q: Why are visitors no longer allowed into the real Lascaux cave?
23236.e: The breath of many visitors brought damp and mould into the cave. That is why it was closed in 1963.
23236.m: The real Lascaux cave stays closed to protect the paintings.

23237.q: What can visitors see at Lascaux today?
23237.e: The cave and its paintings have been copied exactly. The newest copy is called Lascaux IV and opened in 2016.
23237.m: At Lascaux today, you visit a copy of the cave.

23238.q: About how old are the paintings in the Lascaux cave?
23238.e: The paintings were made in the Old Stone Age, about 17,000 years ago.
23238.m: The paintings at Lascaux are many thousands of years old.

23239.q: In which country is the Chauvet Cave?
23239.e: The Chauvet Cave is in the south of France, near the River Ardèche.
23239.m: The Chauvet Cave is a cave in France.

23240.q: When was the Chauvet Cave discovered?
23240.e: Three cavers found the cave in December 1994.
23240.m: The Chauvet Cave was discovered in 1994.

23241.q: Where does the Chauvet Cave get its name from?
23241.e: One of the three discoverers was called Jean-Marie Chauvet. The cave is named after him.
23241.m: The Chauvet Cave bears the name of its discoverer.

23242.q: Which big cats are painted in the Chauvet Cave?
23242.e: In the Chauvet Cave you can see whole groups of cave lions.
23242.m: Lions are painted in the Chauvet Cave.

23243.q: Which animal with a horn on its nose is painted in the Chauvet Cave?
23243.e: Several woolly rhinoceroses are painted in the cave. They also lived in Europe at that time.
23243.m: Rhinoceroses also used to live in Europe.

23244.q: Which animal's bones and skulls lie in large numbers on the floor of the Chauvet Cave?
23244.e: Cave bears spent their winter rest in the Chauvet Cave. Many of their skulls and even paw prints have been found.
23244.m: Cave bears slept in the Chauvet Cave.

23245.q: About how old are the oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave?
23245.e: Tests on the charcoal show that the oldest paintings are over 30,000 years old.
23245.m: The paintings of the Chauvet Cave are among the oldest in the world.

23246.q: Why is the Chauvet Cave so important for research?
a: It contains some of the oldest cave paintings in the world
The first iron tool was found there
It is the deepest cave in the world
23246.e: The oldest paintings in the Chauvet Cave are over 30,000 years old. That is why it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014.
23246.m: The Chauvet Cave contains ancient cave art.

23247.q: What did cave painters make black paint from?
23247.e: Charcoal is what is left when wood is charred in a fire. You can paint black with it very well.

23248.q: What is the yellow or red earth that paint was made from called?
23248.e: Ochre is a coloured earth. Depending on the type, it is yellow, brown or red.
23248.m: People made red and yellow paint from ochre.

23249.q: Which colour almost never appears in cave paintings?
23249.e: The painters had earth and charcoal. These give red, yellow, brown and black, but not blue.
23249.m: You hardly find blue or green in cave paintings.

23250.q: What did people often paint with in the cave?
23250.e: People put the paint on with their fingers, with moss or with brushes made of animal hair.
23250.m: Cave painters often used their fingers as brushes.

23251.q: What was mixed into the colour powder so that it stuck better?
23251.e: The powder made from earth was mixed with water, spit or animal fat to make paint.
23251.m: Colour powder becomes paint when mixed with a liquid.

23252.q: Where did cave painters get light from in the dark?
23252.e: Deep inside the cave it is completely dark. The painters burnt animal fat in stone bowls or carried torches.
23252.m: Deep in the cave, people painted by firelight.

23253.q: Where are the oldest pictures painted by humans found?
23253.e: Cave painting is the oldest painting we know of. The pictures are many thousands of years old.
23253.m: The oldest pictures made by humans are cave paintings.

23254.q: What could white paint be made from?
23254.e: White paint was made from lime or pale clay.

23255.q: What did prehistoric people often put on cave walls next to the animals?
23255.e: In many caves you find outlines and prints of human hands.
23255.m: People left their handprints in caves.

23256.q: How is a hand outline made on a cave wall?
a: You blow paint around your hand
23256.e: You put your hand on the wall and blow paint all around it. Where your hand was, the wall stays bare.
23256.m: For a hand outline, you blow paint around your hand.

23257.q: What could you use to blow paint onto the wall?
23257.e: A hollow bird bone or a plant stem served as a tube for spraying.
23257.m: A hollow bone could be used as a paint tube.

23258.q: What do you call a handprint made by painting the hand itself?
23258.e: For a positive print, the hand is dipped in paint and pressed against the wall.
23258.m: A painted hand pressed on the wall makes a positive print.

23259.q: In which country is the famous “Cave of the Hands” (Cueva de las Manos)?
23259.e: The Cueva de las Manos is in Patagonia in Argentina. There are hundreds of hands on the wall.
23259.m: The Cave of the Hands is in Argentina.

23260.q: What colour are many hand outlines in caves?
23260.e: Many hands were sprayed with red ochre. Others are black.
23260.m: Many hands on cave walls are red.

23261.q: What is striking about some hands in the Gargas cave in France?
23261.e: In Gargas, many hands look as if fingers were missing. Perhaps the fingers were just bent over.
23261.m: In Gargas, many hands on the wall look shortened.

23262.q: What do small handprints on cave walls show?
23262.e: Some hands are so small that they must come from children or teenagers.
23262.m: Children also left handprints on cave walls.

23263.q: What is a prehistoric Venus figurine?
a: A small figure of a woman
23263.e: Venus figurines are small figures of women from the Old Stone Age.
23263.m: Venus figurines are small prehistoric figures of women.

23264.q: In which country was the Venus of Willendorf found?
23264.e: Willendorf is a village in the Wachau valley on the Danube in Austria.
23264.m: The Venus of Willendorf comes from Austria.

23265.q: About how big is the Venus of Willendorf?
23265.e: The figure is only about 11 centimetres tall. It fits easily in your hand.
23265.m: The Venus of Willendorf is as small as a hand.

23266.q: What material is the Venus of Willendorf made of?
23266.e: The figure was carved from limestone and painted with red ochre.
23266.m: The Venus of Willendorf is made of stone.

23267.q: In which museum is the Venus of Willendorf?
23267.e: The figure has belonged to the Natural History Museum in Vienna for a long time.
23267.m: The Venus of Willendorf is in Vienna.

23268.q: What is the Venus of Hohle Fels carved from?
23268.e: The figure was carved from a mammoth's tusk. It is around 35,000 to 40,000 years old.
23268.m: Mammoth ivory was a material for carvings.

23269.q: Where in Switzerland were small Venus figurines made of black stone found?
23269.e: At Monruz on Lake Neuchâtel, tiny figures of women made of jet, a black stone, were found.
23269.m: Venus figurines were found in Switzerland too.

23270.q: How big is the largest Venus of Monruz?
23270.e: The largest figure from Monruz is only 1.65 centimetres long. It was perhaps worn as a pendant.
23270.m: The Venus figurines of Monruz are tiny.

23271.q: What did prehistoric people make flutes from?
23271.e: Bird bones are hollow inside. That is why they are good for flutes.
23271.m: The first flutes were made of bone.

23272.q: Why are bird bones good for making flutes?
23272.e: Bird bones are hollow and light. You can blow air through the hollow bone.
23272.m: Hollow bird bones were made into flutes.

23273.q: About how old are the oldest bone flutes?
23273.e: The oldest flutes from the Swabian Jura are about 40,000 years old.
23273.m: People have been making music for a very long time.

23274.q: In which country were the oldest bone flutes found?
23274.e: They come from caves in the Swabian Jura in southern Germany.
23274.m: The oldest flutes were found in southern Germany.

23275.q: Why does a bone flute have holes?
23275.e: By covering or uncovering the holes with your fingers, you play higher or lower notes.
23275.m: You play different notes with the holes.

23276.q: What did people use to make the holes in a bone flute?
23276.e: Metal was not yet known. The holes were scraped and bored into the bone with pointed stones.
23276.m: The flute holes were bored with stone tools.

23277.q: What kind of instrument is a bone flute?
23277.e: You blow air into a flute. That is why it is a wind instrument.
23277.m: A flute is a wind instrument.

23278.q: What is the bone flute from Hohle Fels for science?
a: One of the oldest musical instruments
23278.e: The flute is one of the oldest known musical instruments in the world.
23278.m: Bone flutes are among the oldest instruments.

23279.q: What did the first wheels look like?
23279.e: The first wheels were disc wheels. They were made by joining wooden planks together.
23279.m: The first wheels were wooden discs.

23280.q: About how many years ago was the wheel invented?
23280.e: The oldest wheels and carts date from around 3500 BC.
23280.m: The wheel is around 5,500 years old.

23281.q: Where was one of the oldest surviving wheels found?
23281.e: In the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, a wooden wheel over 5,000 years old was found.
23281.m: One of the oldest wheels was found in a bog.

23282.q: Which animals pulled the first carts?
23282.e: Strong oxen pulled the heavy carts with wooden wheels.

23283.q: What does a wheel need so it can turn on a cart?
23283.e: The axle is a rod. The wheels turn on it or with it.

23284.q: How did people move heavy loads before there were wheels?
23284.e: Loads were pulled on sledges, or round tree trunks were laid underneath as rollers. Coaches and carts already need wheels.
23284.m: Before the wheel, loads were pulled on sledges.

23285.q: What did potters use a turning wheel for?
23285.e: On the potter's wheel the clay turns round. That way round pots can be shaped quickly and evenly.
23285.m: The potter's wheel is a wheel too.

23286.q: Which wheels came later and were lighter?
a: Wheels made from slices of tree trunk
23286.e: Spoked wheels have rods instead of a solid disc. They are lighter and faster.
23286.m: Spoked wheels are lighter than disc wheels.

23287.q: What can you do better with a wheel and cart than with your bare hands?
23287.e: With a cart you could carry much more, for example wood, stones or the harvest.
23287.m: Carts and wheels are used to transport heavy loads.

23288.q: What material are clay pots made of?
23288.e: Clay is a soft, damp earth. It is easy to shape.
23288.m: Clay pots are made of clay.

23289.q: What do you do to a clay pot to make it hard?
23289.e: In a fire or a kiln, the soft clay becomes as hard as stone.

23290.q: What did people need clay pots for?
23290.e: In pots you could cook porridge and store grain or water.
23290.m: Clay pots were used for cooking and storing supplies.

23291.q: In which period did people in Europe start making a lot of pottery?
23291.e: In the New Stone Age people settled down and grew grain. Now they needed pots.

23292.q: How were the first pots shaped without a potter's wheel?
a: By hand with coils of clay
23292.e: Clay was rolled into long sausages and laid on top of each other in a circle. Then they were smoothed out.
23292.m: The first pots were shaped by hand.

23293.q: What do you call people who make clay pots?
23293.e: Someone who shapes and fires pots from clay is a potter.

23294.q: What is the Linear Pottery culture of the New Stone Age named after?
a: The line patterns on their pots
23294.e: These people decorated their pots with lines in bands. Researchers named them after this.
23294.m: The Linear Pottery culture is named after pots with line patterns.

23295.q: What has often survived from the lake dwellers in Switzerland?
23295.e: Many pieces of the lake dwellers' pots were found in Swiss lakes.
23295.m: Broken pottery tells us a lot about the lake dwellers.

23296.q: What do you get when a clay pot breaks?
23296.e: Fired clay breaks into shards. Researchers put them back together.
23296.m: A broken pot falls apart into shards.

23297.q: From which tree did the lake dwellers take bast for string and cloth?
23297.e: Under the bark of the lime tree there is tough bast. String, mats and cloth were made from it.
23297.m: Lime bast was an important raw material.

23298.q: What is the device for weaving cloth called?
23298.e: On a loom, threads are joined crosswise to make cloth.
23298.m: Cloth is made on a loom.

23299.q: What was hung on the threads of a loom to keep them tight?
23299.e: On a warp-weighted loom, weights of clay or stone kept the long threads tight.
23299.m: Loom weights keep the threads tight.

23300.q: What do you have to make from fibres before you can weave?
23300.e: First you twist the fibres into long threads. This is called spinning.

23301.q: Which simple tool was used for spinning in prehistoric times?
23301.e: The spindle is a stick that turns. A small clay ring helps it turn.
23301.m: You spin threads with a spindle.

23302.q: What are the threads pulled across in weaving called?
23302.e: The long threads are called the warp. The cross thread that goes back and forth is called the weft.
23302.m: In weaving, the weft crosses the warp.

23303.q: What were clothes mainly made of before weaving was invented?
23303.e: Wool, linen and silk have to be spun and woven. Before that, hunter-gatherers sewed their clothes from animal skins.
23303.m: Before weaving, people wore clothes of fur and leather.

23304.q: Which animal later provided wool for weaving?
23304.e: Sheep have a thick coat. Their wool can be spun and woven.

23305.q: What is a dugout canoe made from?
23305.e: A dugout canoe is hollowed out of a single tree trunk.
23305.m: A dugout canoe is made from a single trunk.

23306.e: The dugout canoe is one of the oldest boats in the world.
23306.m: The dugout canoe is an ancient boat.

23307.q: How was a dugout canoe moved forward?
23307.e: People paddled with wooden paddles. Some have been found together with boats.
23307.m: A dugout canoe is moved with a paddle.

23308.q: Which tool was used in the Stone Age to hollow out a tree trunk?
23308.e: The wood was chopped out bit by bit with axes made of polished stone. Iron and bronze were not yet known.
23308.m: Stone axes were important tools for woodwork.

23309.q: What wood are many dugout canoes in Switzerland made of?
23309.e: Oak is hard and lasts a long time in water. Some dugouts are also made of lime wood.
23309.m: Many old dugout canoes are made of oak.

23310.q: Where in Switzerland have dugout canoes been found?
23310.e: Old dugout canoes were found in Lake Biel, Lake Zurich and other lakes.
23310.m: Old dugout canoes were found in Swiss lakes.

23311.q: About how old is the oldest known dugout canoe, from Pesse in the Netherlands?
23311.e: The Pesse canoe was built around 8000 BC. So it is about 10,000 years old.
23311.m: People have been going by boat for about 10,000 years.

23312.q: What did the lake dwellers use their dugout canoes for?
23312.e: They went out on the lake by boat to fish and took goods to the other shore.
23312.m: Dugout canoes were used for fishing and transport.

23313.q: Why did old dugout canoes survive so long at the bottom of lakes?
23313.e: In wet mud there is no air. That is why wood rots only very slowly there.
23313.m: Wood lasts a long time in wet ground.

23314.e: A hand axe is a stone that has been chipped sharp on both sides.
23314.m: The hand axe is a stone tool.

23315.q: Which stone was often used to make a hand axe?
23315.e: Flint has sharp edges when you break it. It is also called silex.

23316.q: How was a hand axe held?
23316.e: The hand axe had no handle. It was held directly in the fist.
23316.m: The hand axe was held in the fist.

23317.q: What was a hand axe used for?
23317.e: With a hand axe people cut up animals, scraped skins and worked wood.
23317.m: The hand axe was a tool for many jobs.

23318.q: How was a hand axe made?
23318.e: Small pieces were knocked off with another stone until the edges were sharp.
23318.m: A hand axe is chipped out of stone.

23319.q: Where was the first hand axe in Switzerland found?
23319.e: It was discovered in 1974 in Pratteln in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.
23319.m: The first hand axe in Switzerland comes from Pratteln.

23320.q: About how old is the Pratteln hand axe?
23320.e: Researchers think it is about 300,000 years old. It is one of the oldest tools in Switzerland.
23320.m: The Pratteln hand axe is ancient.

23321.q: Who found the Pratteln hand axe?
23321.e: The schoolboy Christoph Hauser discovered it in 1974 on a sunken path.
23321.m: Children can make important finds too.

23322.q: What shape does a hand axe usually have?
23322.e: A hand axe is wide and round at the bottom and comes to a point at the top, a bit like a drop or an almond.
23322.m: A hand axe is wide at the bottom and pointed at the top.

23323.q: What do you get when you rub two pieces of wood together quickly?
23323.e: Friction makes the wood hot. If it gets hot enough, a glowing ember forms.

23324.q: What is the way of making fire by spinning a stick quickly called?
23324.e: In fire drilling, you spin a wooden stick quickly in a board until an ember forms.
23324.m: In fire drilling, a wooden stick spins.

23325.q: What can you use to spin the drill stick faster?
23325.e: The string of a small bow is wrapped round the stick. When you move the bow back and forth, the stick spins fast.
23325.m: A bow helps with fire drilling.

23326.q: What do you need to turn an ember into a flame?
23326.e: Tinder is very dry, fine material such as grass or tree bast. It catches fire easily.

23327.q: What do you do with the ember in the tinder to get a flame?
23327.e: Blowing gently gives the ember more air. That makes a flame.
23327.m: Gentle blowing helps an ember become a flame.

23328.q: What must the wood be like for making fire by friction?
23328.e: Wet wood does not get hot enough. That is why you need completely dry wood.
23328.m: You need dry wood for fire.

23329.q: Which fungus did the glacier mummy Ötzi carry for making fire?
23329.e: Ötzi had pieces of tinder fungus with him. This tree fungus keeps smouldering well.
23329.m: Tinder fungus helped with making fire.

23331.q: What do you call a young dog?
23331.e: A young dog is called a puppy. Puppies need lots of sleep and care.
23331.m: A young dog is a puppy.

23332.q: Which wild animal is the dog descended from?
23332.e: All dogs are descended from the wolf. Over time, tame wolves became dogs.
23332.m: The dog's ancestor is the wolf.

23333.q: How did the dog help hunters?
23333.e: Dogs have an excellent sense of smell and hearing. That is why they found wild animals faster than people.
23333.m: With its good nose, the dog helped with hunting.

23334.q: How did the dog later help herders?
23334.e: The dog kept the animals together and drove off predators. That made it very important for herders.

23335.q: What did a dog do when strangers came near the village at night?
23335.e: The dog has very good hearing. By barking, it warned people of danger.
23335.m: The dog was a guard from early on.

23336.q: How long have there been tame dogs?
23336.e: The oldest certain dog bones are around 14,000 to 15,000 years old. Perhaps dogs have existed even longer.
23336.m: Dogs and people have been friends for many thousands of years.

23337.q: What did the dog get from people?
23337.e: The dog got leftovers and a place by the fire. In return it helped people.
23337.m: People and dogs helped each other.

23338.q: What is the small dog whose bones were found in Swiss lake dwellings called?
23338.e: Researchers found the bones of a small dog in the lake dwellings. They called it the peat dog because the bones lay in peat and lake mud.
23338.m: The small peat dog lived in Swiss lake dwellings.

23339.q: What do very old graves with a dog lying next to people show?
a: Dogs only lived in the forest
23339.e: Near Bonn in Germany, a grave about 14,000 years old was found with people and a dog. The dog was buried like a member of the family.
23339.m: The dog was a loyal companion from early on.

23340.q: What did farmers make from the skin of their animals?
23340.e: The skin of sheep, goats and cattle was tanned. That made leather for clothes and shoes.
23340.m: Leather is made from animal skin.

23341.q: Where were sheep and goats first tamed?
23341.e: In the Near East, roughly in what is now Iraq, Syria and Turkey, sheep and goats were tamed about 10,000 years ago. From there they came to Europe.
23341.m: The first tame sheep and goats lived in the Near East.

23342.q: What do you call a young sheep?
23342.e: A young sheep is called a lamb. A calf is a young cow, a foal a young horse.
23342.m: A young sheep is a lamb.

23343.q: What could milk be made into so that it lasted longer?
23343.e: Fresh milk goes sour quickly. As cheese, it lasts much longer.

23344.q: Which wild animal is an ancestor of the domestic sheep?
23344.e: The domestic sheep comes from a wild sheep, the mouflon. Mouflons have large, curved horns.
23344.m: The mouflon is the wild ancestor of the sheep.

23345.q: Which animal did people tame first?
23345.e: The dog is descended from the wolf. Even before the first farmers, dogs lived with people and helped with hunting.
23345.m: The dog is people's oldest domestic animal.

23346.q: Why did the first farmers keep their own animals near the village?
a: So they always had meat and milk
So the animals would build their houses
So the animals would harvest the grain
So the animals would make fire
23346.e: With their own animals, farmers no longer had to hunt for long. Meat, milk and skins were always close by.
23346.m: Their own animals made farmers less dependent on hunting.

23347.q: What do you call a person who looks after sheep and goats?
23347.e: A herder watches over the herd. He leads the animals to good pastures.
23347.m: A herder looks after the herd.

23348.q: What do sheep and goats mainly eat?
23348.e: Sheep and goats are plant-eaters. Goats also like nibbling at bushes.

23349.q: What is the part of a cereal plant where the grains sit called?
23349.e: The ear grows at the top of the stalk. The grains ripen inside it.
23349.m: The grains sit in the ear.

23350.q: Which type of cereal do emmer and einkorn belong to?
23350.e: Emmer and einkorn are old kinds of wheat. They are ancestors and relatives of today's wheat.
23350.m: Emmer and einkorn are early forms of wheat.

23351.q: Where does einkorn get its name from?
a: Each spikelet usually has one grain
It only grows for one year
It only grows in one place
23351.e: In einkorn, each spikelet usually holds only one grain. In German, “einkorn” means “one grain”.
23351.m: Einkorn usually has only one grain per spikelet.

23353.q: What did the cereals we grow come from?
23353.e: Cereals are grasses. Farmers sowed the best grains of wild grasses again and again.
23353.m: Our cereals come from wild grasses.

23354.q: What do you have to do to get the grains out of the ears?
23354.e: When threshing, you beat the ears. The grains fall out.
23354.m: Threshing separates the grains from the ears.

23355.q: What is still made from emmer or einkorn today?
23355.e: Old kinds of cereal are being grown again today. They are used to bake bread or make pasta.
23355.m: Bread is still baked from old cereals today.

23356.q: What had to be removed from emmer and einkorn before grinding?
23356.e: In emmer and einkorn, the grain sits tightly in a hard covering. This covering is called the husk and has to come off first.
23356.m: Emmer and einkorn are hulled cereals.

23357.q: What was a grinding stone usually made of?
23357.e: A grinding stone had to stand up to a lot of rubbing. So hard stones were used, for example granite or sandstone.
23357.m: A grinding stone is made of hard rock.

23358.q: How was a grinding stone used?
a: You rubbed a stone on a big stone
You turned a big wooden wheel
You let water flow over it
You threw it into the fire
23358.e: The grains lay on a large, flat stone. A smaller stone was rubbed back and forth over them until flour formed.
23358.m: With a grinding stone, one stone rubs on the other.

23359.q: What is the small upper stone of a grinding stone called?
23359.e: The large lower stone stays in place. The small upper stone is moved back and forth and is called the handstone.
23359.m: The upper stone of a grinding stone is called the handstone.

23360.q: Why were people's teeth often worn down back then?
a: There were tiny bits of stone in the flour
They ate a lot of sugar
23360.e: During grinding, tiny pieces came off the stone. This grit in the flour wore down the teeth.
23360.m: Grit in the flour wore down teeth.

23361.q: What did the first bread look like?
23361.e: The first breads were flatbreads. They cooked quickly because they were thin.
23361.m: The first bread was a flatbread.

23362.q: Where was the first bread baked?
23362.e: Farmers of the New Stone Age did not yet know metal or ovens. They put the dough on hot stones or in the embers.
23362.m: The first bread was baked on hot stones.

23363.q: What is the least you need to make dough from flour?
23363.e: Flour and water together make a dough. Nothing more was needed for a simple flatbread.
23363.m: Flour and water make a dough.

23364.q: Apart from bread, what did farmers often eat made from grain?
23364.e: Grains or coarse flour were cooked with water or milk. That made a filling porridge.
23364.m: Grain porridge was an important food for farmers.

23365.q: What kind of house did many of the first farmers live in?
23365.e: The first farmers in Central Europe built long wooden houses. They are called longhouses.
23365.m: Many early farmers lived in longhouses.

23366.q: What were the walls of a longhouse made of?
23366.e: Branches and twigs were woven between the posts. Then clay was spread on top.
23366.m: The walls were made of woven branches and clay.

23367.q: What held up the roof of a longhouse?
23367.e: Thick wooden posts stood in rows inside the house. They carried the heavy roof.
23367.m: Wooden posts carried the roof of the longhouse.

23368.q: What was the roof of a longhouse covered with?
23368.e: Straw and reeds were everywhere. Tied tightly, they kept out the rain.
23368.m: The roof was thatched with straw or reeds.

23369.q: How long could a longhouse be?
23369.e: Some longhouses were up to 40 metres long. That is longer than a normal sports hall.
23369.m: A longhouse could be around 40 metres long.

23370.e: Many people lived together in a longhouse. Often a big family lived under one roof.
23370.m: A big family lived in a longhouse.

23371.q: What gave warmth and light in a longhouse?
23371.e: There were no stoves or lanterns yet. An open fire warmed the house and gave light.
23371.m: The fireplace was the heart of the house.

23372.q: Why did farmers build solid houses instead of tents?
23372.e: Farmers had to look after and harvest their fields. So they stayed in one place and settled down.
23372.m: With farming, people settled in one place.

23373.q: What was used to smooth the wall of a freshly shaped clay pot?
23373.e: The coils of clay were smoothed with damp fingers or a wet stone. That made the wall tight and smooth.

23374.q: Why was sand or small stones mixed into the clay?
a: So the pot would not crack
23374.e: Pure clay shrinks a lot when it dries and is fired. Sand and small stones stop the pot from cracking.
23374.m: Sand in the clay prevents cracks.

23375.q: What did you have to do with a freshly shaped clay pot before firing it?
23375.e: A wet pot would burst in the fire. So it was first left to dry well.

23376.q: What colour are many pots from the New Stone Age?
23376.e: In an open fire the clay usually turned brown, grey or black. Colourful glazes were not yet known.
23376.m: New Stone Age pots are usually dark.

23377.q: How did some farmers decorate their pots?
23377.e: Patterns were scratched or pressed into the soft clay. They stayed visible after firing.

23378.q: Why were clay pots good for storing supplies?
a: They protected against mice and damp
23378.e: Mice could not get at the grain in a pot with a lid. Damp did not get in so easily either.

23379.e: Pots and figures made of fired clay are called ceramics. Plates and cups are often ceramic too.

23380.q: What were small loops on some clay pots for?
23380.e: A string was pulled through small loops. That way the pot could be carried or hung up.
23380.m: Loops made pots easy to carry.

23381.q: Why do archaeologists find so many old pieces of pottery?
a: Clay grows back in the ground
The pots were made of gold
23381.e: Wood and cloth rot in the ground. But fired clay survives for thousands of years.
23381.m: Fired clay lasts a very long time.

23382.q: What did New Stone Age farmers use to cut down trees?
23382.e: Metal was not yet known. So axes with a stone blade were used.
23382.m: Trees were felled with a stone axe.

23383.q: What was the handle of a stone axe made of?
23383.e: The handle was carved from a strong branch. The stone blade was fixed firmly into it.
23383.m: The handle of a stone axe was made of wood.

23384.q: How was the blade of a stone axe made smooth and sharp?
a: By grinding it on a stone
By melting it in the fire
By pouring it into a mould
23384.e: The blade was rubbed for a long time on a sandstone with water. That made it smooth and sharp.

23385.q: What did people do when the blade of a stone axe was blunt?
23385.e: A blunt stone blade was rubbed on a grindstone again. After that it was sharp again.
23385.m: A blunt stone blade is ground sharp again.

23386.q: What was the blade of a stone axe made of?
23386.e: Especially hard, tough stones were chosen for the blade. They could stand up to many strong blows.
23386.m: The blade of a stone axe was made of hard stone.

23387.q: In which period did people use polished stone axes?
23387.e: Polished stone axes are typical of the New Stone Age. In the Bronze Age and Iron Age, metal was used instead.
23387.m: The polished stone axe belongs to the New Stone Age.

23388.q: On the lake dwellers' stone axes, what were the sleeves between the stone blade and the wooden handle often made of?
23388.e: The stone blade often sat in a piece of deer antler. This cushioned the blows so the wooden handle did not break.
23388.m: Deer antler protected the handle of a stone axe.

23389.q: What did farmers need the wood of felled trees for?
23389.e: Farmers built houses from tree trunks. Smaller wood was burnt for cooking and heating.
23389.m: Wood was needed for building and heating.

23390.q: Why was harvested flax left lying on damp meadows for a few weeks?
a: So the fibres would come away from the stem
So it would dry out completely
So the flowers would fall off
23390.e: The damp makes the soft parts in the stem rot. After that, the fibres are easier to get out. This is called retting.
23390.m: Damp helps loosen the flax fibres.

23391.q: What colour are flax flowers usually?
23391.e: A flowering flax field glows light blue. The small flowers only bloom for a short time.

23392.q: From which part of the flax plant are the fibres taken?
23392.e: The fibres are in the long stem. They have to be separated with great effort from the woody core.
23392.m: Flax fibres are in the stem.

23393.q: Which plant did the lake dwellers in Switzerland grow to make cloth?
23393.e: The lake dwellers grew flax next to their grain. They made cloth and string from its fibres.
23393.m: The lake dwellers made cloth from flax.

23394.q: What is making cloth from threads called?
23394.e: When weaving, you cross threads lengthwise and crosswise. That makes cloth.

23395.q: About how tall does a flax plant grow?
23395.e: Flax is a slender plant with a thin stem. It grows up to about one metre tall.
23395.m: Flax is a slender, tall plant.

23396.q: What can be made from flax seeds?
23396.e: An oil is pressed from the small brown seeds. It can be eaten or used for paints.
23396.m: Oil is made from flax seeds.

23398.e: Stonehenge is in the south of England. It is one of the best-known stone monuments in the world.

a: A castle from the age of knights
23399.e: At Stonehenge, huge stones stand in a circle. It was built in the New Stone Age.

23400.e: Building began around 5,000 years ago. Stonehenge was rebuilt again and again over many centuries.

23401.q: For which event do especially many people come to Stonehenge?
23401.e: On the longest day of the year, the sun rises in line with the stones. Then many people celebrate there.
23401.m: Stonehenge is lined up with the sun.

23402.q: About how heavy are the biggest stones at Stonehenge?
23402.e: The big stones weigh around 25 tonnes. That is about as heavy as four to five elephants.
23402.m: The big stones at Stonehenge weigh many tonnes.

23403.q: Where did the smaller bluestones of Stonehenge come from?
23403.e: The bluestones come from hills in Wales. They were transported more than 200 kilometres.
23403.m: The bluestones of Stonehenge came from Wales.

23404.q: What lies across two standing stones at Stonehenge?
23404.e: A cross stone lies on top of each pair of upright stones. It looks like a stone gateway.
23404.m: At Stonehenge, lintel stones lie on standing stones.

23405.q: Which special list does Stonehenge belong to?
a: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
23405.e: Stonehenge has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Places like this are meant to be protected for everyone.
23405.m: Stonehenge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

23406.e: A menhir is a long stone that was set upright in the ground. Many menhirs are several metres tall.
23406.m: A menhir is a standing stone.

23407.q: Which language does the word menhir come from?
23407.e: Breton is spoken in Brittany in France. Especially many menhirs stand there.
23407.m: The word menhir comes from Breton.

23408.q: What does the word menhir mean?
23408.e: In Breton, “men” means stone and “hir” means long. So a menhir is a long stone.

23409.q: Where do over 3,000 menhirs stand in long rows?
23409.e: Near Carnac in Brittany, thousands of menhirs stand in rows. It is one of the largest stone arrangements in the world.
23409.m: Thousands of menhirs stand at Carnac.

23410.q: In which Swiss town are the Clendy menhirs?
23410.e: The Clendy menhirs stand on the shore of Lake Neuchâtel near Yverdon-les-Bains. They are over 5,000 years old.
23410.m: There are New Stone Age menhirs near Yverdon-les-Bains.

23411.q: Which comic character often carries a menhir on his back?
23411.e: Obelix is a menhir sculptor and delivers menhirs.

23412.q: What do you call many menhirs standing one behind the other in a line?
23412.e: When many menhirs stand in a line, it is called a stone row. There are often several rows side by side.
23412.m: Many menhirs sometimes form a stone row.

23413.q: Why did people put up menhirs?
23413.e: Nobody knows for sure, because there is no writing from this time. Researchers think menhirs were important for celebrations and beliefs.

a: A tomb made of large stone slabs
23414.e: A dolmen is made of large stones. The dead were buried in it.
23414.m: A dolmen is a tomb made of stones.

23415.q: What does the word dolmen mean?
23415.e: The word comes from Breton. With its flat slab, a dolmen looks like a giant table.

23416.q: What lies on top of a dolmen?
23416.e: Several stones stand upright. A heavy, flat stone slab lies on top of them.
23416.m: A dolmen has a large capstone.

23417.q: What did researchers find in dolmens?
a: Bones of the dead and grave goods
23417.e: Many people were often buried one after another in a dolmen. Jewellery, tools or pots were placed with them.
23417.m: The dead lie in dolmens with grave goods.

23418.q: What is another name for a tomb made of huge stones?
23418.e: A dolmen is a tomb made of very large stones. That is why it is also called a megalithic tomb.
23418.m: A dolmen is a megalithic tomb.

23419.q: In which Swiss town were dolmens from the New Stone Age found?
23419.e: Several dolmens were found in the Petit-Chasseur district of Sion. They belong to a large burial ground.
23419.m: There are dolmens in Sion in Valais too.

23420.q: What were many dolmens once covered with?
23420.e: Many dolmens used to lie under a mound of earth and stones. Today it has often been washed away or removed.
23420.m: Many dolmens lay under a mound of earth.

23421.q: What are the huge stones of dolmens, menhirs and stone circles called?
23421.e: Megalith is Greek for “big stone”. Buildings made of such stones are called megalithic monuments.

23422.q: What can you see at the Unteruhldingen Lake Dwelling Museum on Lake Constance?
23422.e: The open-air museum has houses rebuilt using old finds. It is one of the oldest museums of its kind.
23422.m: Rebuilt lake dwellings stand in Unteruhldingen.

23423.q: What do you call an outdoor museum with rebuilt houses?
23423.e: In an open-air museum the houses stand outside. You can go in and see how people used to live.
23423.m: In an open-air museum, history stands outdoors.

23424.q: On which lake is the Unteruhldingen Lake Dwelling Museum?
23424.e: The museum is right on the shore. Rebuilt lake dwellings stand in the water there.
23424.m: You can visit lake dwellings on Lake Constance.

23425.q: On the shore of which lake is the Gletterens lake dwelling village?
23425.e: Gletterens lies on the southern shore of this large lake in western Switzerland. Rebuilt houses from the New Stone Age stand there.
23425.m: You can experience a lake dwelling village in Gletterens.

23426.q: In which canton is the Gletterens lake dwelling village?
23426.e: Gletterens is a village in the canton of Fribourg. You can visit rebuilt New Stone Age houses there.
23426.m: Gletterens is in the canton of Fribourg.

23427.q: What do researchers go by when they rebuild lake dwellings?
23427.e: There are no photos or texts from the Stone Age. So only the posts, tools and remains that have been found show what the houses looked like.
23427.m: Finds from the ground show what lake dwellings looked like.

23428.q: What do you call a house that has been rebuilt from old finds?
23428.e: A reconstruction is a rebuilt copy. The real old house no longer exists.
23428.m: A rebuilt copy is called a reconstruction.

23429.e: Unteruhldingen belongs to the municipality of Uhldingen-Mühlhofen in the German state of Baden-Württemberg.

23430.q: What can children often try out for themselves at a lake dwelling open-air museum?
a: Putting on a suit of armour
23430.e: In museums like this you can often work as people did in the Stone Age. This includes grinding grain, for example.
23430.m: In an open-air museum you can experience the Stone Age.

23431.q: In which season did Ötzi probably die?
23431.e: Pollen from trees that flower in spring was found in Ötzi's gut. That is why researchers think he died in spring.

23432.q: In which year was Ötzi discovered?

23433.e: The married couple Erika and Helmut Simon from Nuremberg were on a mountain hike. They saw the man in the ice.
23433.m: A couple of hikers discovered Ötzi.

a: In the ice high in the mountains
In a cave in the forest
On the shore of a lake
23434.e: Ötzi lay in the ice of a glacier in the Ötztal Alps. The ice preserved him for over 5,000 years.
23434.m: Ötzi lay in the ice in the mountains.

23435.q: About how many years ago did Ötzi live?
23435.e: Ötzi died around 3300 BC. That is about 5,300 years ago.

23436.q: About how old was Ötzi when he died?
23436.e: Researchers think Ötzi lived to about 45. That was quite old for those times.

23437.e: When he was alive, Ötzi was about 1.60 metres tall. So he was rather short.

23438.q: In which city can you see Ötzi in a museum today?
23438.e: Ötzi lies in the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano in Italy. He is kept in a cold room there.
23438.m: Ötzi is in a museum in Bolzano today.

23439.q: What was stuck in Ötzi's left shoulder?
23439.e: An X-ray showed a stone arrowhead in his shoulder. Someone had shot at Ötzi.
23439.m: An arrowhead was stuck in Ötzi's shoulder.

23440.q: What did Ötzi have on his skin?
23440.e: Ötzi has 61 tattoos made of small lines. They were rubbed into the skin with soot.
23440.m: Ötzi had many tattoos on his skin.

23441.q: Which meat did Ötzi eat shortly before he died?
23441.e: Ibex meat was found in his stomach. He ate about an hour before he died.
23441.m: Ötzi's last meal was ibex meat.

23442.q: What was Ötzi's cap made of?
23442.e: Ötzi wore a warm cap made of bearskin. It had a strap under the chin.
23442.m: Ötzi's cap was made of bearskin.

23443.q: What were Ötzi's shoes filled with inside?
23443.e: There was grass in the shoes. It kept his feet warm like a sock.

23444.q: What was Ötzi's coat made of?
23444.e: The coat was sewn together from goat and sheep skins. It had light and dark stripes.
23444.m: Ötzi's coat was made of goat and sheep skin.

23445.q: What was Ötzi's bow made of?
23445.e: The bow was made of the hard wood of the yew tree. It was not quite finished.
23445.m: Ötzi's bow was made of yew wood.

23446.q: About how long was Ötzi's bow?
23446.e: The bow was about 1.80 metres long. So it was longer than Ötzi was tall.
23446.m: Ötzi's bow was taller than Ötzi himself.

23447.q: What did Ötzi carry his arrows in?
23447.e: A quiver is a bag for arrows. Ötzi's quiver was made of fur and held 14 arrows.
23447.m: Arrows are carried in a quiver.

23448.q: What was the blade of Ötzi's dagger made of?
23448.e: The blade was made of flint, a very hard stone. The handle was made of ash wood.
23448.m: Ötzi's dagger had a flint blade.

23449.q: What did Ötzi carry a birch-bark container for?
23449.e: Ötzi carried embers wrapped in leaves in a birch-bark container. That way he could make a fire quickly.
23449.m: Ötzi carried embers in a birch-bark container.

23450.q: What did Ötzi carry on his back?
23450.e: Ötzi had a frame made of hazel wood. With it he could carry things on his back.
23450.m: Ötzi carried a wooden backpack frame.

23451.q: Why did Ötzi probably carry two fungi on a string?
23451.e: Ötzi had two pieces of a tree fungus with him. People think he used them as medicine.
23451.m: Ötzi probably carried fungi as medicine.

23452.q: Which metal was the blade of Ötzi's axe made of?
23452.e: The blade of Ötzi's axe is almost pure copper. That is why it is called a copper axe.
23452.m: Ötzi's axe had a copper blade.

23453.q: What wood was the handle of Ötzi's axe made of?
23453.e: The handle was made of yew wood. This wood is tough and does not break easily.
23453.m: The handle of Ötzi's axe was made of yew wood.

23454.e: Copper shines reddish like a new coin. That makes it easy to recognise.

23455.q: What was a copper axe mainly used for?
23455.e: With the axe, people felled trees and chopped wood. Ötzi perhaps also needed it for his bow.
23455.m: You chop wood with an axe.

23456.q: How was the blade fixed onto Ötzi's axe?
a: With birch tar and leather straps
23456.e: The blade sat in the wood. It was glued in with birch tar and tied on with leather straps.
23456.m: Birch tar was a kind of Stone Age glue.

23457.q: What is the period Ötzi lived in called?
23457.e: In Ötzi's time the first copper tools appeared. That is why it is called the Copper Age.
23457.m: Ötzi lived in the Copper Age.

23458.q: From which present-day country did the copper for Ötzi's axe come?
23458.e: Tests show that the copper came from Tuscany. Tuscany is in Italy.
23458.m: The copper for Ötzi's axe came from Tuscany.

23459.q: What colour does copper turn when it is left outside for a long time?
23459.e: Over time, copper gets a green layer. It is called patina.

23460.q: What is special about Ötzi's copper axe?
23460.e: From this time, otherwise only blades without handles have been found. On Ötzi's axe, the wooden handle has survived completely.
23460.m: Ötzi's axe has survived with its wooden handle.

23461.q: What do you call a mixture of two metals, such as bronze?
23461.e: When metals are melted together, you get an alloy. Bronze is one of the oldest alloys.
23461.m: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.

23462.q: Which metal do you need the most of to make bronze?
23462.e: Bronze is made of about nine parts copper and one part tin.
23462.m: Bronze contains a lot of copper and a little tin.

23463.q: What is bronze like compared with pure copper?
23463.e: The tin makes the metal harder. That is why bronze tools were better than copper ones.

23464.q: What is the period named after the metal bronze called?
23464.e: In the Bronze Age, people made many things out of bronze. In Switzerland it began around 4,200 years ago.
23464.m: The Bronze Age is named after the metal bronze.

23465.q: Which period came after the Bronze Age?
23465.e: Later, people learnt how to make iron. That is why the Iron Age came next.
23465.m: After the Bronze Age came the Iron Age.

23466.q: Which place in a sports competition gets a bronze medal?
23466.e: Gold is for first place and silver for second. Bronze is for third place.
23466.m: The bronze medal is for third place.

23467.e: Bronze shines golden brown. It is a little lighter than pure copper.

23468.q: Why was tin so valuable in the Bronze Age?
23468.e: Tin was only found in a few places. That is why traders brought it from far away.
23468.m: Tin was rare and had to come from far away.

23469.q: What was made from bronze in the Bronze Age?
23469.e: Weapons, tools and jewellery were made of bronze. For example swords, axes and arm rings.
23469.m: In the Bronze Age, tools, weapons and jewellery were made of bronze.

23470.q: What is the craftsman who works metal called?
23470.e: A blacksmith makes tools, weapons and jewellery out of metal. He works with fire and a hammer.

23471.q: On which heavy block does the blacksmith place the hot metal?
23471.e: The anvil is a heavy block of metal. On it, the blacksmith hammers the metal into shape.
23471.m: The blacksmith hammers on the anvil.

23472.q: What does the blacksmith use to hold the glowing metal?
23472.e: The metal is far too hot to touch. So the blacksmith uses long tongs.
23472.m: The blacksmith holds hot metal with tongs.

a: To blow air into the fire
23473.e: Bellows push air into the fire. That makes the fire much hotter.

23474.q: What was burnt in the smelting furnace to make it very hot?
23474.e: Charcoal burns much hotter than ordinary wood. With it, metal could be melted.
23474.m: Charcoal makes a very hot fire.

23475.e: The liquid bronze went into a mould made of stone or clay. As it cooled, it became hard and took on the shape.
23475.m: Liquid metal is poured into a mould.

23476.q: What was metal melted in, inside the furnace?
23476.e: A crucible is a small clay container. It can stand great heat.
23476.m: Metal is melted in a crucible.

23477.q: At about what temperature does copper become liquid?
23477.e: Copper only melts at about 1,085 degrees. An ordinary campfire is not hot enough for that.
23477.m: Copper only melts at over 1,000 degrees.

23478.q: What does a blacksmith do with a hammer?
23478.e: Glowing metal is soft. With the hammer, the blacksmith beats it into the right shape.
23478.m: The blacksmith shapes hot metal with a hammer.

23479.q: How did people pay before there were coins?
23479.e: In the past, people swapped grain for a tool, for example. This is called barter.

23480.q: Where were the first coins made?
a: In Lydia in what is now Turkey
23480.e: The first coins were made in the kingdom of Lydia. This country lay in what is now Turkey.
23480.m: The first coins came from Lydia.

23481.q: About how many years ago were the first coins made?
23481.e: The first coins were made around 600 BC. That is about 2,600 years ago.
23481.m: Coins have existed for about 2,600 years.

23482.q: What material were the first coins made of?
23482.e: The first coins were made of a mixture of gold and silver. Metal is valuable and lasts a long time.

23483.q: How did the picture get onto a coin?
23483.e: The metal was placed between two dies. Then it was struck with a hammer and the picture was pressed in.
23483.m: The picture is stamped into a coin.

23484.q: Which coins did the Celts copy for their gold coins?
23484.e: The Celts knew the gold coins of a Greek king from Macedonia. They made their own coins based on them.
23484.m: Celtic gold coins were modelled on Greek ones.

23485.q: How did the Celts make their potin coins?
23485.e: Potin is a mixture of copper, tin and lead. The Celts cast coins from it in moulds.

23486.q: Why was a coin more practical than swapping?
a: It was small and easy to carry
It was always made of pure gold
It was bigger than the goods
23486.e: You cannot put a cow in your pocket. Coins are easy to take with you and to count.
23486.m: Coins are small and easy to carry.

23487.q: In which Swiss city was a big lump of Celtic coins melted together found?
23487.e: The Zurich potin lump is made of many Celtic coins stuck together. It was found in Zurich in 1890.
23487.m: A lump of Celtic coins was found in Zurich.

23488.q: What was the Celtic tribe that lived in the area of Switzerland called?
23488.e: The Helvetii were Celts. They lived in the Central Plateau of what is now Switzerland.
23488.m: The Helvetii were Celts in Switzerland.

23489.q: What does the “CH” on Swiss cars stand for?
23489.e: Confoederatio Helvetica is the Latin name for Switzerland. The name recalls a Celtic tribe that lived here.

23490.q: What did the Celts build the walls of their houses from?
23490.e: The walls were made of wooden poles and woven branches. Clay was spread over them to make them tight.
23490.m: Celtic houses had walls of wood and clay.

23491.q: Which drink did rich Celts like to buy from the south?
23491.e: Rich Celts bought wine from Italy and Greece. It came in large clay jars called amphorae.
23491.m: Rich Celts liked to drink wine from the south.

23492.q: What was in the middle of a Celtic house?
23492.e: The fire in the middle gave warmth and light. Food was cooked on it too.
23492.m: The fire burnt in the middle of the house.

23493.q: What do you call a large Celtic town protected by walls?
23493.e: An oppidum was a large settlement with a rampart and wall. In Switzerland, for example, there was one on the Engehalbinsel in Bern.
23493.m: An oppidum is a protected Celtic town.

23494.q: How did most Celts make a living?
23494.e: Most Celts were farmers. They grew grain and kept cows, pigs and sheep.

23495.q: How did the Celts protect their villages?
23495.e: Many villages had a fence of wooden stakes or an earth rampart around them. That protected people and animals.
23495.m: Fences and ramparts protected Celtic villages.

23496.q: Who defeated the Helvetii in 58 BC?
23496.e: The Helvetii wanted to move to Gaul. The Roman Julius Caesar defeated them and sent them back.

23497.q: What was a druid among the Celts?
23497.e: Druids were priests and wise men. They knew a lot about the gods and the stars.
23497.m: Druids were priests and scholars of the Celts.

23498.q: Where did the druids often hold their ceremonies?
23498.e: The Celts had sacred groves. These are pieces of woodland where the druids held their ceremonies.
23498.m: Druids often held ceremonies in sacred woods.

23499.q: According to an old account, what did the druids use to cut mistletoe?
23499.e: The Roman Pliny wrote that druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.
23499.m: Druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.

23500.q: Which tree was especially important to the druids?
23500.e: The oak was a sacred tree. Mistletoe growing on an oak was thought to be very special.
23500.m: The oak was sacred to the druids.

23501.q: How did the druids pass on their knowledge?
a: They carved it on stone tablets
They wrote it in thick books
They painted it on cave walls
23501.e: The druids did not write their knowledge down. Their pupils had to learn everything by heart, often for many years.
23501.m: Druids learnt their knowledge by heart.

23502.q: According to a Roman account, what did druids not have to do?
23502.e: Julius Caesar wrote that druids did not have to go to war. They did not have to pay taxes either.
23502.m: Druids did not have to go to war.

23503.q: What did druids use their knowledge of plants for?
23503.e: Druids knew many plants and what they did. They used them to try to make sick people well.
23503.m: Druids healed the sick with plants.

23504.q: What is the druid in the Asterix comics called?
23504.e: In the comics, Getafix brews the magic potion for the Gauls. The character is based on a Celtic druid.
23504.m: Getafix is the druid in Asterix.

23505.q: According to Pliny, what colour were the druids' robes?
23505.e: Pliny described the druids wearing white robes when they cut mistletoe.

23507.e: The torc is open at the front. The two ends are often thick and beautifully decorated.
23507.m: A torc is open at the front.

23508.q: Who wore a torc among the Celts?
23508.e: A torc showed that someone was rich or powerful. Gods were also shown wearing torcs.
23508.m: A torc showed that someone was important.

23509.q: In which Swiss canton was a gold treasure with neck rings found in 1962?
23509.e: During building work above Erstfeld in the canton of Uri, seven gold rings were found. It is the Erstfeld gold treasure.
23509.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure comes from the canton of Uri.

23510.q: What are the rings of the Erstfeld treasure made of?
23510.e: The Erstfeld treasure from the canton of Uri is made of seven gold rings. The Celts hid it over 2,000 years ago.
23510.m: The Erstfeld treasure is made of gold.

23511.q: Where can you see the Erstfeld gold treasure today?
a: In the Swiss National Museum in Zurich
23511.e: The real rings are on display in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich. There are copies in Altdorf.
23511.m: The Erstfeld gold treasure is in the Swiss National Museum in Zurich.

23512.q: Who found the Erstfeld gold treasure?
23512.e: Two building workers were clearing away a rock with a digger. The rings slid out of the rubble.
23512.m: Building workers found the Erstfeld gold treasure.

23513.q: Among which people was the torc especially popular as a neck ornament?
23513.e: The torc is typical of the Celts. Even the Romans recognised Celts by their neck rings.
23513.m: The torc is a typical Celtic neck ring.

23514.q: What metal were most of the finds from La Tène made of?
23514.e: Most of the weapons and tools from La Tène are made of iron. The Celts were already good at working iron.
23514.m: Most finds from La Tène are made of iron.

23515.q: What was found in 1857 in shallow water at La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel?
23515.e: In 1857 a fisherman pulled many old iron weapons and tools out of the water there. They come from the Celts.
23515.m: Many Celtic iron finds were made at La Tène.

23516.q: Who made the first finds at La Tène?
23516.e: The fisherman Hans Kopp was searching on behalf of Colonel Friedrich Schwab. In a short time he found around 40 old weapons.
23516.m: A fisherman made the first finds at La Tène.

23517.q: Which weapons were found especially often at La Tène?
23517.e: Many swords and lance heads were found. Altogether around 2,500 objects came to light.
23517.m: Many swords and lances were found at La Tène.

23518.q: Why did even more finds come to light at La Tène later on?
a: The lake dried out in summer
A storm washed the sand away
23518.e: During the Jura water correction, the lake level was lowered by more than 2 metres. This left more of the site on dry land.
23518.m: The lower lake level brought new finds at La Tène.

23519.q: Which wooden structures were found at La Tène?
23519.e: The remains of two wooden bridges were found. They led over an old arm of the River Zihl.
23519.m: Celtic bridges stood at La Tène.

23520.q: What is the Celtic period named after the site of La Tène called?
23520.e: Researchers named a period of the Celts after this place. It began around 2,500 years ago.
23520.m: The La Tène period is named after a place in Switzerland.

23521.q: What is the museum that holds many finds from La Tène called?
23521.e: The Laténium is a large archaeology museum. It stands in Hauterive on the lake shore.
23521.m: Many finds from La Tène are in the Laténium.

23522.q: Roughly what does the name La Tène mean?
23522.e: The name means a place with shallow water. At the end of the lake, the water there was not very deep.

a: A grave under a mound of earth
23523.e: Earth and stones were piled up over the grave.
23523.m: A burial mound is a grave under a mound.

23524.q: What was often placed with the dead in a burial mound?
23524.e: The dead were given jewellery, weapons or pots. These things are called grave goods.
23524.m: Grave goods are things given to the dead.

23525.q: What does a burial mound look like from the outside?
23525.e: A burial mound looks like a small round hill. Today, trees often grow on it.
23525.m: A burial mound looks like a round hill.

23526.q: Where in Switzerland are many old burial mounds found today?
23526.e: In the forest, the mounds were not flattened by ploughs. That is why they are often still easy to see there.
23526.m: Many burial mounds lie in the forest today.

23527.q: Who studies old graves to learn more about the past?
23527.e: Archaeologists dig carefully and examine the finds. That is how we learn how people used to live.

23528.q: Who was given an especially large burial mound?
23528.e: A large grave with many grave goods showed that someone was rich and powerful. These are called princely graves.
23528.m: Large burial mounds belonged to important people.

23529.q: What does a Greek bronze vessel in a Celtic burial mound in the canton of Bern show?
a: That there was trade as far as the Mediterranean
That bronze was only made in Bern
23529.e: In 1851 a bronze jug from Greece was found at Grächwil. Goods like this came north along long trade routes.
23529.m: Finds from the south show old trade routes.

23530.q: Why are grave goods important for us today?
a: They show how people used to live
23530.e: Jewellery, tools and pots from graves tell us about everyday life. That is how we know a lot about people who had no writing.
23530.m: Grave goods tell us how people used to live.

23531.q: What was papyrus for writing made from?
23531.e: Papyrus is a plant that grows in marshes. The Egyptians made sheets for writing from it.
23531.m: Papyrus is made from a marsh plant.

23532.q: Where did the papyrus plant grow in Egypt?
a: On the banks of the Nile
In the middle of the desert
23532.e: Papyrus needs a lot of water. That is why it grew in the marshes along the Nile and in the Nile Delta.
23532.m: The papyrus plant grew along the Nile.

23533.q: Which English word comes from the word “papyrus”?
23533.e: The word “paper” comes from the Greek word “papyros”. That was the name of the plant from which the Egyptians made writing sheets.
23533.m: The word paper comes from papyrus.

23534.q: How were long papyrus sheets usually stored?
23534.e: People glued many sheets together into long strips. These were wound up into rolls.
23534.m: Long papyrus texts were stored as scrolls.

23535.q: How were the plant strips turned into a papyrus sheet?
23535.e: Thin strips of the plant were laid across each other in two layers. Then they were pressed and dried.
23535.m: To make papyrus, you lay strips crosswise and press them.

23536.q: Apart from writing sheets, what else did the Egyptians make from papyrus?
23536.e: Papyrus was very useful. People wove sandals, mats, baskets and ropes from it.
23536.m: The Egyptians also wove sandals from papyrus.

23537.q: Why have many old papyri survived until today?
23537.e: Egypt is very dry. So the papyrus often did not rot in tombs and in the sand.
23537.m: Egypt's dry air has preserved many papyri.

23538.q: Which part of the papyrus plant was used for writing sheets?
23538.e: The long stem was cut into thin strips. These were made into the sheets.
23538.m: Papyrus sheets are made from the stem of the plant.

23539.q: What did an Egyptian scribe always have with him for his work?
23539.e: The palette was a narrow board with hollows for the ink. The reed pens were kept in a slot.
23539.m: A scribe carried a writing palette.

23540.q: What did trainee scribes often practise on, because papyrus was expensive?
23540.e: Papyrus cost a lot. So for practice, people wrote on broken pieces of clay pots and on flat pieces of limestone.
23540.m: Trainee scribes often practised on pieces of pottery.

23541.q: Which two colours of ink did Egyptian scribes mostly use?
23541.e: Black ink was made from soot, red from red ochre. Red was used, for example, to highlight headings.
23541.m: Egyptian scribes mostly wrote with black and red ink.

23542.q: How did Egyptian scribes often sit while working?
a: On a chair at a desk
23542.e: Many statues show scribes sitting cross-legged on the ground. They held the papyrus on the stretched kilt over their knees.

23543.q: What is the oval called in which a pharaoh's name was written?
23543.e: The king's name was framed with an oval loop. That way it could be spotted at once in the text.
23543.m: A pharaoh's name is written in a cartouche.

23544.q: In which direction could Egyptian picture writing be read?
23544.e: People wrote from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom. The animals and people in the script face the start of the line.
23544.m: Egyptian writing could be written in several directions.

23545.q: Who could read and write in ancient Egypt?
23545.e: Only a small number of people learned to write. That is why scribes were very important and respected.
23545.m: In ancient Egypt only a few people could write.

23546.q: What did scribes write down for the pharaoh, for example?
a: How much grain had been harvested
How many stars are in the sky
The names of the children playing in the village
Which fish swim in the Nile
23546.e: Scribes kept lists of harvests, taxes and supplies. That way the state knew how much grain there was.
23546.m: Scribes counted and recorded the harvest, for example.

23547.q: Which dangerous animals did cats keep away from Egyptian homes?
23547.e: Cats hunted not only mice but also poisonous snakes. That made them very useful in the house.
23547.m: Cats also protected the Egyptians from snakes.

23548.q: Why were cats so popular with farmers?
23548.e: Mice and rats ate the grain in the storehouses. Cats kept these animals away.
23548.m: Cats protected the grain from mice.

23549.q: What did the Egyptians often do with dead cats?
a: They threw them into the Nile
They left them lying in the desert
23549.e: Many thousands of cat mummies have been found. The cats were preserved and wrapped like people.
23549.m: In ancient Egypt many cats were mummified.

23550.q: According to the Greek writer Herodotus, what did families do when their cat died?
a: They ate nothing for three days
They moved to a new house
23550.e: Herodotus reported that the family shaved off their eyebrows in mourning. This shows how much cats were loved.
23550.m: Egyptians shaved off their eyebrows in mourning for their cat.

23551.q: What did the ancient Egyptian word for cat sound like?
23551.e: The word for cat was pronounced something like “miu”. It sounds like a cat's miaow.
23551.m: The Egyptian word for cat sounded like “miu”.

23552.q: What was the name of the ancient Egyptians' cat goddess?
23552.e: Bastet was often shown with a cat's head or as a cat. She protected home and family.
23552.m: Bastet was the Egyptians' cat goddess.

23553.q: Which wild cat are our pet cats descended from?
23553.e: The African wildcat lives in Africa and Arabia. It became tame and so turned into the house cat.
23553.m: Our pet cats are descended from the African wildcat.

23554.q: What kind of animal is a scarab?
23554.e: The scarab is a beetle. It is also called a dung beetle.

23555.q: What does the dung beetle roll along in front of it?
23555.e: The beetle shapes a ball from animal dung and rolls it away. It also lays its eggs inside it.
23555.m: The dung beetle rolls balls of dung.

23556.q: According to Egyptian belief, what did the beetle god Khepri roll across the sky?
23556.e: The Egyptians thought of the beetle with its ball. So they imagined that Khepri rolled the sun up into the sky every morning.
23556.m: The god Khepri rolled the sun across the sky.

23557.q: Why did many Egyptians wear small figures of a scarab?
23557.e: The scarab was seen as a sign of protection and good luck. So people wore it as an amulet.
23557.m: A scarab was a popular lucky charm.

23558.q: What else were scarabs with writing on the underside used for?
23558.e: Names or signs were carved on the flat underside. People pressed them into soft clay like a stamp.
23558.m: Scarabs were also used as stamps.

23559.q: Where was the heart scarab placed on a mummy?
23559.e: The heart scarab was placed on the chest near the heart. It was meant to protect the dead person in the afterlife.
23559.m: The heart scarab lay on the mummy's chest.

23560.q: What was the scarab a symbol of?
23560.e: Young beetles crawled out of the dung ball. That made the Egyptians think of new life and rebirth.
23560.m: The scarab stood for new life.

23561.q: What kind of body does the Sphinx of Giza have?
23561.e: The Sphinx lies there like a huge lion. Only the head is different.
23561.m: The Sphinx of Giza has the body of a lion.

23562.q: What kind of head does the Sphinx of Giza have?
23562.e: The Sphinx has the face of a human with a royal headcloth. People think it shows a pharaoh.
23562.m: The Sphinx has the head of a human.

23563.q: How was the Sphinx of Giza built?
23563.e: The workers chiselled the figure straight out of the limestone rock. Only a few parts were added with stone blocks.
23563.m: The Sphinx was carved out of the rock.

23564.q: What is missing from the face of the Sphinx of Giza today?
23564.e: The nose broke off many hundreds of years ago. It was about one metre wide.
23564.m: The Sphinx of Giza is missing its nose.

23565.q: Roughly how long is the Sphinx of Giza?
23565.e: The Sphinx is about 73 metres long and about 20 metres high. It is one of the largest statues in the world.
23565.m: The Sphinx of Giza is about 73 metres long.

23566.q: In which direction does the Sphinx of Giza face?
23566.e: The Sphinx looks east. That is where the sun rises every morning.
23566.m: The Sphinx faces the sunrise in the east.

23567.q: Which pharaoh probably had the Sphinx of Giza built?
23567.e: Most experts think the Sphinx was made in the time of Khafre. His pyramid stands very close by.
23567.m: The Sphinx probably dates from the time of Pharaoh Khafre.

23568.q: For a long time, what covered the Sphinx of Giza up to its shoulders?
23568.e: The desert wind kept blowing sand over it. Only in the 20th century was the Sphinx fully uncovered.
23568.m: For a long time the Sphinx was buried in sand up to its shoulders.

23569.e: Cleopatra ruled Egypt as pharaoh. She is one of the best-known women in history.

23570.q: Which number does the famous Cleopatra have in her name?
23570.e: There were other queens called Cleopatra before her. That is why she is called Cleopatra VII.
23570.m: The famous Cleopatra is called Cleopatra the Seventh.

23571.q: Which famous Roman was allied with Cleopatra and had a son with her?
23571.e: Cleopatra and Julius Caesar had a son called Caesarion. Caesar helped her stay queen.
23571.m: Cleopatra and Julius Caesar had a son together.

23572.q: With which Roman general did Cleopatra have three children?
23572.e: Cleopatra and Mark Antony had three children. Together they fought against Octavian.
23572.m: Cleopatra and Mark Antony had three children.

23573.q: In which city on the Mediterranean did Cleopatra have her palace?
23573.e: Alexandria was the capital of Egypt at that time. The city had a famous lighthouse and a great library.

23574.q: Which language did Cleopatra learn as the first ruler of her family?
23574.e: Cleopatra's ancestors had only spoken Greek. According to the historian Plutarch, she was the first in her family to also learn the language of the people of Egypt.
23574.m: Cleopatra was the first in her family to speak Egyptian.

23575.q: Where did Cleopatra's family originally come from?
23575.e: Cleopatra belonged to the Ptolemy family. They came from Macedonia in the north of Greece.

23576.q: Roughly how many years ago did Cleopatra live?
23576.e: Cleopatra lived from 69 to 30 BC. That is a little more than 2000 years ago.

23577.q: Roughly how long did Pharaoh Ramesses II reign?
23577.e: Ramesses II reigned from about 1279 to 1213 BC. That is about 66 years.
23577.m: Ramesses II reigned for about 66 years.

23578.q: Which nickname was Ramesses II given?
23578.e: Ramesses II built a lot and reigned for a very long time. That is why he is called Ramesses the Great.
23578.m: Ramesses II is also called Ramesses the Great.

23579.q: Against which people did Ramesses II fight at the Battle of Kadesh?
23579.e: The Hittites had a large empire in what is now Turkey. At Kadesh in Syria they fought against Egypt.
23579.m: Ramesses II fought the Hittites at Kadesh.

23580.q: What did Ramesses II later make with the Hittites?
23580.e: In 1259 BC the two empires made peace. The treaty is seen as the oldest known written peace treaty.
23580.m: Ramesses II made one of the oldest peace treaties in the world.

23581.q: Roughly how many sons and daughters of Ramesses II are known?
23581.e: About 45 sons and 40 daughters are known. Ramesses II had several wives.
23581.m: Ramesses II had over 80 known children.

a: In the Valley of the Kings
In the temple of Abu Simbel
In the Valley of the Queens
23582.e: Ramesses II was buried in a rock tomb in the Valley of the Kings. His mummy was later hidden and only found again in 1881.
23582.m: Ramesses II was buried in the Valley of the Kings.

23583.q: Who is shown by the four giant seated figures in front of the rock temple of Abu Simbel?
23583.e: Ramesses II had the temple carved into the rock. In front of the entrance sit four giant figures of himself.
23583.m: Ramesses II sits four times in front of the temple of Abu Simbel.

23584.q: How were the temples of Abu Simbel originally built?
23584.e: The workers chiselled the rooms and figures straight out of a sandstone mountain. That is why they are called rock temples.
23584.m: The temples of Abu Simbel were carved into a mountain.

23585.q: How many giant seated figures sit in front of the great temple of Abu Simbel?
23585.e: Four figures of the pharaoh sit in front of the entrance. Each one is about 20 metres high.
23585.m: Four giant figures sit in front of the great temple of Abu Simbel.

23586.q: Which pharaoh had the temples of Abu Simbel built?
23586.e: Pharaoh Ramesses II had the rock temples built. The four giant figures in front of the great temple show him.
23586.m: Ramesses II had Abu Simbel built.

23587.q: Why were the temples of Abu Simbel moved in the 1960s?
a: They would have sunk in a reservoir
They were in the way of a road
A king wanted them in Cairo
23587.e: The new Aswan Dam created a huge lake. The water would have flooded the temples.
23587.m: Abu Simbel was moved so that it would not sink in the reservoir.

23588.q: How were the temples of Abu Simbel moved to higher ground?
a: Lifted in one piece with cranes
23588.e: Workers cut the temples into over 1000 large blocks. Higher up, they put everything back together exactly.
23588.m: The temples of Abu Simbel were cut up and rebuilt.

23589.q: Where in Egypt is Abu Simbel?
23589.e: Abu Simbel is in the south of Egypt, close to the border with Sudan. The area is called Nubia.
23589.m: Abu Simbel is in the far south of Egypt.

23590.q: What happens twice a year in the great temple of Abu Simbel?
23590.e: In February and October the morning light falls through the entrance. It lights up the statues of the gods at the very back of the temple.
23590.m: Twice a year the sun shines deep into the temple of Abu Simbel.

23591.q: Which organisation helped rescue the temples of Abu Simbel?
23591.e: UNESCO called on many countries to help. Today the temples are World Heritage.
23591.m: UNESCO helped to save Abu Simbel.

23592.q: Every year the Egyptians measured how high the water in the Nile rose. What did this tell them?
a: Whether the harvest would be good
How many fish were in the river
23592.e: If the water rose enough, the fields got plenty of water and mud. Then there was a good harvest.
23592.m: The level of the Nile showed whether the harvest would be good.

23593.q: What did the farmers use to cut the ripe grain?
23593.e: A sickle is a curved knife. In the past, sickles often had sharp blades made of flint.
23593.m: The farmers harvested the grain with sickles.

23594.q: Where was the harvested grain stored?
23594.e: Granaries were buildings made of mud bricks. There the grain stayed dry and safe for bad years.
23594.m: The grain was stored in granaries.

23595.q: Which sweet fruits did the Egyptians harvest from palm trees?
23595.e: Date palms grew well along the Nile. The sweet dates were eaten fresh or dried.
23595.m: The Egyptians harvested dates from palm trees.

23596.q: How many seasons did the ancient Egyptian year have?
23596.e: There was the season of flooding, the season of sowing and the season of harvest. Each lasted about four months.
23596.m: The Egyptian year had three seasons.

23597.q: What is the device with a long lever that farmers used to lift water from the Nile called?
23597.e: A shaduf has a long beam with a bucket and a counterweight. This made it easy to lift water up.
23597.m: Farmers lifted water from the Nile with a shaduf.

23598.q: Which animals pulled the Egyptian farmers' plough?
23598.e: Cattle were strong and patient. They pulled the wooden plough across the fields.
23598.m: Along the Nile, cattle pulled the plough.

23599.q: The farmers had to give something to the pharaoh. What did they give?
23599.e: For a long time there were no coins. The farmers gave part of their grain to the state.
23599.m: Egyptian farmers handed over part of their harvest.

23600.e: Senet was played on a board with squares. It is one of the oldest known board games.
23600.m: Senet is an ancient Egyptian board game.

23601.q: How many squares does a Senet board have?
23601.e: The Senet board has three rows of ten squares each. That makes 30 squares altogether.

23602.q: In Senet, what decided how far you could move?
23602.e: Instead of a dice, people threw flat sticks or bones. The side that landed facing up showed the number.
23602.m: In Senet, people threw sticks instead of dice.

23603.q: How many people played Senet together?
23603.e: Two people played against each other. Each had their own pieces.
23603.m: Senet is played by two people against each other.

23604.q: Who played the board game Senet in ancient Egypt?
23604.e: Senet was popular all over Egypt. Ordinary people scratched the board into stone, while pharaohs had precious boards.
23604.m: Both poor and rich people played Senet.

23605.q: What did the Egyptians later think of when playing Senet?
23605.e: The game came to be linked with the journey of the dead to the afterlife. That is why Senet boards were often placed in tombs.
23605.m: Senet stood for the journey to the afterlife.

23606.q: Roughly how old is the game Senet?
23606.e: Senet pieces have been found in very early royal tombs. They are about 5000 years old.

23607.q: Which part of the face did the ancient Egyptians make up in a particularly striking way?
23607.e: In pictures and statues you can see thick dark lines around the eyes. This was typical of Egypt.
23607.m: The ancient Egyptians mainly made up their eyes.

23608.q: What is the black eye make-up called that the Egyptians already used?
23608.e: Kohl was made from a dark mineral. It was put on with a small stick.
23608.m: Kohl is a black eye make-up.

23609.q: What did the Egyptians make green eye make-up from?
23609.e: Malachite is a green rock. People ground it into powder and mixed it with fat.
23609.m: Green make-up was made from malachite.

23610.q: What else did dark eye make-up help with in ancient Egypt?
23610.e: The dark colour around the eyes reduced the glare in the strong sun. People also believed it protected against eye diseases.
23610.m: Eye make-up helped against the glaring sunlight.

23611.q: Who wore make-up in ancient Egypt?
23611.e: In ancient Egypt both women and men wore make-up. Pharaohs wore eye make-up too.
23611.m: In Egypt men wore make-up too.

23612.q: Who wore especially large and elaborate wigs in ancient Egypt?
23612.e: Large wigs made of real hair were expensive. So rich people used them to show how important they were.
